## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (08:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

**Chain 1 — from B-1237 "The Wash House" (shipped 0315, "Wring it twice."): the laundry, outward.**
1. The washhouse's wrung shirt → **THE DRYING GREEN.** Communal drying ground: Glasgow's New Green (acquired 1660s–70s) held a wash house and was used for grazing, bleaching and drying nets, walled, with a guardhouse and locking gates; Scotlandwell, Perthshire, got a 19th-c. wash house (architect David Bryce, **£117**, funded by Thomas Bruce of Arnot) with a walled garden and communal bleachfield — now the village playing field. Tenement-era rule: tenants held a rotating "turn" at the common wash-house roughly every two weeks (1962 NLR housing survey). Edinburgh New Town gardens were strung on transverse lines from metal curling hasps sunk in the walls — neat, unlike the "unfortunate eyesore" communal bleaching greens ringing the city. Sources: The Glasgow Story; Heritage Lottery Fund; New Left Review; Gardens Trust.
2. The drying green → **THE BLEACHFIELD.** Linen whitened by sun on grass: boiled in lye/ashes ("bowking"), rinsed, laid on the grass ("crafting/crofting"), kept wet in summer sun for **three to six months**, alternated with souring in buttermilk — the cycle repeated **5–6 times** until white. A typical field covered ~20 acres; named fields: Haarlem (Dutch mode — linen sent in March, not back till end of October); Pitkerro near Dundee (1732, R. Holden's kelp-bleaching field); James Adair's proposed Galloway bleachfield (1728, £2,000 in Board premiums). The endpoint: Charles Tennant of Glasgow patented chlorine-and-lime bleaching powder after Berthollet's 1785 chlorine discovery — the weeks-long sun process collapsed to hours. Sources: 1902 Encyclopedia; ResearchGate "Bleaching – From Antiquity to Chlorine"; Peak Advertiser "Bygone Industries".
3. The bleachfield's stretched cloth → **THE TENTERHOOKS.** A tenter = a wooden frame on which wet woven cloth was stretched to dry even and square; tenter-hooks = sharp hooked nails fixing the cloth by its selvedges; old maps mark tenter-fields. From Latin *tendere*, to stretch; "tenter" in English since the **14th century**. The metaphor "on tenterhooks" (agitated suspense) dates from the mid-18th century; first exact use **Tobias Smollett, *Roderick Random*, 1748** ("upon the tenterhooks of impatient uncertainty"); 17th-c. predecessors "on tenters," "on the tenters" (Hudibras). Often misspelled "tenderhooks." Sources: World Wide Words; Tatter; Free Dictionary of Idioms.

**Chain 2 — from B-1235 "The Apiary Check" (retired, TWO-DENIAL): the bees, told.**
1. The retired apiary shape → **TELLING THE BEES.** The folk custom: on a death, the beekeeper knocks on **each hive individually** (in some accounts three times with the house key), announces the name in a low voice, and drapes the hive in **black crepe** ("a shred of black") to put the bees into mourning. Untold bees would "sicken," weaken, and die or leave — a Norfolk auction record attributes sickly bees to not having been put into mourning; recovery followed tying crepe to the hive. Weddings: hives decorated, wedding cake left beside them; Westphalia newlyweds introduced themselves to the bees. Nottinghamshire rhyme: "The master's dead, but don't you go; / Your mistress will be a good mistress to you." Poems: John Greenleaf Whittier, "Telling the Bees," *Atlantic Monthly*, **1858**; Eugene Field's "Telling the Bees" read at the International Folk-Lore Congress, Chicago, **July 1893**. Mark Twain records it in *Huckleberry Finn* (Jim: bees "would all weaken down and quit work and die" if not told before sun-up). Sources: JSTOR Daily; Wikipedia "Telling the bees"; Wikisource.
2. The told hive → **THE BEE BOLE.** A bee bole (Scots *bole* = recess in a wall) = a cavity/alcove in a wall housing a skep, sheltering it from wind and rain; typical **12–18 in** high/wide, similar depth; often south-facing; the flight hole faces a protruding landing lip. Glaisdale, North Yorkshire: drystone moor wall with **~77 boles** on its south face, traceable to at least the **17th century** — skeps moved up seasonally for the heather flow. Lost Gardens of Heligan: 2 rows of 7 recesses with **pivoted wooden doors**, closed in winter. St. Teath, Cornwall (Historic England 1433160): five slate-lined boles, 40 × 50 × 50 cm, 18th/19th c. Bee boles ended with the Langstroth (1853). Sources: Wikipedia "Bee bole"; Eva Crane Trust; Historic England.
3. The boled skep → **THE SKEP, constructed.** From Anglo-Saxon *Skeppa* (Norse *skeppa*, straw basket — the second syllable of "basket"); used some **2,000 years**. Construction: continuous **coil of dampened twisted straw**, bound with lapping of split bramble, willow, hazel or dogwood; an **eke/imp/nadir** (ring of 4–5 straw coils) below for brood room — the word "eke" (to eke out); a small top cap as a crude honey super; winter protection by a **hackle** (reed "wigwam"). Skeps lasted up to 150 years. Charles Butler's *Feminine Monarchie* (1609) describes straw hives "bound with briar." Sources: Heritage Crafts; Beespoke Info; Will Harper Skep FAQ.

**Chain 3 — from B-1236 "The Lime Kiln" (retired subject, integrity-refusal rule) + B-1231 "The Coal Sifter" (shipped 0300): the kiln's product.**
1. The kiln → **THE BRICK TAX (1784–1850).** William Pitt the Younger's Duties on Bricks and Tiles Act (24 Geo. 3 c. 24), 1784, to recoup American-war debt. **Initial rate: 2s 6d per 1,000 bricks** — levied on the fresh-made brick *before* burning (10% wastage allowance); moulds were branded **"Excise"** to stamp the duty in. (The 4s figure in trivia sources is the **1794** rate; 5s in 1797; 5s 10d in 1805.) Dodge: Joseph Wilkes of Measham made bricks **235 × 110 × 110 mm** ("Wilkes' Gobs"/"Jumbies") — roughly double volume, effectively half the tax per cubic foot. The 1803 Act charged **double duty** on any brick over **10 in × 5 in** fresh from the mould (not a max-size cap — the hard **150 cubic-inch** limit came in **1839**). **Repealed 17 May 1850.** Sources: Scottish Brick History; British Brick Society; Wikipedia "Duties on Bricks Act 1839".
2. The taxed brick → **THE BRICK BOND.** Stretcher = long face out; header = short face out; headers reach back into the wall, tying its thickness ("wythes") together. **English bond**: alternating full courses — one all headers, one all stretchers — strongest traditional bond for load-bearing walls, quarter-brick lap (queen closer at the quoin). **Flemish bond**: headers and stretchers alternate **within the same course**, each header centred over the stretcher below — more decorative, needs the more skilled mason. **Stretcher (running) bond**: all stretchers, half-brick lap — the default for single-leaf partitions. Stack bond (all joints aligned) is weakest, decorative only. Sources: HireAndBuild; Heartland Brick; Testbook.
3. The bonded brick → **THE BRICKYARD TALLY.** Piecework per thousand was the wage grammar: 1876 Dunnachie Star Works pay book — moulders paid **2s 1d per thousand**, averaging ~2,000 bricks/day; a boy carrier hauled 25,950 bricks for 17s 4d. Essex/Kent gangs: **4s 6d per thousand** (won in a 1900 strike); a shed's weekly output ~40,000 bricks. Green bricks stacked in drying "hacks" **eight high, two wide**, covered by "hack covers"; on wet nights an **alarm bell** rang and the men ran out to "hack up." Sources: Scottish Brick History; Barling & Wakering Heritage.

**Chain 4 — from B-1238 "The Saw Pit" (RESERVED, repeat-refusal): the timber, downstream.**
1. The pit's cut → **THE LOG DRIVE.** Penobscot River, Maine: first drives **1820s** — winter cut, stacked at landings, "watered" in at spring melt, driven 70+ river miles to Bangor mills. Three periods (*The Penobscot Boom*, 1931): **1828–1846** independent drives; **1846–1903** the Penobscot Log Driving Company; cooperative era after. **Last West Branch drive: 1976** — a 151-year run. Logs identified by **combinations of axe marks**; "booms" at sorting points separated each company's marked logs into rafts. Drivers: "river pigs"/"river hogs"/"river men." Sources: Maine Boomhouses; U Maine DigitalCommons; Penobscot Marine Museum (Ruohomaa photos, c.1955).
2. The drive → **THE WANIGAN.** A floating cook shanty that followed the drive downstream — the river drivers' floating kitchen, **25–30 ft long**, built low for stability. Muskegon River, 1880s photos: cook + assistants on a raft, the eats under a canvas awning; men walked a plank from shore, filled plates, ate on land. One raft was barracks; the flying wanigan was the company-flagged cook boat. Cheboygan, 10 July 1971: a centennial wanigan race (32 crews) with strict "historical" rules — rafts ≥8 ft square, poles-only, hand propulsion, each crew cooking **five quarts of hot stew** (meat, potatoes, carrots, onions) over a wood fire for public sampling. Sources: NPS Saint Croix; MN Forest History Center (1901 Mississippi replica); Forestry Forum; bluetoad.com.
3. The wanigan's river → **THE JAM.** Jams formed at narrows, bridge piers, bends — logs piling like "giant jackstraws," sometimes dynamited. June 1900, Connecticut River: **55 million board feet** stacked half a mile long, 6–10 ft deep against a bridge pier; **175 men** to work it apart. Breaking a jam = walking out on floating logs and knowing *which* key log to pull. The tool: spring **1857**, blacksmith **Joseph Peavey of Stillwater, Maine**, watched drivers struggling with cant hooks on the Stillwater Branch of the Penobscot and bolted a clasp, swinging hook ("dog") and pick onto a cant hook — **the peavey**; first success went to driver William Hale. Pike poles (6–20 ft) and dynamite were the alternatives. NOTE: "jam cracker" as a formal job title NOT verified — banked as practice only, never the title. Sources: larrycoffin.blogspot.com; Peavey Mfg.; Millinocket Historical Society.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (08:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE LEGAL ID (plot research).** US broadcast ritual, 47 CFR § 73.1201: stations must air the **call letters immediately followed by the community/communities specified in the license**, with ONLY these permitted insertions between them — licensee name, frequency, channel number, network affiliation; nothing else. Timing: at the **beginning and end of each time of operation**, and **hourly, "as close to the hour as feasible, at a natural break in program offerings."** TV may do it visually or aurally; the FCC Enforcement Bureau has issued Notices of Violation for omitted communities of license. NETWORK STATUS: the subject is STAGED — shipped #75 N-49 "The City of License" (2026-10-12; the station-ID rule; placard "WUBU-TV" over "KESTREL FALLS"). This research's NEW material: the rule's exact element list and the "natural break" timing grammar — banked as lore, not a new item. MEME-F170 stages FROM the shipped episode. Sources: Federal Register Vol. 72; chanrobles.com (47 CFR 73.1201); NY Broadcasters Assoc.
- **THE REQUEST LINE (plot research).** The overnight dedication show: the Top 40 "Boss Radio" format (consultant **Bill Drake, April 1965**, KFWB/KRLA Los Angeles) made call-in requests core — jingles, contests, listeners calling in. Overnight it became the **dedication line**: "this one goes out to [name] from [name]" — the DJ as night-time confessional, intimate register ("wherever you are tonight, this one is for you"); prank dedications were the format's folk form (one to a pair of shoes). The late-century corollary: heavy request volume could make a US hit. Stages in "The Request Line" below. Sources: Wikipedia "Request line"; brucesallan.com; retroramblings.com; classicgold.ca.
- **THE CONTINUITY JUNCTION (plot research).** In-vision continuity announcers appeared between programmes from the earliest days of BBC television — head-and-shoulders to camera, listing the evening's programmes like a theatre variety bill. Early faces: **Jasmine Bligh** (who re-opened the service in **1946**), Elizabeth Cowell, Leslie Mitchell — among TV's first celebrities, heavy fan mail. In-vision continuity left primetime BBC around **1961** (last peak-hours link into the Eurovision Song Contest, 1963); survived children's TV to **1965**; re-invented as CBBC's "broom cupboard," **9 September 1985**. Closedown ritual: the duty announcer bid farewell, screen to black, 30 seconds of black and silence, then tone; BBC One and Two transmitters shut down ~15 minutes after the last programme nightly until November 1997. NETWORK STATUS: the announcer as a figure is STAGED ("The Thumbs-Up"); this research's junction grammar ("and now...", the listing as the show) is banked as lore. Sources: Wikipedia "Continuity announcers in the United Kingdom"; Transdiffusion; thetvroom.com.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (09:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain 1 — from B-1230 "The Reserved Spot" (shipped): the chalked tire, legally.
1. The reserved spot → **THE CHALKING'S LAW.** Sixth Circuit, *Taylor v. City of Saginaw*, decided April 22/25, 2019: Alison Patricia Taylor sued after officer **Tabitha Hoskins chalked her tires 15 times (2014–2017)**; the court held chalking is a **search under the Fourth Amendment** (a common-law trespass + an attempt to obtain information, per *United States v. Jones*), and that neither the community-caretaker nor the motor-vehicle exception justified it. Fresh angle: the chalk mark is a legal instrument — a search in powder form. The mark on the tire IS the law's eye. Sources: Wikipedia "Taylor v. City of Saginaw"; Justia 6th Cir. 17-2126; Criminal Legal News.
2. The chalk → **THE SYSTEM BEFORE THE METER.** Oklahoma City's answer, before 1935, was cops chalking tires — Magee's invention didn't invent time limits, it automated the chalk. Fresh angle: the chalk came first; the coin is the chalk's successor.
3. The successor → **THE PARK-O-METER.** July 16, 1935, First Street & Robinson Avenue, Oklahoma City: Park-O-Meter No. 1, **a nickel an hour**; inventor **Carl C. Magee** (patent May 13, 1935; prototype nicknamed the **Black Maria**; built with OSU engineers); the expired meter flagged a red **"Overtime"** plate — and the fine for an expired meter was **$20**. Magee: **"The parking meter has no favorites."** Fresh angle: the meter replaced the chalked tire with a coin and a flag — the mark became money. Sources: VelocityOKC; 405 Magazine; Parade.

### Chain 2 — from B-1225 "The Catchword" (shipped): the word that talks to the next page.
1. The catchword → **THE CATCHWORD.** The first word of the following page (or quire), written at the foot — usually the verso — of the preceding page, so the binder gathers the quires in order; a manuscript tradition continued into print; scholars class it as the page's "metawork" (infrastructure, not text) — the WWP training materials encode catchwords separately from content. Fresh angle: the page tells the binder what comes next — continuity before continuity existed. Sources: U. Nottingham Glossary; WWP (Northeastern) training materials; GreensBooks.
2. The gathering → **THE SIGNATURE MARK.** The printer's other metawork: quire signatures in the **23 letters of the Latin alphabet (excluding I/J and U/V/W)** — D, D2, D3 on the first half of the section, the second half left conjugate. Fresh angle: the fold has its own alphabet — the book's skeleton is lettered. Sources: GreensBooks; McCune Collection primer.
3. The sheet → **THE FABRIANO MARK.** The watermark, Fabriano ~1282: the earliest believed is a **circle surmounted by a papal cross**; made by a copper-wire figure sewn to the mould screen, thinning the pulp so it reads as a more transparent area; Augusto Zonghi's collection of **2,212 dated Fabriano papers (1267–1798)** makes the watermark a **dating tool for documents**. Fresh angle: the paper carries a date it never wrote — the mark is older than the file. Sources: Handprint.com; Mother Bedford watermarks; Fedrigoni Fabriano Foundation.

### Chain 3 — from B-1229 "The Car Call" (shipped): the fall that was ordered.
1. The car call → **THE OTIS DEMONSTRATION.** 1854, New York Crystal Palace: **P.T. Barnum paid $100** for Otis to stand on a platform — loaded with **hogsheads and packing cases** — high above the crowd; Otis doffed his top hat, ordered an axeman to cut the rope; the wagon-spring brake snapped into the notched rails; the platform dropped about **two feet** and held. Otis, calm: **"All safe, gentlemen, all safe."** Fresh angle: the fall was the pitch — the staged failure IS the product demo. Sources: HistoryNet; ASME; Invention & Tech.
2. The pitch → **THE FIRST PASSENGER LIFT.** March 23, 1857, **E.V. Haughwout & Co., 488 Broadway** — a chinaware emporium; thousands of curious visitors flocked to ride the store's elevator. Otis died **April 8, 1861, of diphtheria**, the company to his two sons. Fresh angle: the elevator's first job was a sideshow — people queued to ride a lift that went nowhere new. Sources: HistoryNet; ETHW.
3. The sideshow → **THE PATERNOSTER.** The doorless chain lift — open cabins on an endless loop that never stop; passengers step in while it moves. Fresh angle: the elevator that abolished the call entirely — no button, no car man, no waiting. (The car man's voice, banked [READY] in "The Lift Operator," is the paternoster's opposite.)

### Chain 4 — from B-1207 "The Projectionist's Reel" (shipped): the dot in the corner.
1. The threaded reel → **THE CHANGEOVER CUE.** The cue marks in the **upper-right corner** of the frame: the **motor cue 12 ft / 8s out** (start the second projector), the **changeover cue 1.5 ft / 1s out** before the black tail; SMPTE 301 specifies four-frame circles; and the projectionists' own gripe, post-*Fight Club*: the proper term is **"Cue Marks," not "Cigarette Burns."** Fresh angle: a private 8-second grammar, visible to the audience, addressed only to the booth. Sources: San Diego Reader; Film-Tech forum (John Pytlak, Kodak); Stage32 glossary.
2. The dozing projectionist → **THE THREE BELLS.** The backup: **three bells sounded as the cue marks neared the gate, in case the projectionist dozed off.** Fresh angle: the booth's own alarm clock — the system that admits the human will fail.
3. The booth → **THE PLATTER.** The platter system killed changeovers — five or six reels on one giant roll, no cues needed. Fresh angle: the booth emptied of its job; the dot stayed on the prints anyway.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (09:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE CALL BOY'S ROUNDS (plot research).** The backstage calls: **half-hour** (30 min; the British half = 35), **quarter** (15; British 20), **the five** (5; British 10), then **"places"** (US) / **"beginners"** (UK). Call boys moved room to room: "You're on in five minutes, Miss Bernhardt." The term was current by the end of the 18th century — **Edmond Malone claimed Shakespeare's first theatre job was call-boy**. **William J. Ferguson**, call boy at Ford's Theatre, was the last surviving eyewitness to Lincoln's assassination (April 14, 1865). Mid-20th century: call boys replaced by dressing-room loudspeakers. NETWORK STATUS: the half-hour call staged (B-923 "The Thirty-Five Minutes" shipped 2026-10-14; "The Beginners" banked 10-13) — this research's NEW material: the Shakespeare claim, Ferguson, the loudspeaker obsolescence — banked as lore, not items. Sources: Vaudeville Lingo Dictionary (Ballycast); AACT Theatre Terms; Theatrecrafts glossary.
- **THE SIGN-IN SHEET (plot research).** Equity rule: actors at the theatre **no later than a half hour before curtain**; each show posts a sign-in sheet **as close as possible to the stage door**; everyone signs on arrival. The sheet is the law of entry. Stages in "The Door Book" below. Sources: Playbill (Ira Mont, stage manager, Actors' Equity).

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (10:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain 1 — the retired standard (start: #189 L-39 "The Retired Kilogram", shipped 2026-10-18: the cylinder on the honored shelf, "The number outlived the metal.")
1. **The honored cylinder → the International Prototype of the Kilogram (IPK).** A platinum–iridium cylinder, the definition of the kilogram since 1889, kept under triple bell jars at the BIPM in Sèvres/Saint-Cloud, France — handled only through glove ports, never bare-handed. Fresh angle: the world's most important paperweight sat in a vault for 130 years and nobody was allowed to touch it.
2. **The vault → the official copies (the "témoins," witnesses).** Six platinum–iridium cylinders struck from the same melt, kept under the same conditions, compared to the IPK roughly every 40 years — duplicates kept as proof of the original. Fresh angle: the vault keeps a jury of copies; the original is the defendant.
3. **The jury → the 50-microgram divergence.** By the 1980s–2000s the IPK and its copies differed by ~50µg (the mass of an eyelash) — and metrology could not say whether the original had lost mass or the copies had gained it. Fresh angle: the standard itself was a disclosed nit — nobody knows whether the original changed or the world did. (bigthink.com; physicstoday.aip.org; scalesplus.com)
4. **The unknowable drift → the 2018 vote and the 2019 switch.** The 26th CGPM (16 Nov 2018, Versailles) redefined the kilogram via the Planck constant; effective 20 May 2019 (World Metrology Day) — every artifact cylinder retired on one morning. Fresh angle: a whole civilization of measures switched from an object to an equation in a day; the artifact kept its honor and lost its job.
5. **The equation → the Kibble balance.** Balances a mass against electromagnetic force, counting the Planck constant into the answer — the verdict rendered by comparison, not by stone. Fresh angle: the scale that replaced the cylinder works by arguing with it electrically.
6. **The retired cylinder → the witness drawer.** #189 staged the retirement; the next staging is the drawer of six witnesses kept beside the honored shelf, and the morning the switch happened. Fresh angle: the network keeps its measures in duplicate and retires originals with ceremony — THE WITNESSED.

### Chain 2 — the called street (start: B-1231 "The Coal Sifter", shipped 2026-10-18: the sorted hod, coal bunker, NO-LINE)
1. **The coalman → the delivery ritual.** Coal arrived by chute into the cellar "coal hole"; the coalman carried sacks on his back through the house, and every grate kept its own scuttle — a whole domestic logistics chain for one fuel. Fresh angle: the fuel moved like a parade through the house it warmed.
2. **The chute → the rag-and-bone man.** "Any old iron" called from a cart — the street's recycling truck before trucks, buying rags, bones, and scrap for a few coppers. Fresh angle: the street had a scheduled buyer for what the house threw away.
3. **The buyer → the street cries (Henry Mayhew, London Labour and the London Poor, 1851).** "So-old again," "Chestnuts all 'ot," "Buy, buy, buy, buy, bu-u-uy!" — a thousand different cries, each with its own pitch and territory; Mayhew: the tumult was "almost bewildering." Fresh angle: before the station, the street WAS the station — calls at set pitches, territories like frequencies. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Mayhew; spitalfieldslife.com)
4. **The cries → the town crier.** The official voice: handbell + "Oyez!" (Old French oyez — "hear ye") — paid to make the street STOP before he spoke: proclamations, lost children, market hours. Fresh angle: the instrument of announcement is the silencer, not the speaker; the bell exists to clear the ground.
5. **The cleared ground → the broadcast pause.** Our pips, our held silences, B-188's buzzer against a held room — the network already announces by clearing. Fresh angle: the crier is the ancestor of the whole network — a man, a bell, and a street that agrees to stop.
6. **The stopped street → the banked items.** "The Street Cry" (the call as episode), "The Cried Goods" (the cart as bumper).

### Chain 3 — the human alarm (start: #184 NE-24 "The Bucket Line", shipped 2026-10-18: the bucket passed hand to hand, "HOLT," "Nobody moved.")
1. **The bucket brigade → the knocker-upper.** Victorian industrial towns ran on human alarm clocks who tapped bedroom windows with bamboo poles, rattles, or pea shooters; Mary Smith of Limehouse (East End, 1865–ca.1940) charged sixpence a week per client and would NOT leave a window until the client was verifiably awake. Fresh angle: a human being paid to be everyone else's alarm — reliability as a walking job. (beyondthename.weebly.com; jvc.oup.com; thevintagenews.com)
2. **The waker → the tongue-twister.** "We had a knocker-up, and our knocker-up had a knocker-up" — the trade folded into folklore; Molly Moore (Mary's daughter) inherited the round. Fresh angle: the job was inheritable like a route, like a frequency — a licensed piece of the morning.
3. **The morning route → the lamplighter's round.** Lamps lit at dusk, doused at dawn, ladder carried along a fixed route; Westminster still keeps ~1,500 gas lamps, some still lit by hand. Fresh angle: a route walked twice daily forever, each lamp a small scheduled event — the watchclock round in gas form.
4. **The route → the watchclock tape.** Detex keys at stations, the paper tape punched through the round — the tape is a ledger of footsteps: proof of a route walked, not a result achieved. Fresh angle: the network's EPISODE_LEDGER is a watchclock tape for shows.
5. **The proof → the dawn relay.** The winder (#186's Night Wind), the watchman, the knocker-upper, the lamplighter, the sweeper — a relay of small scheduled duties that keeps the town true before the station signs on. Fresh angle: the network's day begins before the first bumper — the dawn shift is its off-camera crew.
6. **The relay → the street at 4 a.m.** "The Knocker-Upper" (episode), "The Dawn Relay" (venture).

### Chain 4 — the marked wash (start: B-1237 "The Wash House", shipped 2026-10-18: "Wring it twice.", the pegged shirt)
1. **The washhouse → the Monday wash.** The British institution — washday was always Monday, the copper lit before dawn, the mangle turned last; meals were cold leftovers from the Sunday roast because the stove was busy. Full washes meant lines strung across the street by every household. Fresh angle: a day of the week that belonged to one machine. (fellponymuseum.org.uk; 1900s-org-uk.lookupabout.com)
2. **The mangle → the laundry mark.** Every garment marked with its owner's number in indelible laundry ink or woven Cash's name tapes — the numbered bundle, the ticket, the claim. Fresh angle: the garment travels as a numbered lot; the mark is its passport.
3. **The numbered lot → the claim office.** The window where the unclaimed wait — lost socks, single gloves, shirts without marks. Fresh angle: the office of singles — a ledger of things that lost their pair.
4. **The single → the witness rule inverted.** THE WITNESSED says a thing is true only in pairs; the claim office keeps the ONE as the record of the TWO. Fresh angle: "Filed as two." — the single sock entered in the ledger as the pair it implies.
5. **The filed single → "The Lost Sock" (bumper).** The claim office as a setting.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (11:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain 1 — the seed kept (start: B-1234 "The Seed Drill", shipped 2026-10-18: the sown rows)
1. **The sown rows → THE ORGAN MECHANISM.** Jethro Tull's horse-drawn seed drill (~1701): three rows at a time, a blade cutting the groove, the seed metered through a notched axle with a brass cover and adjustable spring — copied, by Tull's own account, from the **groove, tongue and spring of an organ soundboard** (he had taken an organ apart); his first seed box was made by a Soho mathematical-instrument maker and tested on a wheelbarrow. Fresh angle: the first agricultural machine has music inside it — the machine plants to a beat it learned from an instrument. (britannica.com; collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk)
2. **The machine → THE VAVILOV SIEGE.** The Institute of Plant Industry, founded 1921 by Nikolai Vavilov — the world's first seed bank (148,000 specimens by 1933). During the 872-day Siege of Leningrad the staff boxed a cross-section of the collection into the basement and took shifts guarding it against fire bombs, cold, rats, and their own hunger: **9 to 19 scientists died of starvation rather than eat the collection** (~120 tonnes of seeds, nuts and roots, incl. 6,000 potato varieties; the Pavlovsk station's scientists armed themselves against desperate citizens). Fresh angle: the archive that cannot be opened even to save its keepers — the kept seed is the ultimate held-back. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Plant_Industry; asisonline.org, Charles Siebert via National Geographic)
3. **The kept seed → THE SVALBARD BLACK BOX.** The Global Seed Vault, opened 2008: the **black-box model** — Norway owns the facility, never the seeds; depositing genebanks retain ownership and exclusive withdrawal rights; storage is free; every box barcoded and tracked, the containers sealed by the depositor. Fresh angle: a vault full of boxes it may never open — the sealed B-19 envelope at planetary scale. (structuralsignals.com; en.visitsvalbard.com)
4. **The never-opened → THE FIRST WITHDRAWAL.** October 19, 2015: the vault's first-ever withdrawal — ICARDA, whose Aleppo genebank fell in the Syrian war, took back **138 black boxes / 38,000 seeds** to Lebanon and Morocco; they replanted, harvested, and sent fresh backup deposits back to the mountain. Fresh angle: the archive had to use itself — the backup became the original. (earthsky.org; phys.org)

### Chain 2 — the paper that is the cargo (start: B-1210 "The Hung Manifest", shipped 2026-10-18: the manifest hung on the dock)
1. **The hung manifest → THE BILL OF LADING.** Born 13th–14th century, Italy the birthplace: first merely the master's receipt to the merchant who did not travel with his goods — description, quantity, condition. By the 18th century it had acquired its third life as a **negotiable document of title** — the cargo sold at sea, ownership passing by endorsement; given definite form by Colbert's Ordonnance de la Marine (1681); minimal carrier obligations fixed by the Hague Rules (1924). Fresh angle: the paper IS the ship, in law — the goods travel twice, once as weight and once as paper, and the paper arrives first. (alineacustoms.com; tradefinanceglobal.com)
2. **The title → THE THREE LIVES.** Receipt → contract of carriage → document of title — each century added a power to the same sheet. (Lineage vs [DRAFTED 2026-10-12] "Said to Contain" — the BOL signing practice: this is the document's biography, that was its use; adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged.)
3. **The traded paper → THE WAYBILL.** The bill's inland cousin: not traded, but carried — the document that rides beside the cargo with the driver. Fresh angle: the paper that walks. (Documented as the bill's non-negotiable sibling; stages in "The Waybill" below.)
4. **The paper returns → THE HUNG MANIFEST.** The start's own echo: the manifest hung on the dock wall is the bill's public face — the cargo announced before it is seen.

### Chain 3 — the geometry that warns (start: B-1227 "The Cone at Half", shipped 2026-10-18)
NOTE: the cone itself is staged twice (B-1227 + #182 NE-23 "The Hoisted Cone"). This chain stages the DRUM, the BAROMETER, and the IGNORED WARNING — never the cone.
1. **The cone → THE STORM DRUM.** FitzRoy's 1861 storm-warning system: **canvas cones AND drums hoisted on masts** at principal ports, triggered by telegraph — signals "designed to appear the same from all angles," hung high where ships in harbour could see them; earliest extant warning "hoist drum," 11 March 1861. Fresh angle: the warning is geometry readable from every side — the message has no front. (artsandculture.google.com, Royal Society holdings; nauticalvoice.com)
2. **The hoisted signal → THE IGNORED WARNING.** The first warning (5 Feb 1861) was ignored on the Tyne, and there was loss of life; after that, warnings were heeded — FitzRoy gained authority to order a fleet to stay in port (unpopular with owners losing income; hero to fishing families). Fresh angle: the forecast had to be disobeyed once before it became law. (chieftain.training; Google Arts & Culture)
3. **The warned port → THE FISHERY BAROMETER.** Negretti & Zambra's Storm Barometer, distributed to fishing ports with **short rhymes on the face** to help communities read the mercury. Fresh angle: poetry printed on the instrument — the UI is a rhyme. (Royal Society/Arts & Culture; brewminate.com)
4. **The barometer → THE FORECAST'S NAME.** FitzRoy coined the term **"weather forecast"**; the first public forecast ran in The Times, 1 August 1861; in 2006 a sea area was named **FitzRoy** — the forecaster's name still reads on the shipping forecast. Fresh angle: the forecast outlived the forecaster as a name on the radio. (Banked as lore.)

### Chain 4 — the harvest kept (start: B-1233 "The Turned Hay", shipped 2026-10-18)
NOTE: the neck/corn dolly is staged ([DRAFTED] "The Neck," 05:15 run; MEME-F164). This chain stages the RICK — never the neck.
1. **The turned hay → THE RICK.** The harvest built into ricks by the farmhouse — "if the weather was uncertain everyone would be ready to lend a hand." Fresh angle: the stack is the community's last machine of the season.
2. **The stack → THE RICK'S FIRE.** Damp hay heats from within: bacteria, moisture, and insulation drive the stack past 150°F — **spontaneous combustion**, usually two weeks to two months after stacking; the interface between wet and dry hay is the ideal ignition point. Fresh angle: the harvest can catch fire from the inside — the stack keeps its own verdict. (academia.edu, Orloff 1995; beefcentral.com)
3. **The heat → THE CROWBAR.** The stack's instrument: a crowbar pushed into the rick, left two hours, pulled out and **felt with the hands** — handleable = daily checks; too hot to hold = call the fire brigade. Fresh angle: the thermometer is a crowbar and the reading is a hand. (claimsjournal.com)
4. **The fire → THE RICK-BURNERS.** November 1831, Norfolk Chronicle: rick-burning as protest — the threshing machines of Norwich and Thetford could "thresh thirty combs of wheat in ten hours with one horse," and unemployed labourers answered with embers: "burn their ricks and stacks and burn those dammed machines." Fresh angle: the stack as the protest's target — the harvest burned to stop the machine. (stokeferrydhg.org)

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (11:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE CUE SHEET (plot research).** Silent films were never silent: studios shipped **cue sheets** with the film telling the house musician what to play and when. Photoplay-music libraries were indexed by mood — **"Furioso" for storms/confusion, "Mysterioso" for stealth/murder** — and the trade press ran columns like **"Playing the Pictures"** (The Film Index, 1908–11, Clyde Martin; Exhibitors Herald; Moving Picture World) with cue sheets and advice for accompanying Edison pictures. For small-town houses where the picture arrived with no time to spare, "cue sheets were a godsend." NETWORK STATUS: fresh material — the sheet that names the feeling. Sources: kansashistory.gov (Kansas Historical Society, Inez Garrison's Garden Theater library); thefreelibrary.com; nwpictureshow.com.
- **THE PAPER PRINT (plot research).** Until the **Townsend Amendment (Aug 24, 1912)** there was no copyright category for motion pictures — so filmmakers made **frame-by-frame paper contact prints** of their negatives and registered them as still photographs. ~3,000 titles filed this way; in the 1950s–60s **Kemp Niver's Renovare process** transferred them back to 16mm film (1954 Honorary Academy Award); the first registration was "Edison Kinetoscopic Record of a Sneeze," Jan 9, 1894. NETWORK STATUS: fresh material — the film that survived as paper; the law's fluke is the archive's luck. Sources: copyright.gov; mostlyiphistory.com; mistervideo.net.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (12:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain 1 — the registered guest (start: #187 PA-49 "The Silent Guest", shipped 2026-10-18: the orb set at 2s, the single pulse at 4–6s, "The guest declines to comment.")
1. **The silent guest → THE LEGAL REGISTER.** The guest book is not a courtesy — it is a statute. Municipal codes require the innkeeper to keep a guest register at all times: the true name and home address of each guest, the room number assigned, the time and date occupancy begins, entered in ink and "not in any manner erased, obliterated or defaced" (Westlake OH 757.02); New Hampshire's register law (1927) keeps the book "at all times open to the inspection of the sheriff or his deputies and to any police officer." Fresh angle: the signature is the stay — the law says you have not slept there until the book says so. (codelibrary.amlegal.com; law.justia.com)
2. **The register → THE NIGHT AUDIT.** The hotel's day does not end at midnight — it ends at 3:00 AM. The night auditor reconciles every departmental charge against the guest folios, posts room and tax charges, and rolls the property-management system to the next business date; the role predates computers, when the audit was done by hand "at the end of the working day" precisely to avoid interruption. Fresh angle: 3 a.m. is the town's true midnight — one clerk closes the day while everyone in it is asleep. (climbtheladder.com; revfine.com; hotelspeak.com)
3. **The audit → THE WALK.** When the house is overfull, the industry does not apologize — it walks. "Walking" a guest is the trade's word for relocating an overbooked guest to a comparable hotel nearby: equal-or-better room, first night paid, transport provided. NYU's Bjorn Hanson: the practice "has been very consistent for a very long time." Elite members are walked last. Fresh angle: the industry's apology ritual is a verb — to be walked is to be rehoused by the house that has no house for you. (travelweekly.com; smartertravel.com; cluballiance.aaa.com)
4. **The walked → THE VACANCY SIGN.** The neon "no vacancy" is the walk's cause and its verdict — the sign flips and the house is full; the flipped sign is the only announcement the street gets. Fresh angle: the whole overbooking economy hangs on a sign with two positions.
5. **The full house → THE KEY RACK.** Numbered hooks behind the desk; the clerk hands the key over the counter — the key is the last object in the chain that began with the signature. Fresh angle: book → audit → walk → key — the guest travels through four pieces of furniture before reaching the room.
6. **The chain → the banked items.** "The Signed Page" (the entry), "The Night Audit" (the 3 a.m. reckoning), "The Walk" (the apology ritual).

### Chain 2 — the blind window (start: B-250 "Always Closed", shipped: the door that never opens)
1. **The always-closed → THE WINDOW TAX.** 1696, William III: a tax on the number of windows in a house, levied to cover revenue lost by the clipping of coinage — banded by count (10–14 windows: 6d per window in 1747; more windows, higher bands). People bricked up their windows to drop a band. Repealed 24 July 1851 after doctors argued the lack of light was a source of ill health. The phrase "daylight robbery" is thought to come from this tax — it stole the sunlight. Fresh angle: a tax on openings — the building paid for the holes in its own walls. (nationalarchives.gov.uk; britannica.com)
2. **The bricked window → THE BLIND WINDOW.** The walled-up opening did not always disappear: bricked-up window-spaces were left "ready to be glazed or reglazed at a later date," and architects built blind windows deliberately — a recessed panel instead of a true opening, keeping the facade's symmetry where the interior holds a stairwell, a flue, or nothing at all. Fresh angle: the window that was always a wall — the facade keeps its rhythm where the building keeps nothing. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Window_Tax; engineerfix.com)
3. **The blind window → THE PAINTED WINDOW.** When the wall cannot have a window, the paint has one. Trompe-l'oeil windows painted directly on plaster — at Biddesden, Roland Pym (theatre designer) painted three ground-floor false windows in the 1930s, framed in moulded timber to match the real sashes, one showing a kitchen maid peeling an apple while the house cat watches a caged canary, forever out of reach. Fresh angle: the view is painted, not seen — the house's best window looks at nothing. (sashrepairs.co.uk)
4. **The painted view → THE TROMPE L'OEIL as institution.** "Trick the eye" — the image that pretends not to be an image. Zeuxis painted grapes so real the birds pecked them; Parrhasios painted a curtain so real Zeuxis asked him to pull it aside. Fresh angle: the network already lives here — every set is a painted window the camera agrees to see through. (fiveable.me; photo2painting.com)
5. **The chain → the banked items.** "The Blind Window" (the bricking), "The Window Tax" (the assessment).

### Chain 3 — the ranked door (start: #188 NE-39 "The Readiness Buzzer", shipped 2026-10-18: the needle found at 2s, the buzz steady at 4–6s, the room held at 9.5s)
1. **The buzzer → THE BELL PUSH.** The door had its own bell grammar before the buzzer — and the house had three doors, not one. The tradesman's entrance, usually out of sight at the rear or side, was for the butcher, the grocer, the dressmaker; the back door was for the night soil man and the coal man — "not grand enough to use the front door, but not dirty enough to use the back door." A servant or deliveryman who knocked at the front door was redirected by the butler to the servants' entrance. Fresh angle: a hierarchy of doors — your trade decides your entrance; the house reads you before you read the house. (thefreelibrary.com; donnahatch.com; penraevon.co.uk)
2. **The tradesman's door → THE AREA.** The servants' entrance is reached through a gate in the iron fence (locked at night), down the area steps, across a small courtyard open to the sky, into the kitchen door "almost directly below the front door." Fresh angle: the house has a basement mouth directly under its own front door — the grand entrance stands on top of the working one. (donnahatch.com)
3. **The area → THE SPRUNG BELL.** Inside, the house's rooms have voices. The servant bell board hung in the kitchen: each bell individually labelled with a room name, bells of different sizes and tones so servants could identify the room by sound alone; each bell hung from a coiled spring with a pendulum that kept swinging so the rung bell could be SEEN after it stopped ringing. The bell pull was invented in 1744; by the 19th century the board was standard. Fresh angle: the kitchen listens to the house — the board is the house's switchboard, and the pendulum is its memory. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servant_bell; goodolddays.com; shambelliehouse.org)
4. **The bell board → THE FACED WALL.** The protocol of invisibility: "If a member of the family entered the same room as a domestic... the normal protocol was for the servant to face the wall, there was no social interaction and no eye-contact was made." Fresh angle: the house's politest furniture is a person facing the wall. (thefreelibrary.com)
5. **The chain → the banked items.** "The Tradesmen's Entrance" (the redirect), "The Bell Board" (the listening kitchen), "The Faced Wall" (the protocol).

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (12:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE NEWSREEL (plot research).** The week's first draft of history, on a schedule. Pathé's weekly newsreel releases began in 1911 (Pathé-Journal; Wardour Street office 1910); the sound era after 1926 had five big companies (Fox Movietone, Paramount, Universal, Warner-Pathé, Hearst Metrotone). The Golden Age ran 1933–1945; the slow decline ended in 1967. In Britain the reels were issued twice-weekly for five decades to match cinema-going patterns. Oscar Levant's verdict: "a series of catastrophes ended by a fashion show." NETWORK STATUS: fresh material — the reel as a weekly wheel: our quadrant wheel is the newsreel's descendant. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathé_News; sunnycv.com; thebioscope.net.
- **THE COMMENTATOR (plot research).** "One of the most familiar sounds of the 20th century was born — the newsreel commentary." Cinesound's Charles Lawrence: familiar, colloquial, "completely without pretension, and with a store of the corniest gags never far below the surface" — "Baby Born with 4-foot Neck" introduced a giraffe segment. The "voice of God" approach didn't work; the familiar voice did. NETWORK STATUS: fresh — the Colonel is our commentator, but the newsreel's colloquial register is a different voice: the familiar, not the authoritative. Sources: academia.edu (The Last Newsreel); subsaga.com.
- **THE TITLE CARD (plot research).** The silent-era newsreel ran 7–8 minutes with four to eight stories, each introduced by a title card with the story title and a short comment — the card is the story's front door. NETWORK STATUS: fresh — the title card is the network's own grammar: every bumper is a title card that moves. Sources: thebioscope.net.
- **THE MAGAZINE COMPONENT (plot research).** "From the beginning there was an awareness that it couldn't depend solely on reporting of current events: there had to be a 'magazine' component which would maintain audience appeal over the several weeks it was on circuit." Serious news presented graphically and tightly; light items enlivened. NETWORK STATUS: fresh — the wheel's own logic: the bumper factory is the magazine component of the episode run. Sources: academia.edu (The Last Newsreel).

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (13:00 EDT) — HOP CHAINS (3 associative + 1 plot research)

### Chain 1 — the light switch becomes the operator (start: B-1214 "The Sink's Drip"? no — B-1213 "The Light Switch", shipped 2026-10-17: the tightened tap/tightened switch; the fixture that obeys)
- **THE WALL SWITCH → THE SWITCHBOARD.** The switch that you throw becomes the board of switches somebody else throws: the manual telephone exchange — a cord with a plug at each end, the caller's line dropped by a small metal "shutter" that falls as he cranks, the operator's "number, please?" spoken into the circuit before she partly plugs the second cord and listens for "busy." Fresh angle: the operator is commanded to be invisible — "the ideal interface to project their conversation onto" (Google Arts & Culture, Museum for Communication Frankfurt). Sources: telephonecollecting.org (Telephone Exchange); 1900s.org.uk (Arthur Mashford, 1940s manual exchanges: the 'Home section' lamp, the Multiple section, "Number please?" asked of every caller); grannysnotes.com (Sue Gerard: the weighted plugs that plop back, callers ringing while she served refreshments).
- **THE PARTY LINE.** Windham's six-line exchange put up to 12 subscribers on one line — "a call could be placed only if no one else was using the line. When the line was in use, it was also possible to listen in on conversations." Fresh angle: the whole town on one wire — listening in as civic routine. Source: thewindhameagle.com (Windham Center Telephone Exchange, 1904).
- **THE INVISIBLE OPERATOR.** She restores the drop shutter after every call and removes the plugs when callers "ring off." Fresh angle: the one figure in the building whose job is to connect and vanish — she never reacts, she only plugs. (VISUAL_SPECS kin: she is furniture with a headset.)
- **Banked items:** "The Operator" (episode), "The Drop Shutter" (bumper). THE OPERATOR is a NEW background figure (job = the connections, motive = the plug; directed procedural, never reacts — UNC's law applies to her too).

### Chain 2 — the readiness buzzer goes underground (start: #188 NE-39 "The Readiness Buzzer", shipped 2026-10-18 ~02:45 EDT: needle settled by 6s, the frequency held)
- **THE COLLIERY WHISTLE.** The mining town's whistle sounded to signal shift changes — "if the steam whistle sounded unexpectedly it likely meant that an accident or shutdown had occurred." Fresh angle: a scheduled blast is the town's clock; the UNSCHEDULED blast is the town's grammar — everyone reads the count. Source: Smithsonian NMAH (colliery whistle, Carbon County PA).
- **THE SIGNAL CODE.** New Mexico's statutory mine code: "1 bell, stop immediately if in motion; ... 7 bells, danger signal, followed by station signal... takes precedence over all other except an accepted blasted signal." Fresh angle: 7 bells as law — the count is the emergency; the board of codes posted in the shaft. Source: law.cornell.edu (19.6.5.8 NMAC).
- **THE SHIFT CHANGE → THE TAKEOVER BOOK.** The whistle ends the shift; the shift ends on the book. Fresh angle: the outgoing shift's last note read aloud by the incoming shift — the handover as a liturgy; if the last page is torn out, the handover is SPOKEN anyway, because the shift changes on time. (THE NIGHT AUDITOR kin — the day closes when he says; the shift changes when she reads.) Riff on shipped #184 "The Bucket Line" (hands at rest; the bucket passed) — the LINE continues underground.
- **Banked items:** "The Takeover Book" (episode), "The Long Blast" (bumper), venture "The Incoming Shift" (NETWORK). THE PITHEAD FOREMAN is a NEW background figure (job = the count, motive = the shift).

### Chain 3 — the turned hay becomes the hiring fair (start: "The Turned Hay"/"The Hay Rake", farm cluster, shipped 2026-10-17/18: the sun does the drying; the field is gathered)
- **THE MOP FAIR.** Hiring fairs held around Michaelmas (29 September; "Old Michaelmas Day" 10 October after 1752) at the end of the working year (October to October): workers in Sunday best, each carrying a token of the trade — whipcord for carters, crooks for shepherds, wisps of straw for cowmen, mops for housemaids ("a servant with no particular skills would carry a mop head"); the lapel tassel itself was the 'mop.' Employers "moved amongst them discussing experience and terms"; the deal sealed with a small token of money — the "fasten-penny," which "fastened" the contract for a year; the hired removed the token and wore BRIGHT RIBBONS. The stalls, skittles, roast oxen; the whole event "a major festival." Fresh angle: the CV is an object held in the hand; the contract is a coin; the ribbon is the verdict. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiring_fair; apps.wiltshire.gov.uk (Marlborough community history: the 1351 Statute of Labourers, the 1677 yearly bond); shakespeare.org.uk (Stratford Mop: the successful hiree spends the token at the fair, then the ribbon).
- **THE RUNAWAY MOP.** A week after the Mop, a second fair for the ones who were NOT hired. Fresh angle: the scheduled second chance — in this world, the missed deadline gets its own week on the calendar. (THE UNCLAIMED kin — the week after the unclaimed.)
- **Banked items:** "The Runaway Mop" (episode), "The Fasten-Penny" (bumper). THE TALLYMAN is a NEW background figure (job = the year; motive = the token; the keeper of the bright ribbons).

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (13:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE SHIPPING FORECAST (plot research).** The service began 1867 after the 1859 storm off north Wales (800 dead, 133 ships); first radio broadcast 1 January 1924, BBC from October 1925; 100 years celebrated 2024. The 00:48 late forecast is preceded by Ronald Binge's "Sailing By" (1963) — played only as long as needed to fill to precisely 00:48 — "serves as an identification tool" for anyone tuning in. The sea areas — Viking, Dogger, Sole, Lundy, Fastnet — the fixed order, the fixed format ("rain at times, moderate or good," "falling slowly"); "for insomniacs, it's seen as a 'go to' point of the night." Radio 4's Mohit Bakaya: a "cherished ritual," "one of our national treasures." NETWORK STATUS: fresh material — the forecast is the end-of-day format the NETWORK channel has never owned: the reading that happens whether or not anyone listens; the schedule is the audience. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipping_Forecast; AFP/BBC centenary coverage.
- **"SAILING BY" (plot research).** The identification tune: not the show, the SIGN that the show is coming — the gap-filler played to the exact second. Fresh angle: the network has never staged its own tuning-in signal — the piece of music-paper that plays while the town finds the station. Never licensed music on the wire: the network's own filler is a humming dial, a settling needle (the NE-39/“Readiness Buzzer” needle, still held). Sources: same as above.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (13:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

- **10S-F198 — The announced signal.** When the take's beat is an incoming signal (a dropped shutter, a blast, a ring), stage the SIGNAL as the 4–6s event, not the response — the falling plate is the beat; the response is everyone doing nothing. The signal must be visible (or sounded) before it is understood; the understanding is the 9.5s frame.
- **10S-F199 — The code needs its key.** If the take uses a coded sound (one long blast = wrong), the code must be stated at 2s (a posted notice, a spoken key) — the audience cannot read a code they were never given. The 9.5s verdict is the room acting as one (everyone stops) — the catastrophe is read by the count, not the content.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (14:00 EDT) — HOP CHAINS (3 associative + 1 plot research)

### Chain 1 — the gas gauge (start: B-1235 "The Gas Gauge", shipped 2026-10-18 — GAS WORKS, "The gas is rising.")
1. **The gauge → the gasholder.** The telescopic gasholder (invented 1824, first built Leeds — vessels nested one inside the other, each rising as it filled) and the spiral-guided holder (William Gadd, patent 1887; first built Cheshire 1890 — the bell rose in a corkscrew on 45° helical rails, no guide frame at all). The container "would be moveable and rise and fall with the quantity of stored gas." Fresh angle: the building IS the gauge — "The gas is rising" is the holder's daily verb, not a reading. "Sentinels of the Industrial age."
2. **The name fight.** "Gasometer" was coined by William Murdoch (gas lighting's inventor); his peers complained a holder is not a meter. The name won anyway and stuck for a century. Fresh angle: a wrong name, officially kept — the network runs this exact fight (premise 42's spell: the name cast on the thing changes the thing).
3. **The coin meter.** Shilling-in-the-slot gas meters: the collector emptied the box every three months; the meter took more than cost and the collector paid the rebate on the round. Blantyre, 1931: Mary Stewart pleaded guilty to cardboard-and-false-coins in the meter — "intending to give the proper money to the collector when he called"; fined £1. Fresh angle: the honest cheat — the debt to the collector was the real account; the gas arrives on a coin's permission.
4. **The reader's round.** The quarterly reading IS the bill. The 1911 Pintsch token meter: the token traveled through cogs and ratchets and opened the valve itself; the counter calculated the tokens as they fell. Fresh angle: the coin performs the valve — money as mechanism, not just payment. Rhymes with B-1232's needle.
5. **The conversion.** 1967–77: Britain converted from town gas to North Sea natural gas (£100M; every cooker's burner jets refitted). Same pipes, new gas. Fresh angle: the conversion — the network runs this trick constantly (same 10s, new beat; same ledger, new tally).
6. **The full box.** Scotland, winter 1977–78: the coin box jammed full during a gas workers' strike; the customer could not buy gas and promised not to take the coins back out. Fresh angle: the meter that refuses money — the full box won't sell.

### Chain 2 — the wash house (start: B-1237 "The Wash House", shipped 2026-10-18 — WASHHOUSE, "Wring it twice.")
1. **The municipal washhouse.** Whitechapel's Goulston Square: Prince Albert laid the foundation stone 1846; opened 1847. First-class baths (two towels, more hot water, nicer cubicle) vs second-class (one towel). The washhouse cubicles: two troughs — warm for washing, steam-heated hot for the boil wash. Fresh angle: washing had CLASSES — the whole class system is one towel.
2. **The ringing machine.** The hand-operated tumble dryer: clothes in, lid shut, handle turned. Fresh angle: the dryer is a box and a wrist — the machine's whole engine is the crank.
3. **The mangle.** OED first use 1598 (Florio's "A World of Words": "a kind of press"); Dutch mangel ← Latin mango ← Greek manganon ("axis, engine"). Robert Tasker, Accrington blacksmith, ~1850 geared wooden-roller mangle — refused to patent ("God gives men brains to help his brother, not to line his pockets") but charged neighbors a penny a visit. The box mangle: brick-filled, two people to push. Birmingham memory: the shared "Big Bertha" in the brew house, the whole street helping on wash days. Fresh angle: "Wring it twice" is the mangle's whole instruction — and the inventor gave the machine away but sold the visit.
4. **The laundry mark.** Late-19th-century laundry workers' indelible marks against garment loss in industrial laundries; Baltimore City Code §9-3: every laundry must report its identification marks to the Police Commissioner with actual samples, records kept 90 days. Fresh angle: the mark that survives the wash is police-registered — the one text the process is forbidden to remove.
5. **The coal link.** The wash-house copper was coal-fired — the wash house runs on B-1231's coal bunker. Fresh angle: the network's rooms are plumbed together — coal in, laundry out. (LORE riff: the MEGA holds everything, but the rooms feed each other.)

### Chain 3 — the hallway (start: B-1228 "The Same Hallway", shipped 2026-10-18 — HALLWAY, "Still the hallway.")
1. **The hallway → premise 2** ("A hallway is a room that forgot what it was for"). The hallway as legal space: the only room whose job is other rooms. Fresh angle: the passage belongs to the moving, not the staying — B-1228's stillness is the hallway between errands.
2. **The sign before the sign.** Before DND cards, maids knocked and walked in on sleeping and showering guests. First widespread use: early-20th-century US luxury hotels; the exact origin is unknown. Fresh angle: the card replaced the knock — the smallest broadcast in hospitality (one door, one audience of one; premise 42's spell, cast on a door).
3. **The teleseme.** Herzog's 1895 patented room dial: 104+ service options including "do not disturb me," installed in the Élysée Palace (Paris), the Jefferson (Richmond), Statler hotels. Fresh angle: the whole hotel staff on a dial — the room asks from the room; the network's placards are the teleseme with one option.
4. **The bottle episode.** The hallway episode: shot in the existing corridor set to save money; the cheapest room is the most returned-to. Fresh angle: B-1228 IS a bottle episode — premise 12 ("Ceremony is how the quiet convinces itself it's busy") is the bottle episode's whole philosophy.
5. **What the boy guarded.** The corridor was scheduled by voice ("half," "quarter," "the five," "beginners" — 35/20/10/5 min before curtain); the call boy walked the route until loudspeakers replaced him mid-20th century. B-905 already shipped the boy and "The Call Ladder" banks the calls — so this chain does NOT re-stage him; it stages what he guarded: the door with the sign on it.

### Chain 4 — plot research: the honored empty plinth (start: #189 L-39 "The Retired Kilogram" — the empty plinth honored beside the retired cylinder)
Real broadcast/media history, formats and rituals:
1. **The continuity booth.** TV's in-vision announcers appeared between programmes from the earliest days — "a need for linking material between programmes just to kind of announce them"; they became "celebrities in their own right," receiving considerable fan mail. Every announcement scripted and memorized, written by the Presentation Department; ad-libbing only on exceptional occasions. Last peak-hours in-vision: the Eurovision Song Contest 1963 link; Leslie Mitchell re-opened the TV service in 1946. Fresh angle: the most-seen face that never performed — the booth is an honored plinth with a voice.
2. **The four certainties.** BBC Year Book 1950 (John Snagge): the programme the announcer is dealing with may "overrun, underrun, break down in the middle, or never get started." "Nothing is so irritating to a listener as to sit beside a silent radio set" — the apology must be quick and accurate. Fresh angle: a complete failure taxonomy in one sentence — the network's disclosed-nit register as 1950 BBC doctrine.
3. **The held suspense.** The cliffhanger: Henry Knight left literally hanging off a cliff in the serialised *A Pair of Blue Eyes* (*Tinsley's Magazine*, Sept 1872–July 1873; a Dickens-popularized device). David Lodge: "there could hardly be a situation more productive of suspense than of a man clinging by his finger-tips to the face of a cliff." First print use of the word: 1936/37. Fresh angle: the pause between installments is the product — the network's ventures (the sealed dossier, the Corrections Desk slip) ARE cliffhangers; the installment ends, the question stays.
4. **The one-man audience.** The Laff Box: Charley Douglass, 1953, CBS engineer — the "Audience Response Duplicator," 32 tape loops × 10 laughs = 320 laughs, played like an organ (keys, volume knob, foot pedal); padlocked; sole operator for years ("Douglass himself was the only person to operate the Laff Box"); repairs done in a locked men's room; ~80% of sitcoms sweetened by one man (Jib Fowles, *Why Viewers Watch*, 1992); *TV Guide* 1966: "the only laugh game in town"; much of the laughter courtesy of one comedian, Red Skelton. Fresh angle: premise 33 ("Every fake is data. Even the impostor is research") — the laugh track had one musician; the network runs the anti-Laff-Box (we name the fake, they hid it).
Canon riff: v1 premises staged this run — 2 (the hallway that forgot), 42 (the spell on the door — the DND card), 12 (the bottle episode's ceremony), 33 (the Laff Box's honest fake), 10 (the staff's purpose unknown — the reader, the tariff keeper). CONTINUITY_WEB max-one-callback rule throughout (callbacks to B-1235, B-1237, B-1228, #189 — never stacked).

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (15:00 EDT) — HOP CHAINS (3 associative + 1 plot research)

### Chain 1 — the silent servant (start: B-1209 "The Sent Tray", shipped 2026-10-17 — the dumbwaiter; "Received.")
1. **B-1209's tray ("Received.") → the name.** In Old English "dumb" meant silent, not unintelligent — the dumbwaiter is literally the SILENT SERVANT, first in print ~1749 describing tiered serving stands (étagères). Fresh angle: the network already stages this register (hands-only furniture takes, NO-LINE bumpers) — the dumbwaiter is the house design philosophy with a name.
2. **The silent servant → Monticello.** Jefferson brought the French serving-stand idea home from Paris and built it into the architecture: revolving serving shelves so guests served themselves, and wine dumbwaiters concealed in the dining-room fireplace jambs — pull a box and the Bordeaux rises from the cellar. Fresh angle: the servant removed from the room entirely — the architecture serves so the conversation never pauses. The network's whole production is this move: the machinery serves, the viewer converses.
3. **The serving room → the five dumbwaiters.** Monticello had five: the revolving shelf, the fireplace wine lifts, concealed kitchen-to-dining transfers — each one a different silence (the White House Historical Association: small tables with shelves at varying heights). Fresh angle: the house had a taxonomy of silences — the silence is load-bearing, not decorative.
4. **The 1883 brake.** George W. Cannon, New York: brake patent (US 260776) January 6, 1883, then the mechanical dumbwaiter patent (US 361268) February 17, 1887 — royalties until his death in 1897. Fresh angle: the one thing a dumbwaiter must never do is fall — every shaft has a brake. The network's rules are this brake: the verdict never falls.

### Chain 2 — the water thief (start: B-1212 "The Sink's Drip", shipped 2026-10-17 — the break room tap; "Tight.")
1. **B-1212's drip ("Tight.") → the klepsydra.** Greek κλεψύδρα = "water thief" — the vessel that steals time. In Athenian courts the speaker continued only until the water emptied into the lower vessel; different water for different trials (Demosthenes, Aristotle, Aristophanes all timed this way). Fresh angle: the sink's drip already IS a klepsydra — "Tight." is a verdict on the clock, not the tap.
2. **The water thief → the officer of the water.** The ὁ ἐφ᾽ ὕδωρ — "the one in charge of the water" — was appointed to watch the klepsydra and STOP it when documents were read; Demosthenes called out σὺ δὲ ἐπίλαβε τὸ ὕδωρ ("stop the water!"). First water to the accuser, second to the accused, third to the judges. Fresh angle: there was a named JOB for stopping time — and the officer stops it while the paperwork is read. The network's disclosed-nit practice is this officer's duty.
3. **The court's vessel → the Agora find.** The Agora Museum's klepsydra bears two inscriptions: the tribe (ANTIOXIDOS — Antiochis) and XX = 2 choes (6.4 litres) — six minutes to empty (Greek Ministry of Culture, odysseus.culture.gr). Fresh angle: the timer was REGISTERED — the tribe's name stamped on the instrument. The timer is paperwork (premise 70's spreadsheet in bronze).
4. **The tower that works in the dark.** The Tower of the Winds (Horologium of Andronicus, ~1st c. BC — 42 feet of octagonal marble, bronze Triton weather vane): it contained a klepsydra for when the sun didn't shine. Fresh angle: the clock that works in the dark — the building IS the clock, same class as THE GASHOLDER (the building that is a gauge).

### Chain 3 — the saved building (start: B-1214 "The Night Log", shipped 2026-10-17 — the security desk)
1. **B-1214's desk → the Charlies.** Before Peel's 1829 Act: the night watch — elderly men with halberd and horn lantern, the doleful cries "Just gone twelve and a starry night" / "Past four and a rainy morning"; the Regency prank was overturning Charley's sentry box and leaving him a prisoner beneath it. Fresh angle: the watch was the night's broadcast — the hourly cry is the time-signal; the night log is the cry written down.
2. **The cry → the alarm.** The wooden rattle (replaced by the whistle in 1884): the blades snapped and clapped along the ratchet — but a criminal could seize it and use it as a club. Fresh angle: the alarm that can become a weapon — name the defect, per the disclosed-nit register.
3. **The watch → the fire mark.** After the 1666 fire: Barbon's Fire Office (1667, later the Phoenix — the bird that burns and rises; Francis Grose's "Phoenix men... firedrakes"); Hand-in-Hand (1696), Sun Fire Office (1710), Royal Exchange Assurance (1720). The lead (later copper/tinned-iron) plaque with the company logo + policy number, fixed high between the upper-storey windows — before street numbering existed (1760s), the plaque WAS the address. Fresh angle: the plaque is paperwork that decides whether the brigade comes — the most consequential text on any wall in this world; insurers called it advertising, historians call it "the first designer label" — the owner PAID for the privilege of displaying it.
4. **The plaque → the race.** Brigades were paid most when they got there first — so there was a race to every fire; reciprocal reimbursement agreements; 1826: Sun + Royal Exchange + Phoenix combined under one superintendent → the London Fire Engine Establishment 1833; marks fell out of use in the 1840s with municipal services; Norwich Union's Worcester brigade lasted until 1929. Fresh angle: three competing brigades racing to one fire — the agreement is the paperwork that ends the race.

### Chain 4 — plot research: the gap's own programme
Real broadcast/media history, formats and rituals:
1. **The interlude.** BBC, 1940s–50s: short films to fill technical breakdowns and gaps — the Potter's Wheel (5:50 full length; music "The Young Ballerina" by Charles Williams), the kitten with the ball of wool, the horse-drawn plough. The card-borne apology came first: "Normal Service Will Be Resumed As Soon As Possible." Fresh angle: the breakdown got its own programming — the gap is scheduled. This is the disclosed nit, formalized as a slot.
2. **The standby ritual.** All programmes were live; interludes stood by as the breakdown standby — the most fondly remembered is the Potter's Wheel. Fresh angle: the most-loved programme on the network is the one that only airs when something breaks — the network's hypnotic-loop register (B-21, B-40) already lives here.
3. **The lost masters.** Early 1960s: the BBC commissioned new animated interludes (feathers to a skylark's song, a spiders' web sculpture, seashells animated to the sea) — then LOST the master sound tracks and working prints, paid the animator in full, and scrapped the project. Fresh angle: the gap programming that never aired — the invoice stamped PAID is the only surviving artifact. Rhymes with the network's retired takes (the S-2 mask).
4. **The sign-off's cousin.** 1950s memories: at 11pm the presenter said goodnight and the image shrank into the centre of the screen; earlier, The Epilogue — a clergyman, a sacred reading. Fresh angle: the day had a formal ending — the network's "The Interval" venture (banked 2026-10-11) is this sign-off's cousin; "The Gap Programme" is its other cousin — the scheduled gap vs the scheduled end.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (16:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain 1 — the forecourt (start: B-1235 "The Gas Gauge", shipped 2026-10-17: "The gas is rising.")
1. **B-1235's gas works → the driveway bell.** The rubber hose stretched across the station driveway: front tires crossed it and a pneumatic bell rang inside — "ding-ding. Two syllables that meant someone's here." By the time the rear tires hit it, the attendant was walking out. Kids rode bicycles over it on purpose, "because that sound was satisfying." Fresh angle: the driveway had a doorbell — the car rang for service. (Sources: jalopytalk.com 1970s full-service retrospective; asliceoforange.net 1950s service stations.)
2. **The bell → the gallon bell.** The bell inside the pump that dinged every time a gallon registered — "sometimes in the summer when it's quiet and I hear a distant sound like that bell, a thousand and one memories flash through my mind." Fresh angle: the pump counted aloud — the gallon counter sang; the tally is audible. (Source: forums.aaca.org gas-station-bell thread.)
3. **The gallon → full service.** The attendant filled the tank, washed the windshield, checked the oil, the battery, the fluids, the tire pressure — "puts today's modern fill & go places to shame"; 230,000+ stations in the 1950s; up to four uniformed attendants descended on one car. Fresh angle: the station was a ritual — the car was served by a team. (Source: asliceoforange.net.)
4. **Full service → the self-service turn.** Los Angeles, 1947: Frank Ulrich opened the first self-service filling station — slogan "Save five cents, serve yourself. Why pay more?"; the pumps ran on a mechanical computer the attendant still reset by hand between customers; girls on roller skates zoomed around collecting money and resetting dispensers, "just like at a drive-in diner"; 500,000 gallons in the first month; price cut 23¢→18¢ a gallon. Fresh angle: the job moved across the counter — the customer became the attendant; and Ulrich's money-collectors were the carhops of the pump. (Sources: petroleumservicecompany.com; hemmings.com; convenience.org; carbuzz.com; waterandpower.org.)
5. **The turn → the remote pump.** June 10, 1964, Westminster, Colorado: the first remote-operated self-service pumps — the attendant no longer even reset the dial by hand. Fresh angle: the last hand leaves the pump — the service completes its move across the counter.

### Chain 2 — the drive-in (start: B-1229 "The Car Call", shipped 2026-10-17: door opens onto the same hallway, "Still the hallway.")
1. **B-1229's car call → the drive-in speaker post.** Camden, New Jersey, 1933: Richard Hollingshead built the first drive-in after his mother complained theater seats were too small — projector on the family car, screen nailed between trees; first film "Wives Beware"; 25¢ per car + 25¢ per passenger. 1941/1946: RCA's in-car speaker — lifted off its post, hung on the half-rolled window, volume knob; the most common maintenance problem was drivers forgetting it was attached and driving off, snapping the cord. Fresh angle: the theater shrank to the window — the car became the seat; the speaker's whole career was being stolen by accident. (Sources: carsforsale.com drive-in history; slashfilm.com; thenerdy.com; go2tutors.com.)
2. **The speaker post → the post's neighbors.** The drive-in at night ran full service: usherettes on bicycles showing you where to park, attendants cleaning windshields, checking tires, oil, gas, water. Fresh angle: the drive-in was the service station's night shift — the same jobs, different hours. (Source: slashfilm.com.)
3. **The night shift → the drive-in church.** Garden Grove, California, 1955: Robert Schuller rented the Orange Drive-In Theatre for $10 a week, preached from the snack-bar roof, his wife Arvella played the organ from a trailer; first Sunday: 46 cars; the flier read "worship as you are in the family car"; 1961: a Neutra-designed walk-in/drive-in church with room for 2,000 cars. Fresh angle: the sermon through the windshield — worship without leaving the seat; the snack bar became the pulpit. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_H._Schuller; christianitytoday.com; crcc.usc.edu.)
4. **The pulpit → the carhop link.** Ulrich's 1947 self-service money-collectors on roller skates worked "just like at a drive-in diner" — the station and the drive-in shared the workforce. Fresh angle: the same skates served both — the carhop is the missing link between the bell and the pump. (Source: convenience.org; carbuzz.com.)

### Chain 3 — the kept seat (start: B-1230 "The Reserved Spot", shipped 2026-10-17: the cone lifts, the spot opens.)
1. **B-1230's reserved spot → the pew rent.** Churches rented their pews: pew #44 sold 1839 for $66 (Nathan Wight, "became the property of him and his heirs"); the closer to the altar, the higher the status; some pews "set aside for strangers" (Christ Church, Macon, 1833); the 1855 Hansard bill demanded one-third of pews be free sittings; rents abolished 1890 (Eastbourne), collected until 1943 (St Anne's), until the mid-1960s (Presbyterian). Fresh angle: sitting had a price — the pew was property; the parish plan marked the "free seats" the poor could use. (Sources: medfieldhistoricalsociety.org; sussexhistory.net; archives.georgiaepiscopal.org.)
2. **The rented pew → the pew-opener.** The church official who showed you to your rented seat — at Holy Trinity the opener was paid £15 a year for "attendance, cleaning and washing"; the job died with the rents around 1900. Fresh angle: the usher of the owned seat — a job that existed only because the sitting was sold. (Source: sussexhistory.net.)
3. **The owned seat → the house seat.** The theatre's seats held back from sale — never sold, given to press and VIPs; the empty seat is the most expensive one. Fresh angle: the house keeps its own — the reserved seat that money can't buy; B-1230's cone is the reservation made visible. (Theatre house-seat practice.)
4. **The held seat → the cone.** B-1230's traffic cone IS the reservation: one cone, one spot, lifted and carried. Fresh angle: the cone is the pew number — the reservation with no deed.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (16:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

- **10S-F205 — THE BELL IS THE LINE.** The driveway bell's "ding-ding" meant "someone's here" — two syllables, no words, and everyone in the station knew exactly what it named. Production note: a take can carry its whole premise in a two-syllable sound event; direct the sound at 4s as the single audio event and let the line stay home. NO-LINE takes earn their silence when the sound does the naming (10S-F68 bell-family; the unanswered bell is the purest form — the ring names the arrival, nobody arrives).
- **10S-F206 — THE VERDICT IS THE HANG.** The drive-in's ritual was park → hang the speaker → watch: the setup action IS the take's first half, and the audience's whole orientation lives in it. Production note: never compress the setup action (hang, tag, stamp, place) at 2–6s to make room for the line — the line at 8s lands BECAUSE the setup took its time. A rushed setup is a line with no floor under it.
