## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (03:00 EDT) — LORE DEEPENING

- **THE CHALLENGE.** Bramah's 1784 patent; the Challenge Lock in the Piccadilly window from 1790 under the gold-ink placard — "The artist who can make an instrument that will pick or open this lock shall receive 200 guineas the moment it is produced." Stood 67 years; outlived Bramah (d. 1814). Lore ruling: a reward posted in a shop window for sixty-seven years is a standing order, not a contest — the notice is filed, not paid. (Chains: 5.)
- **THE PICKING.** The summer of 1851: Hobbs picked the Chubb detector in 25 minutes before eleven witnesses (the vault door at the Depository of Valuable Papers, Westminster, 22 July), then the Bramah in 51 hours across 16 days. Bramah paid the 200 guineas and protested in the Morning Chronicle; Hobbs showed the gold sovereigns in a glass case with a policeman. Lore ruling: the lock that resisted two generations fell twice in one summer, to the same American — the time is the argument. (Chains: 5.)
- **THE GRAND MASTER.** The keyed-alike hierarchy: the change key opens one door, the master opens the floor, the grand master opens the building — and is used for none of them. Lore ruling: it hangs on the Auditor's ring, counted but never turned — the most powerful key in the building is the one that never enters a lock. (Chains: 5.)
- **THE WASTE IS THE PRODUCT.** What the machine throws away is what the machine is for — 1833: cottonseed, a pollution problem, became an industry (oil, linters, meal). Lore ruling: the second product was garbage until it wasn't; the gin makes two things and the valuable one is the one it was trying to discard. (Chains: 1.)
- **THE TOLL IN COTTON.** The gin is paid in what it makes — Whitney & Miller's two-fifths, Piazzek's fifth. Lore ruling: the machine takes its share off the top, in the thing itself — the toll is never money. (Chains: 1.)
- **THE SAW FILE.** The machine eats its own teeth; a man with a file keeps it sharp — light and frequent, never heavy. Lore ruling: the file is older than the machine, and the machine knows it. (Chains: 1.)
- **THE TURNED PIKE.** The first gate went up at Wadesmill in 1663; "turnpike" is the gate, not the road. Lore ruling: the road charges for the road; the pike turns, the road opens, the transaction is the turn. (Chains: 2.)
- **SHUNPIKING.** The recognized art of leaving the road; gates ~5 miles apart made it possible; the trusts answered with side-bars. Lore ruling: every gate creates its by-road; every by-road gets its gate. (Chains: 2.)
- **REBECCA'S DIALOGUE.** Before the smash, the scripted line — "It feels like a big gate put across the road to stop your old mother… Off with it then, my children." Lore ruling: the riot had a script; the dialogue is part of the demolition, not the prelude to it. (Chains: 2.)
- **THE MEASURED MILE.** 80 chains to the mile; the milepost is where the promise is kept; the "TAKE OFF" stone releases the hill-horse, which walks home alone. Lore ruling: the mile is measured before it is marked; the marker is the trust's receipt. (Chains: 2.)
- **THE SHRINK.** The contract forgives the journey before it begins — pencil shrink 2–3%. Lore ruling: the scale expects the loss; the loss is forgiven in advance, never after. (Chains: 3.)
- **THE DEAD LINE.** 1864: the line inside the stockade — twenty feet from the fence, cross it and be shot; the word exploded with Andersonville. Lore ruling: the pen has a line in it; the line is older than the network and nobody crosses it. (Chains: 3.)
- **THE TICKET.** Nothing is sold until the paper says so; the seal pressed on the ticket IS the sale; unused numbered tickets are locked up like money. Lore ruling: the paper is the transaction — the animal, the weight, the money are all secondary. (Chains: 3.)
- **THE MOURNING.** Grief is registered with cloth, not tears — a Norfolk hive "sickly" until crepe on a stick; an untold Oxfordshire keeper lost all seventeen hives. Lore ruling: the official diagnosis for a failing hive is missing protocol, not disease. (Chains: 4.)
- **THE SPENT HOUSE.** The skep was built to be spent — sulfur smoke, the colony killed, only the comb surviving. Lore ruling: the old house was a consumable; the harvest was the house itself. (Chains: 4.)
- Background figures inventoried: THE SHOPMAN (job = the window display, motive = the lock has been unopened longer than he has been alive); THE WITNESSES (job = watching the lock be opened, motive = the proof is the watching); THE SAW-FILER (job = the thousand teeth, motive = light and frequent, never heavy); THE PIKEMAN (job = the gate, motive = the cry in the dark; counts your sheep at midnight); THE SHUNPIKER (job = the by-road, motive = the gate is a suggestion); THE WEIGHMASTER (job = the seal, motive = the ticket is the sale); THE TALLYMAN (job = the deduction, motive = the loss was expected).

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (04:00 EDT) — Kevin Bacon chains + studies

**Chain 1: #203 L-52 "The Claim Check" (the torn ticket, matched halves) → the 900-year-old split.**

1. **THE CLOAKROOM.** The torn claim ticket IS a cloakroom claim check — paired-number systems where a paper half stands in for a garment. Fresh angle: c.1900 New York, restaurants sold hat-check concessions to entrepreneurs, and fancy-dress balls ran "hat check affairs" — tickets were free and the mandatory $2 hat check WAS the true price of admission. Separately, the 1901 Builder account of Covent Garden's rebuild shows stalls getting dedicated cloakrooms as part of entrance/fire-egress rearrangement — cloakrooms as architecture, not furniture. (Sources: restaurant-ingthroughhistory.com "Check your hat"; arthurlloyd.co.uk, The Builder May/June 1901; V&A Theatre and Performance Collection, 1874 ivory Royal Italian Opera token accession S.533-1985.)
2. **THE PAWN TICKET.** The claim check becomes a pledge ticket — paper that IS the claim, made bearer. Fresh angle: British Columbia's Pawnbrokers Act prints verbatim on every ticket that if it is lost "the pawnbroker will be bound to deliver the pledge to any person who produces this ticket" — the holder of the paper IS the owner by statute. The same Act mandates a "Sale Book of Pledges for Loans of More Than $5" — the official register of the unclaimed. Albemarle & Bond's founder took a WOODEN LEG as a pledge for 10 shillings in the 1960s; never redeemed — the man simply got another leg from the NHS. Unredeemed pledges auctioned; surplus over the debt goes back to the pawner. (Sources: bclaws.gov.bc.ca Pawnbrokers Act; topcash.co.za History of Pawn Brokering; NY General Business Law §44 — "the holder of such memorandum or note shall be presumed to be the person entitled to redeem the pledge"; lost tickets cured by a "stop ticket" backed by a lost-instrument bond.)
3. **THE BAGGAGE CHECK.** The pledge ticket goes to the station — railroads ran the same claim-by-number system in brass. Fresh angle: the first known US maker, James Hendley of Boston (1835), hand-cut tin checks IN PAIRS — one strapped to the bag, one for the passenger, and the passenger's half was literally called "the duplicate"; a star stamp marked which half the passenger kept. Metal checks gave way to paper in the 1880s, gone by WWI. Behind them the left-luggage office and its caged guards' vans — the institution that holds what nobody collects. (Sources: tagtown.net; ohiometaldetecting.com 1860s railroad check; blog.railwaymuseum.org.uk.)
4. **THE DIVIDED TOKEN.** The baggage check is a 900-year-old idea: the Exchequer split tally stick, foil and stock. Fresh angle: notches cut to width by denomination (£1000 down to a penny), the stick split lengthwise, and the natural wood grain meant only the two original halves would ever fit — fraud-proof from Henry I's reign until 1826. The word "stocks" for government debt IS the tally's stock. And the payoff: in 1834 the abolished Exchequer ordered six centuries of tally sticks burned in two furnaces at the Houses of Parliament — the bonfire escaped and burned down the Palace of Westminster. The receipt destroyed its own archive. (Sources: lot-art.com Christie tally stick; medievallondon.ace.fordham.edu; W.T. Baxter, Accounting Historians Journal via egrove.olemiss.edu; thebookandpapergathering.org, Parliamentary Archives conservation note.)
5. **THE MODERN STUB.** The tally stick's descendant is the punched ticket stub — split-verification in the conductor's hand. Fresh angle: each railway conductor carried a punch cutting a DISTINCTIVELY shaped hole (Smithsonian example: a Bonney-Vehslage punch making an "L"), so a stub could be traced to exactly which conductor cancelled it. And: Herman Hollerith watched a conductor punch a "punch photograph" (light hair, dark eyes, large nose) into a ticket — and that observation became the IBM punch card. The stub is a proto-computer. (Sources: americanhistory.si.edu, ticket punch nmah_1061199; cprr.org; lascrucesdigest.com.)

**Chain 2: #202 PA-57 "The Lost Property Office" (the shelves of the forgotten) → the institution of the unclaimed.**

1. **200 BAKER STREET.** #202's filed umbrella is one of the million-shelf umbrellas at TfL's Lost Property Office — founded 30 October 1933, now Europe's largest, 200,000+ items a year; every item logged on an internal system named **"Sherlock."** Only ~one-fifth ever reclaimed. Fresh angle: the office kept an urn of cremated ashes for SEVEN YEARS before returning it to its German owner — the long clock for the irreplaceable. (Sources: TfL 90th-anniversary press release; London Transport Museum history page; manager Diana Quaye tour reporting.)
2. **TOKYO — OWNERSHIP ROTATES BY STATUTE.** Japan's lost-property law dates to a code written in **718**. The finder must hand items in within seven days, gets 5–20% (usually 10%) if the owner is found, and may claim the thing itself if unclaimed for six months. Tokyo police took in ¥4.5 billion (~$29M) in lost cash in 2025 and returned **72.3%** to owners. Fresh angle: the category breakdown — **75% of cellphones returned, 72% of IDs, but only 0.3% of 330,000 umbrellas** — the umbrella is the world's most consensually abandoned object. (Sources: Tokyo Metropolitan Police stats via EINPresswire; chareidi.org law history; notlost.com Tokyo FAQ.)
3. **THE MTA'S TIERED CLOCK.** New York holds items three months up to three years by estimated value, then auctions per NY Personal Property Law §10-106; guns were never resold — **dumped in the sea** (except wartime scrap drives). In the 1940s: 16,000 items a year, umbrellas auctioned in lots of ten dozen for $6.50–$8.50. Fresh angle: artist Rose Salane bought a lot of **94 unclaimed rings** from MTA Asset Recovery and calls the lots "an accidental archive" — the catalog as a portrait of the city. (Sources: mta.info; newsbeep.com "A Fortune in Flotsam"; urbanomnibus.net "Lost in Transit".)
4. **ESCHEATMENT — THE STATE AS CUSTODIAN, NEVER OWNER.** Under the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act the dormancy clock (typically 3 years) transfers custody to the state treasurer, which must list it publicly and hold it **in perpetuity with no claim deadline** — the state uses the funds but must keep an equivalent available. Fresh angle: Nebraska's treasurer auctioned abandoned safe-deposit contents (a 1934 $500 Federal Reserve note, a 1961 Roger Maris card, a 2-carat diamond ring) and **records the proceeds under the original owner's name** — the hammer sells the thing but keeps the name on the money. **$41.7 billion** waits unclaimed nationwide (NAUPA). (Sources: legalclarity.org; onbe.com Escheatment 101; froggy981.com Nebraska auction report.)
5. **THE AUCTION AS RITUAL.** TfL's unclaimed go to **Greasby's auction house (est. 1919, South London) every fortnight** alongside Met Police and Heathrow lost property — devices wiped, ~20% of resale. Brisbane Airport's annual auction bundles ~700 lots with **100% of proceeds donated** to a children's hospital. Alabama's Unclaimed Baggage runs an annual weirdness report (2026: a fully assembled robot, a bionic knee, $43,000 diamond earrings, a suitcase of rat poison, a bag of rocks). Fresh angle: MTA Asset Recovery lots are **numbered with material descriptions "in case their owner returned to claim"** — the catalog is addressed to the absent. (Sources: eastlondonadvertiser.co.uk; newsroom.bne.com.au; thefreelibrary.com unclaimed-baggage report.)
6. **THE LOST THAT MUST NOT BE CLAIMED.** Some categories the institutions refuse — TfL **throws away perishables** (the cooked frogs, the Victoria Line sandwich, the chocolate bar: "We didn't keep them"); the MTA sea-dumped guns; most finders never exercise their claim (Charleston, 2015: $200k in Revolutionary War-era pistols behind a false panel, still sitting in a police evidence locker because neither the finder nor the landlord filed the claim petition); California stopped auctioning safe-deposit contents in 2003 — now a dual-key-swiped vault of Civil War diaries and a 1906 "SF in Ruins" newspaper. Fresh angle: a taxonomy of the unclaimable — **the perishable, the dangerous, the inconvenient, the guilty.** (Sources: obnews.co TfL tour; discoverwildscience.com Charleston pistols; laketahoenews.net California vault.)

**Chain 3: #201 L-51 "The Regulator" ("The cycle holds.") → the planet's own time audit.**

1. **THE TIME BALL.** The Regulator's pendulum keeps the contact closed by swinging; the time ball is the pendulum scaled into a public institution. Fresh angle: the time is recorded at the moment the ball BEGINS descending, not when it hits bottom (Admiralty notice, Oct 1833, signed by command of John Barrow); the preparatory choreography — half-mast at 12:55, top at 12:58, drop at 13:00 — and 1pm was chosen only because the astronomers were busy observing the sun at noon. Hoisting was done BY HAND until 1960 — an assistant on a winch, three floors of chains below. (Sources: rmg.co.uk RMGC object 247981; redice.tv time-balls; en.wikipedia.org time ball.)
2. **THE OBSERVATORY'S MASTER CLOCK.** The ball needed a reference; observatories kept a pendulum more accurate than the Earth itself. The Shortt–Synchronome free pendulum (1921): the primary swings in a vacuum tank, touched only 1% of the time by a 0.3-second impulse every 30 seconds, accurate to ~1 second/year; used in 1926 to detect seasonal changes in the Earth's rotation — **the clock caught the PLANET being wrong.** A 1984 test of a 1932 Shortt against atomic clocks found 200 microseconds/day and detected lunar/solar tidal distortion. Fresh angle: the mechanism is a division of labor — a "free" master that does nothing but swing undisturbed while a slave does all the work of driving the hands. (Sources: museum.seiko.co.jp; en.wikipedia.org Shortt–Synchronome clock.)
3. **RUTH BELVILLE, THE GREENWICH TIME LADY.** The human version of the master clock. For 48 years (1892–1940) Ruth Belville walked London carrying her father's 18th-century pocket watch "Arnold," delivering correct time to subscribers weekly, by foot. When the speaking clock arrived in 1936 she called "Tim" a vulgar name; the News of the World headlined her 1943 obituary "Human 'TIM' Found Dead." Fresh angle: electric telegraph time (her "modern" rival) was actually LESS accurate and LESS reliable than her pocket watch — subscribers complained about the Post Office service while Ruth turned up weekly "as regular as clockwork." Old tech coexisted with new for decades. (Source: blog.sciencemuseum.org.uk.)
4. **THE SPEAKING CLOCK (TIM).** Belville's walker becomes a voice. Launched 24 July 1936 by the General Post Office; dial TIM (846), hear "At the third stroke, it will be…" — a fully automated networked information service (arguably the first mass-market electronic data service). 13 million calls in its first year. The first voice, Ethel "Jane" Cain, auditioned from 15,000 operators, held the job 1936–1963; the machinery was "a large-scale blending of a record player and a cuckoo clock" with glass disks holding 79 time designations. Fresh angle: people called it just to check their phone line was working — the voice became the dial tone's proof of life. (Sources: sitepoint.com talking-clock; designyoutrust.com speaking-clock.)
5. **THE RADIO TIME SIGNAL (WWV/WWVH).** The speaking clock's voice untethered from the phone line and beamed as infrastructure. NIST station WWV (Fort Collins, licensed 1 Oct 1919) broadcasts ticks, tones, and spoken UTC every minute on 2.5/5/10/15/20/25 MHz; WWVH Hawaii uses a female voice on the same frequencies — male/Colorado, female/Hawaii, distinguishable at a distance. Voice announcements began 1 Jan 1950. Fresh angle: WWV only got permission to broadcast time-of-day in the 1940s because the US Navy — holder of the nation's radio-time monopoly — cut its own transmissions during WWII. The baton passed mid-war. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org WWV; thebdr.net.)
6. **THE LEAP SECOND.** Time itself needs a correction slip. Since 1972, the IERS inserts a 61st second whenever atomic time drifts >0.9s from Earth's rotation — 27 added, last at end of 2016. The 2012 one took down Reddit and delayed Qantas flights; the 2022 vote (confirmed Oct 2025, 69 countries, Versailles) abolishes it by 2035, effective World Metrology Day 20 May 2027, because a NEGATIVE leap second (Earth is currently spinning FASTER, nobody knows why) has never been tested and nobody dares. Fresh angle: instead of correcting every second, the plan lets the gap widen to a full HOUR and then adds it all at once, centuries from now. The Corrections Desk deferred to our descendants. (Sources: astronoo.com; korben.info; newscientist.com.)

**10S STUDY:** 10S-F224 (KISHŌTENKETSU — the four-beat 10s: ki (introduction) / shō (development) / ten (twist) / ketsu (conclusion) maps to the 10s as 0–2 / 2–5 / 5–7 / 7–10. The engine is the turn, not conflict — "tension isn't the heart of the story… the twist is the high point" (Nelson Agency). The network's deadpan beats already run this way: the 06:00 finding (the line re-edits the first five seconds) is the ten followed by the ketsu. The 2026-10-18 "skip the introduction" finding covers ki; the 0–6s Vine grammar covers shō. Production note: draft every 10s as ki-shō-ten-ketsu; make 4–6s the recontextualizing event (the ten), 7–10s the settling line (the ketsu); never spend the ten on a second setup. Sources: skdesu.com kishōtenketsu; en.wikipedia.org act structure; nelsonagency.com). 10S-F225 (THE DEESCALATING KETSU — the kishōtenketsu conclusion can "amp up conflict or completely deescalate it into nothing" (Nelson Agency); the network's register already ships the deescalation as verdict: B-40's silence, B-153's card, "The Warning Position" (prepare — never). Production note: when the verdict is absence, end before the take does — hold the final 1.5s empty; the nothing is the ketsu; do not chase a punchline onto a beat whose whole point is the warning position).

**MEME STUDY:** MEME-I-k (THE COPYPASTA — text that must not change: copypasta spreads by exact duplication; "the only real rule is that the same text travels intact, or close to intact"; the joke is the repetition; meaning shifts by placement — oral tradition with the text fixed and the context swapped. Network-native: publish lines verbatim as text units — the Colonel's correction slips, the Control Voice announcements, ledger entries as copypasta blocks. The verbatim text is the artifact; viewers paste it whole into new contexts and the familiarity does the work. Deadpan + lore-heavy + paperwork-flavored; never a licensed rant. Production note: any line that has shipped verbatim twice becomes paste-ready canon — post it as text, unaltered). Network-native invented form: THE KIT — one panel per character, tools laid out, each labeled in locked text syntax. UNC's kit, the Auditor's kit, the Restocker's kit, the Winch Assistant's kit. Remix-ready: viewers assemble their own kits ("the winch assistant's kit, as submitted by @waefrebeorn"); lore-heavy; never licensed templates. Production note: ship one KIT card per background figure when they are introduced — the kit is the character's filing).

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (04:00 EDT) — LORE DEEPENING

- **THE DIVIDED TOKEN.** The Exchequer split tally stick, foil and stock, fraud-proof by wood grain from Henry I to 1826; the word "stocks" is the tally's stock. Lore ruling: the two halves only ever fit each other — trust, in this world, is a broken thing, and the tear is the signature. (Chain 1.)
- **THE BEARER-PAPER RULE.** Whoever holds the ticket is the person — by statute (BC Pawnbrokers Act; NY GBL §44). Lore ruling: the network's claim law — identity is a held object; the paper is you. (Chain 1.)
- **THE LOST-INSTRUMENT BOND.** A lost ticket is cured by a "stop ticket" backed by a lost-instrument bond. Lore ruling: paperwork repairs paperwork — there is a form for losing the form. (Chain 1.)
- **THE TALLY BURN.** 1834: the abolished Exchequer burned six centuries of tally sticks; the bonfire escaped and burned down the Palace of Westminster. Lore ruling: the institution that destroyed its own records — the MEGA's founding trauma, referenced whenever an archive burns. (Chain 1.)
- **THE DORMANCY CLOCK.** Three years (typical) and custody transfers to the state; Nebraska records auction proceeds under the original owner's name. Lore ruling: every lost thing the network stages has a visible clock — the ∞:0 scoreboard of the unclaimed. (Chain 2.)
- **THE CODE OF 718.** Japan's lost-property law predates the network by 1,300 years; the finder gets 5–20%, usually 10%. Lore ruling: the network's lost-and-found practice is older than the network — the Colonel cites the code number aloud. (Chain 2.)
- **THE UNCLAIMABLE TAXONOMY.** The perishable, the dangerous, the inconvenient, the guilty. Lore ruling: filing rules for what the office refuses to keep — the perishables officer is the only person allowed to decide something is officially garbage. (Chain 2.)
- **THE NUMBERED LOT TAG.** A paper tag with a lot number and a one-line description, tied to an object whose owner is absent; MTA lots are described "in case their owner returned to claim." Lore ruling: the tag is the only voice the absent owner still has. (Chain 2.)
- **THE NEGATIVE SECOND.** 27 one-second slips filed since 1972; the 28th — the first removal — has never been attempted; the vote abolishes corrections by 2035. Lore ruling: the Corrections Desk's own correction slips have a history, and the Desk's bravest act is the one it deferred to our descendants. (Chain 3.)
- **RUTH'S ROUND.** 48 years, the watch "Arnold," weekly by foot, more accurate than the Post Office's telegraph time. Lore ruling: the network's corridors have a standing route; the roundsman corrects the clocks by hand because the automated voice announces the wrong hour. (Chain 3.)
- **THE PREPARATORY SIGNAL.** Half-mast at 12:55, top at 12:58, drop at 13:00; the time is recorded when the descent BEGINS. Lore ruling: readiness itself is announced — nothing happens in this world without its warning position first. (Chain 3.)
- **THE SHORTT DIVISION.** A free master that does nothing but swing undisturbed; a slave that does all the work of driving the hands. Lore ruling: network doctrine — one clock works, one clock is true; the standard nobody is allowed to look at. (Chain 3.)

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (05:00 EDT) — Kevin Bacon chains + studies

**Chain A: #205 NE-54 "The Night Porter" (the single ring, the empty lobby) → the audited night.**

1. **THE ROUND THAT MUST BE PROVEN → the Detex Newman watchclock.** Newman's 1901 US patent: the embossing type on a station key mating with a die inside the carried clock; the 1902 "Newman" portable was the first with a full-face dial and the first portable watchclock approved unqualified by the insurance rating organizations; consolidated 1923 as the Detex Watchclock Corporation; manufacture ended 31 December 2011. Mechanism: the watchman turned a uniquely-coded key at each of up to 40 stations, each turn embossing the station number onto a paper dial at the exact time — no ink, no ribbons; opening the case punched a hole at the current time; missed stations showed as visible gaps. First portable watchman's clock: Johannes Bürk's 1855 German patent. Fresh angle: the watchclock dial is a paper ledger of the night — the roundsman brings the hour back to the ledger, embossed. (Sources: Detex official history watchclocks.org; en.wikipedia.org Watchclock; Locksmith Ledger.) Nothing banked from this hop.
2. **THE MAN WHO WAKES THE WAKER → the knocker-up.** Mary Ann Smith, 71 Brenton Street, Limehouse, 1900s–1934: woke East End dock workers with a pea-shooter and dried peas, sixpence a week per client, hundreds each morning, never leaving a window until the client confirmed awake; 1911 census: "tin box maker," 16 children, two surviving; 1921: occupation "caller up," husband a watchman; her son invented the pea-shooting technique (killed in WWI), her daughter Molly Moore one of the last knocker-ups. Fresh angle: a profession whose whole job was not letting the night win. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org Mary_Smith_(knocker_upper); Oxford JVC blog.) 3. **THE BELL FOR THE NEVER-CLOSED SERVICE → the night call.** An 1827 aquatint, "The Surgeon-Apothecary summon'd to a Night-Call": the practitioner who lives above his shop roused late, cat and flower-pot flying; German pharmacy museums confirm the institutional version — pharmacies legally required to keep a night-duty room; modern after-hours practice retains the fixture literally — at a German Apotheke after hours, you "ring the bell at the entrance and wait for the pharmacist." Fresh angle: the night call is medicine's oldest on-call contract — a bell that must be answered even when the shop is dark. (Sources: 1827 aquatint via ResearchGate/Old Bailey context; museum.de pharmacy night-duty; army.mil after-hours bell.) 4. **THE SINGLE RING AS A CODE → the servant bell-board.** Internal bell systems invented 1744; 19th-century standard in larger households: wires from bell pulls (braided silk, tasselled, hidden in tapestry) to a board of individually labelled bells by the servants' quarters — Library, Dining Room, Master Bedroom; bells in different sizes and tones so servants identified the room by ear; electric versions from the 1860s used indicator boards with named apertures and a moving coloured disc. National Trust historian Marilyn Palmer: "No object is more evocative of historic household communication than the sprung bell." Fresh angle: one ring is a complete sentence with a room's name on it — #205's single 4–6s ring is addressed, not decorative. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org Servant_bell; National Trust "Country house communication through the ages.") **Chain B: B-1237 "The Wash House" ("Wring it twice.") → washday.**

1. **THE LAW THAT BUILT WASHHOUSES → the Baths and Washhouses Act 1846.** Committee for Promoting the Establishment of Baths and Wash-Houses for the Labouring Classes (1844); Sir George Grey's bill; Royal Assent 26 August 1846 — first legislation empowering British local authorities to fund public baths and washhouses; permissive, funded from the Poor Rate; twice as many baths for the labouring classes as for the upper; fees capped at 1d cold bath, 2d warm, 1d per hour's washing place. London's first: Goulston Square, Whitechapel (Prince Albert laid the foundation stone; opened 1847; model establishment 1851); seven bath houses in London by 1851; Liverpool's Pier Head wash house (1828) predates the Act. Fresh angle: Parliament legislated cleanliness into existence at a penny an hour — the wash as a civic institution with a published price list. (Sources: London Metropolitan University wash-houses history; Victorian Web; Baths and Washhouses Act 1846 — Wikipedia.)
2. **THE WASH-HOUSE THAT FLOATED → the Paris bateaux-lavoirs.** An 1805 ordinance banned women from washing on the Seine banks (they blocked navigation); an 1813 Préfet de Police order made bank-washing fully illegal. In 1880 Paris still held ~94,000 washerwomen (blanchisseuses/lavandières), in the Corporation of Washerwomen of the City of Paris, 12–15 hour days, six days a week, no sick leave — "bent with rheumatic limbs, ruined joints and scaly rough red hands." Once a year the city crowned them: at Mid-Lent each lavoir elected a queen; from the 1890s the Queen of Queens paraded the boulevards — interrupted by WWII, never fully revived; the last washing boat disappeared during WWII. Fresh angle: the river was the factory floor — a wooden barge of kneeling women kept a city of two million presentable. 3. **THE WEEKLY COPPER → Monday washday.** London houses got fresh water twice a week from 1682 — Monday among them — and Monday has been wash day ever since. "Blue Monday": the day's drudgery AND the bluing agent — bluing (indigo, Prussian blue, ultramarine, kept in a cloth bag swished in the final rinse) masked the yellowing of soap-washed whites, making them read whiter. The copper: the domestic boiler — clothes boiled in the scullery copper, lifted with a laundry stick or "ponch," hands left red raw. Fresh angle: the week itself was built around the copper — Monday owned the steam, and the colour blue owned Monday. (Sources: DigitalNZ "When washday was Monday"; The Frick Pittsburgh "Laundry Day"; Old Treasury Building Melbourne; PioneerGirl bluing bag.)
4. **THE MACHINE BETWEEN PEOPLE → the mangle.** Wooden rollers in a frame, hand-cranked, feeding washed laundry through to squeeze it dry — "murder to use," hands red raw; smaller versions sat on table edges or buckets; also called "wringers." Fresh angle: the mangle is B-1237's machine ancestor — "wring it twice" was a sentence spoken to a machine that only understood squeezing. 5. **THE MARK THAT SURVIVES THE WASH → the laundry mark.** 18th century: linens cross-stitched with initials — girls learned marking alphabets as first needlework; Old Bailey transcripts record marks picked out after thefts. A 1767 advert sold "the new invented Liquid for marking Linen, that will stand Washing and Boiling... and cannot be picked out." US Patent 598,520 (Marker's record for laundrymen): a notation system of 42,875 three-character numbers giving every garment in a public laundry a unique identity. 1935: the National Marking Ink Co. patented invisible marking inks — colourless in daylight, glowing under ultraviolet, later police-forensic. Codified locations: shirt, front inside shirttail; handkerchiefs were NEVER marked — they travelled in a net with a marked strip tag pinned on. Fresh angle: the shirt carries its own ledger number through the wash, and the net carries the unmarkable. **Chain C: B-1276 "The Attic Window" (the unopened paper plane) → mail that travels.** (Per task: transport, not seals — the 17th-c. locked letters untouched.)

1. **THE THROWN MESSAGE → the Siege of Paris balloon post, 1870–71.** 17 September 1870, two days before the encirclement completed: Nadar wrote to the Council for the Defence proposing balloons; first flight 23 September — the Neptune, 125 kg of mail, three hours, landed at Craconville 83 km out. Regular service at 20 centimes a letter; two balloon factories — Nadar's in the Élysée-Montmartre dance hall, Godard's in the Gare d'Orléans; silk short, women varnished cheap cotton calico at long tables while sailors made ropes, nets, baskets. 66 balloons flew, ~2.5 million letters and 102 passengers; five captured, three lost at sea. Léon Gambetta escaped in the Armand-Barbès on 7 October 1870 before a crowd at Place Saint-Pierre, Montmartre, to run the government from Tours. Many of the letters now sit in the Smithsonian's National Postal Museum. Fresh angle: the first airmail was a siege improvisation — the post office became a dance hall, a railway station, and 66 canvas envelopes. (Sources: The Paris Review "All Aboard L'Armand-Barbès"; Amusing Planet; Encyclopædia Britannica 9th ed. via Wikisource.)
2. **THE MAIL THAT CAME BACK → the siege pigeons.** The balloons carried homing pigeons out; they were the only way messages could reach the besieged city (the Seine telegraph cable cut 27 September; couriers intercepted). Of 360 pigeons flown out, 57 returned — each carrying multiple messages on photographic microfilm, delivering over 60,000 of 95,000 messages. Not one balloon ever made the return trip. Fresh angle: the pigeon was the reply — the siege's outbound post was the only post that could never come home. (Sources: Amusing Planet; US Army signal-corps pigeon history.)
3. **THE BIRD THAT SAVED A BATTALION → Cher Ami.** 4 October 1918, the Argonne: Whittlesey's 77th Division "Lost Battalion" — surrounded, out of runners, shelled by its own guns — down to its last pigeon of seven. The leg-capsule message: "We are along the road parallel to 276.4. Our own artillery is dropping a barrage directly on us. For heaven's sake, stop it." Cher Ami was shot through the breast, fell, rose again, flew 25 miles in 25 minutes, arriving with the leg hanging by a tendon and the capsule intact; the barrage stopped, 194 men rescued. French Croix de Guerre; US Distinguished Service Cross; Pershing: "There isn't anything the United States can do too much for this bird." Mounted at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. Fresh angle: the most important message of 1918 hung on by a tendon — the carrier was worth more than the envelope. (Sources: National Museum of the US Army Cher Ami biography; ArmyHistory.org; Smithsonian Magazine.)
4. **THE LETTER AS A CAPSULE → the Paris pneumatic post.** Opened 1866 (borrowed from London's 1853 Stock Exchange tube): a 1 km experimental stretch, Bourse to Grand Hôtel; first official line 1868 (ministries to Central Post Office); official-only "closed" network until 1878, public "petit bleu" from 1879. Capsules on compressed air at 40–70 km/h through tubes laid in the sewers, finished to doors by dedicated couriers called tubistes. 1934 peak: 427 km of pipe, 130 offices; volume peaked 1945 at 30 million. Killed by fax and telex, closed 1984; a parallel government network (Senate–National Assembly–Journal Officiel) ran to 2004. Fresh angle: for 118 years Paris had an underground machine whose only job was moving folded paper at the speed of compressed air. (Sources: Paris pneumatic post — Wikipedia; Bonjour Paris; Vanessa Couchman.) P. Exhibition Allahabad" with an aeroplane-and-mountains vignette; recipients included a young Jawaharlal Nehru and King George V; Péquet flew with a compass strapped to his lap. 1. **THE NIGHT'S TIMEKEEPER → the Greenwich Time Signal.** First broadcast 5 February 1924, 9:30 p.m. — Astronomer Royal Sir Frank Dyson's idea, BBC head John Reith's approval (after Dyson proposed regular signals following the 1924 New Year Big Ben broadcast). Two mechanical pendulum clocks at the Royal Observatory with electrical contacts on their pendula sent a signal each second down a GPO line, converted to a 1 kHz tone — five 0.1s pips and a final 0.5s pip, the last marking the exact hour; the line tone was inverted (steady tone = silence) so faults showed instantly. Dent built the clocks — the same firm as Big Ben's turret clock. After ~13 years the Admiralty billed the BBC £520 a year — "no guarantee attaches to the service" — and a vice-admiral replied with a tongue-in-cheek invoice for the BBC's free naval broadcasting. Fresh angle: the whole nation set its watches to two pendulums in Greenwich — time as a sound the entire country agreed to hear at once. (Sources: British Online Archives; miketodd.net.) 2. **THE LAST VOICE OF THE DAY → the continuity announcer's closedown.** A full BBC closedown: tomorrow's schedule rundown, the national weather forecast, a public information film (Mon–Thu), a closing announcement wishing goodnight over the station clock, then God Save the Queen over the globe ident. Richard Straker's 14 April 1985 closedown (12:57 a.m.): cue the anthem as the clock's second hand hit 57, 12, 27, or 42 seconds, mix to the globe on the quarter minute; Peter Brook's 14 October 1981 closedown: PIF ("Motorway Fog") → closedown → globe → anthem. Variants: the anthem over a portrait of the Queen (Christmas 1977, 1992); in Wales, three bars of the Welsh anthem and one of the English. Fresh angle: a human whose whole nightly job was saying goodnight to a nation on a clock cue — the last scheduled sentence of the broadcast day. (Sources: Television closedown routines in the UK — Wikipedia; The TV Room Rewind; BBC1 closedown 14 Oct 1981.)
3. **THE LAST PROGRAMME → the end of closedowns.** BBC One's closedown ritual ended November 1997 when BBC News 24 filled the overnight hours; the sequence had run since the 1950s (ending with Eric Coates's "Television March" before the anthem). ITV's regional closedowns were similarly elaborate — tomorrow's précis, weather, the anthem. Fresh angle: the anthem marked the exact moment television stopped being a public utility and became a room with the lights off. (Sources: Television closedown routines — Wikipedia.) LINEAGE: banked venture "The Closedown" owns the ritual as a series; this run banks only the SENTENCE ("The Goodnight"), flagged.
4. **THE PICTURE AFTER THE PICTURE → Test Card F.** Introduced 1967 with colour on BBC Two's 625-line service; designed by BBC engineer George Hersee, who brought in his eight-year-old daughter Carole for the dummy run (paid £100); she poses with a noughts-and-crosses board — the X in the left-centre square sits at the exact middle of the screen — and her clown doll Bubbles, repainted blue-to-green for colour calibration. Carole Hersee became the most-aired face in British TV history (~70,000 hours, 1967–1998). Test-card music from library-music tapes (pop crept in late 1970s); BBC One's ident tone 1 kHz, BBC Two's 440 Hz, so engineers told channels apart by ear. Myth-bust (trade historians): Test Card F was NOT broadcast overnight in the 1960s–80s — after closedown came 30 seconds of black, then tone, then the transmitters were pulled; the card lived in daytime trade-test gaps (last BBC One daytime slot 29 April 1983; Ceefax took the rest 1998). Fresh angle: the most-watched face in television history is an eight-year-old who was paid £100 — and she never once spoke. (Sources: The TV Room Rewind; Design Observer; Vivu.tv/Fandom Carole Hersee.) LINEAGE: banked venture "The Still Hour" (THE HELD IMAGE) owns the off-hours picture; this run banks only the SOUND AFTER THE SOUND ("The Night Transmitter"), flagged.
5. **THE SOUND AFTER THE SOUND → the closedown tone.** After the anthem faded: thirty seconds of black and silence, then ten minutes of tone on BBC One (two minutes on BBC Two — English regions couldn't opt back to network without a valid feed, so network stayed up for them). Then, about fifteen minutes after the last programme, the transmitter networks were shut down for the night. Fresh angle: the night had its own broadcast — half a minute of nothing, ten minutes of one note, then the engineers pulled the plug on the country. (Sources: The TV Room Rewind.)

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (05:00 EDT) — LORE DEEPENING

- **BLUE MONDAY.** London houses got fresh water twice a week from 1682 — Monday among them — and Monday has been wash day ever since; "Blue Monday" is the drudgery and the bluing. Lore ruling: the week itself was built around the copper — Monday owned the steam, and the colour blue owned Monday. (Chain B.)
- **THE BALLOON POST.** 66 balloons, ~2.5 million letters, 102 passengers; the post office became a dance hall and a railway station. Lore ruling: the first airmail was a siege improvisation — the mail leaves by air because the ground is closed. (Chain C.)
- **THE COPPER.** The domestic boiler; clothes lifted with a laundry stick or "ponch," hands red raw. Lore ruling: the week's liturgical object — lit every Monday regardless of who runs the washhouse. (Chain B.)
- **THE REPLY.** 57 of 360 siege pigeons returned with 60,000+ microfilm messages; Cher Ami flew 25 miles in 25 minutes with the leg hanging by a tendon. Lore ruling: the pigeon was the reply — the siege's outbound post was the only post that could never come home; the carrier is worth more than the envelope. (Chain C.)
- **THE NIGHT CALL.** The 1827 aquatint; the legally-required night-duty room; the bell that must be answered even when the shop is dark. Lore ruling: medicine's oldest on-call contract — the call is logged before it is answered; the bell outranks the dark. (Chain A.)
- **THE GOODNIGHT.** The closedown's last scheduled sentence, cued on the clock's second hand, then the anthem over the globe. Lore ruling: a human whose whole nightly job was saying goodnight to a nation — the sentence is the schedule. (Chain D.)
- **THE STAND-BY.** NBC's peacock interstitial (1957–79); the British apology caption. Lore ruling: the apology is the programming — the gap has a card, and the card is scheduled. (Chain D.)
- **THE WARM VALVES.** Thirty seconds of black, ten minutes of tone, then the plug pulled; the engineers kept the valves warm overnight. Lore ruling: the night had its own broadcast — and then the engineers pulled the plug on the country. (Chain D.)
- Background figures inventoried: THE COPPERMAN (job = the copper, motive = Monday is Monday); THE POSTMASTER OF THE ROOF (job = the balloon manifest, motive = the wind is the only signature); THE PIGEON MASTER (job = the loft, motive = the reply has feathers); THE APOTHECARY (job = the night drawer, motive = the bell outranks the dark); THE ANNOUNCER (job = the last sentence, motive = the schedule ends with him); THE STAND-BY OPERATOR (job = the card, motive = the gap is scheduled); THE TRANSMITTER KEEPER (job = the warm valves, motive = the night has a carrier).

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (06:00 EDT) — HOP CHAINS

**Chain A (THE KEYS — from shipped #204 "The Detected Lock," whose true key will not turn in the lobby lock).** Hop 1: #204's key → the WARDED LOCK (medieval–19th-century: fixed internal wards block the wrong key; the correct key's cutouts navigate them). Hop 2: the SKELETON KEY (a real key filed to its essential parts — Wikipedia: "reduced to its essential parts" — so it passes every ward configuration in a family; the minimal blade bypasses rather than picks; housekeeping skeleton keys are the legitimate form). Hop 3: BRAMAH'S CHALLENGE LOCK (Joseph Bramah, patent 1784; challenge lock displayed in the window at 124 Piccadilly from 1790 — "The artist who can make an instrument that will pick or open this lock shall receive 200 guineas the moment it is produced"; stood unpicked 67 years). Hop 4: HOBBS TAKES IT (Great Exhibition 1851 — American locksmith Alfred Charles Hobbs, working for Day & Newell, opened it after 51 hours spread over 16 days; arbitrators awarded him the 200 guineas 2 Sept 1851; Bramah paid under protest; Hobbs displayed the reward as gold sovereigns in a glass case guarded by a policeman — the win WAS the advertisement). Hop 5: THE DETECTOR (Jeremiah Chubb, patent 1818: after a 1817 Portsmouth Dockyard burglary with false keys, the government offered £100 for a lock openable only by its own key; the detector spring jams the bolt when any lever is lifted too high — the lock TELLS on the tamperer; early versions needed a separate REGULATOR key to reset it; a convict locksmith on a prison hulk was promised a free pardon + £100 and after two or three months admitted defeat; Hobbs picked it too — ~25 minutes before eleven witnesses at the Depository of Valuable Papers, Westminster — the Great Lock Controversy). (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bramah_lock, /wiki/Chubb_detector_lock; Linda Hall Library; daniellucian.com; antiqueboxes.org.) **Chain B (THE UNCLAIMED — from shipped #202 "The Lost Property Office," Laura filing the umbrella).** Hop 1: #202's umbrella → the real TFL LOST PROPERTY OFFICE (created 1933; 86 years at 200 Baker Street; ~330,000 items a typical year — ~900 a day; Europe's largest; held THREE MONTHS, then auctioned/donated — higher-value items auctioned, proceeds fund the service; ~25% reclaimed). **Chain C (THE DUST — from shipped #190 "The Soil" (three piles: soil, breeze, salvage) + #191 "The Thirty Miles" (the ragman)).** Hop 1: #190's "breeze" pile → the REAL dust-trade vocabulary (Dickens Project sketch of the dust-yard sorters: the finer cinders left after the wind blows through the upright sieve are called "breeze" and are SOLD TO THE BRICKMAKERS — the leftover that builds; the full sort: coal picked for resale; soft-ware/hardware; bones to the soap-boiler; woollen rags for hop-manure, white linen rags washed for paper; broken pottery sold to make new roads). Hop 2: the GREAT DUST HEAP (Battle Bridge/King's Cross — E. H. Dixon watercolours 1837/1840; contemporary accounts say it was sold to the Russian government for rebuilding Moscow after the Napoleonic wars for ~£20,000; removed 1848 for King's Cross Station). Hop 3: BOFFIN (Dickens's Our Mutual Friend — Nicodemus Boffin inherits dust heaps and becomes THE GOLDEN DUSTMAN; the heaps were real fortunes). Hop 4: the DUSTMAN'S BELL (dustmen drove wagons ringing a bell to summon the bins; Camden Railway Heritage Trust: householders complained the dustmen were never there when needed and had their own way of making it known the service was not free — the dust got in their throats, "an abnormal thirst... allayed by copious quantities of beer"). (Sources: onlondon.co.uk; londonopia.co.uk; dickens.ucsc.edu; crht.thinknewr.com; hornseyhistorical.org.uk.) Lineage: #190 owns the sort; this chain owns the heap, the market, and the bell.

**Chain D (THE LIGHT — from shipped B-763 "The Unlit Lamp" + the never-staged dark stage).** Hop 1: the GHOST LIGHT (a single bare bulb on a stand in a wire cage, down centre on the empty stage; safety — the orchestra pit, the scenery; also called the EQUITY LIGHT — Actors' Equity demands it in contracts; the 19th-century gas theory — a burning light vented gas-line pressure; during the COVID closures it became the symbol of resilience — the theatre refusing to go completely dark). Hop 2: the BURGLAR'S FALL (legend: an unlucky burglar fell into the orchestra pit in the dark house and sued — the light as the precaution that outlived the lawsuit). Hop 3: the superstition (nearly every theatre claims a resident ghost; the light keeps the space inhabited rather than abandoned — ghosts perform their own shows at night — or wards the mischievous ones). (Sources: halgill.substack.com; dramatics.org; shakespearetheatre.org; broadwayforbros.com.) **10S STUDY:** 10S-F228 (THE SECOND RING — 10s takes can borrow the theatre's call ladder: two identical sound events spaced ~4s apart (the bell at 2s and 6s) give the audience a clock INSIDE the take; the line then reads as the last call, not an interruption. Production note: stage the event twice — the first is the setup, the second is the cue — and keep the line window 7.5-8.75s as the third beat; the audience's counting does the setup work). 10S-F229 (THE QUIET VERDICT — a take that withholds its end-button reads louder than a loud one: B-1276's folded plane, #205's still bell, B-1274's folded map. - **THE DETECTOR.** Chubb 1818: the £100 government reward; the detector spring that jams the bolt on tampering — the lock tells on the tamperer; the regulator key that resets it. Lore ruling: the regulator is the only forgiveness. (Chain A.)
- **THE UNEARNED PARDON.** The convict locksmith on the Portsmouth prison hulk: promised a free pardon + £100, two or three months of trying, then he admitted defeat. Lore ruling: the pardon was never earned — the defeat is the pardon; he stays. (Chain A.)
- **THE LOST QUARTER.** The real institution's rule: ~330,000 items a year, held three months, then the high-value unclaimed are auctioned and the proceeds fund the service; ~25% reclaimed; created 1933. Lore ruling: the quarter is the institution's patience — the gavel is the funeral. (Chain B.)

- **THE GREAT DUST HEAP.** Battle Bridge/King's Cross; ~£20,000 to the Russian government for rebuilding Moscow; removed 1848 for the station; Boffin's fortune. Lore ruling: the heap is the fortune — the mountain stays. (Chain C.)
- **THE BREEZE.** The dust-trade's word for the wind-blown finer cinders through the upright sieve, sold to the brickmakers. Lore ruling: the leftover is the load-bearing material — what the wind takes builds the city. (Chain C.)
- **THE DUSTMAN'S BELL.** The wagons' ring to summon the bins; the complaints; the throat-dust thirst. Lore ruling: the bell empties the house — the ring is the route. (Chain C.)

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (07:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain A — the returning tray (start: B-1275 "The Dumbwaiter, Returning", shipped 2026-10-18)
1. **B-1275's returning tray → the London Pneumatic Despatch Company.** 30 June 1859: Rammell & Clark form the company "for the more speedy and convenient circulation of despatches and parcels"; the 452-yard Battersea trial (1861) ran a 2-foot gauge track inside the tube, rubber-flapped capsules up to 3 tonnes at 40 mph off a 21-foot Waddle fan; the permanent Euston–Eversholt Street line opened 20 Feb 1863 — a capsule with up to 35 bags of mail made the third-of-a-mile run in one minute, thirteen journeys a day. Fresh angle: the capsule that RETURNS — a reversible fan pushes it one way, exhausts it back; the East Kent Times (1864) called the tunnel "the pea-shooter, and the train the pea."
2. **The pea-shooter tunnel → the tube as the dumbwaiter's big brother.** The dumbwaiter's tray and the pneumatic capsule are the same machine at different pressures — the building sending things to itself through its own walls. Fresh angle: the network already owns the tray grammar (B-1275, "The Capsule, Held" B-405); the tube is the tray with weather inside.
3. **The one-minute ride → the 1874 verdict.** The Post Office abandoned the system after its trials: transport underground was indeed faster, but hauling the mail in and out of the cars and up to the surface was a protracted process — no substantial time savings. Fresh angle: the machine won the race and lost the errand; the stairs beat the tube.
4. **The abandoned tube → the company that outlived the machine.** Disused by 1874, liquidated 1875, the old plans lost; the company was restored to the register in 1897 "as if it had never been removed," and the Postmaster General bought the tubes outright in 1921. Fresh angle: the paperwork outlived the machine by decades — the despatch company existed on paper longer than it ever ran.

### Chain B — the night porter's ring (start: #205 NE-54 "The Night Porter", shipped 2026-10-19)
1. **#205's porter and his ring → the watchclock.** Abraham A. Newman's Clock Company (1878); the 1901 embossing patent — the station key's embossing type meets a mating die inside the clock and presses the station number into the paper chart; up to 40 stations, each key chained at its post. Fresh angle: the key CANNOT travel — the watchman must come to the key. Presence is the whole mechanism; the round is a ceremony of being there.
2. **The chained key → the tamper puncture.** Every time the case is opened or closed, a mechanical device punctures the disk at the current time — more than two perforations proves the clock was opened and the record possibly forged. Fresh angle: the clock confesses on its own dial. The witness cannot be coached.
3. **The hourly rounds → the 130-year witness, retired.** Detex built the Newman watchclock for over a century; the mechanical line was discontinued 31 Dec 2011. Fresh angle: a machine watched the night for 130 years and was retired by electronics — the rounds continue, the witness changed.
4. **The retired witness → the recursion (bridge to Chain D).** The watchclock watches the watchman — so who keys the key-keeper? The tongue-twister answers: "we had a knocker-up, and our knocker-up had a knocker-up."

### Chain C — the attic's mail (start: B-1276 "The Attic Window" — "The attic has mail.", shipped 2026-10-19)
1. **The attic has mail → the pigeon loft on the roof.** Siege of Paris, 1870–71: 302 pigeons left the city by balloon; 57 returned. René Dagron shrank whole newspaper pages to 11×6mm collodion films weighing 0.05gm each — twenty films to a bird, rolled into tubes fastened on the wings. Fresh angle: the attic's mail has feathers; the loft is the attic with a sky door.
2. **The film on the wing → the magic-lantern reading.** On receipt the film was slipped between glass and projected on a wall; teams of clerks transcribed the contents for delivery by regular post. Fresh angle: the archive reads by shining, not by opening — the projection IS the reading.
3. **The million letters → the Prussian hawks.** The besiegers flew hawks and falcons around Paris to strike the feathered messengers down. Fresh angle: the sky had counter-programming — the pigeon's enemy is another bird with a job.
4. **The 57 returns → the auction.** On 6 Feb 1871 the service ended; surviving pigeons sold at public auction for three francs each — a fraction of the 36,000 francs negotiated in compensation for the breeders. Fresh angle: the heroes were remaindered; the compensation paperwork out-valued the birds.

### Chain D — the pea at the window (start: Chain B's knocker-upper node)
1. **The human alarm clock.** Industrial Britain ran on knocker-uppers — batons, bamboo poles, rattles on bedroom windows. Mary Smith of East London used a long tube to shoot dried peas at windows — sixpence a week; the pea woke the client without waking the street. Fresh angle: the pea is precision address — one pea, one window, the whole street spared.
2. **The pea → the candle in the window.** A lit candle in the window meant the client was home and the payment secured — no candle, no knock. Fresh angle: the candle is the knock's permission slip; the signal precedes the service.
3. **The candle → the snuffer-outer.** The knocker-up's second tool put out the gas lamps at dawn — the same walk both woke the town and darkened it. Fresh angle: one walk, two jobs — the dawn round is a relay (lineage: the banked "Dawn Relay" — flagged).
4. **The relay → the recursion.** "We had a knocker-up, and our knocker-up had a knocker-up" — the accountability chain is itself accountable. Fresh angle: the watcher is watched; the key-keeper has a key-keeper. This is THE WATCHED motif's third staging (first: the crowd at the challenge window; second: the eleven witnesses).

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (07:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

- **10S-F230 — CUT ON THE IMPACT, NOT AFTER IT.** Derek Lieu's Vine editing lesson (the "Krispy Kreme" vine): the clip cuts at the exact frame the feet hit the sign — the viewer never sees the aftermath, so the emotion freezes in the "OH MY GOD" instead of sliding into horror at the damage. The cut is the joke's punctuation. Production note: in 10s, place the beat boundary AT the event's peak — the landing, the thunk, the flare — not in the settling after. The take's end feeds the loop, so the last frame is also the first frame's promise: end on the impact, never on the recovery.
- **10S-F231 — REPETITION IS THE MEMORY DEVICE.** Poynter/Poeppel on six-second loops: the endless repetition helps the viewer remember, especially when the information is set to a pattern — "you remember those because of the repetition in music." The loop IS the repetition. Production note: one repeated gesture inside the 10s (the ring at 2s, the ring at 6s) reads as three on replay — the loop doubles the count for free. Design the repeated beat so the SECOND pass reads as the answer to the first: the call-and-answer grammar the network already runs (the Dust Bell's ring/wait/ring, the tally's 3→4).

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (07:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: MEME LITERACY

- **THE MISSED STATION.** The watch dial as a remix template: pre-printed times with embossed station numbers, and the GAP — a missed station — is the most readable thing on it. Network-native format: "STATION __: ______" — the audience fills their own missed station; the incompleteness is the remix handle (Shifman). Production note: publish the blank dial card; the viewers' missed stations are the content. Never licensed, always paperwork-flavored.
- **THE PEA GRAMMAR.** "Wake the one, spare the street" — meme caption grammar in two clauses: the addressed subject, then the spared world ("The window woke. The street slept."). This is the network-native adaptation of top-text/bottom-text: the first line names the target, the second names what was left alone. Production note: the Colonel's corrections already run this grammar (the named error, then the undisturbed record) — formalize it as the house caption shape.

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (07:00 EDT) — LORE DEEPENING

- **THE PNEUMATIC DESPATCH.** Founded 30 June 1859 by Rammell & Clark "for the more speedy and convenient circulation of despatches and parcels"; the 452-yard Battersea trial (1861) — 2-foot gauge, rubber-flapped capsules to 3 tonnes at 40 mph off a 21-foot fan; the Euston–Eversholt Street line opened 20 Feb 1863 — 35 bags, one minute, thirteen journeys a day; the East Kent Times' pea-shooter comparison ("the pea-shooter, and the train the pea"); abandoned 1874 — faster underground, but handling the mail in and out took longer. Lore ruling: the tube won the race and lost the errand. (Chain A.)
- **THE FIRST DESPATCH.** The inaugural capsule run — 35 bags of mail through the tube from Eversholt Street to Euston, illustrated in the Illustrated London News, 28 Feb 1863; the Post Office charged a nominal fee "to encourage them to accept the technology." Lore ruling: the demonstration is the product — the first run is always for the audience. (Chain A.)
- **THE CONFESSING DIAL.** Newman's 1901 embossing patent: the station key's type meets a mating die inside the clock and presses the number into the paper chart; every case-opening punctures the disk at the current time — more than two perforations proves tampering. Lore ruling: the dial is the witness; the puncture is the confession. (Chain B.)
- **THE SIEGE PIGEON POST.** 302 pigeons left Paris by balloon, 57 returned; Dagron's 11×6mm collodion films at 0.05gm each, twenty to a bird, rolled into wing-tubes; on receipt the film went between glass and was projected by magic lantern while clerks transcribed; twenty-word messages at five francs each. Lore ruling: the bird is the mail; the film is the message; the return is the verdict. (Chain C.)
- **THE MAGIC-LANTERN READING.** The archive's reading method: projection, not opening — the wall becomes the page, the clerks' hands become the type. Lore ruling: the reading is the performance; the transcript is the delivery. (Chain C.)
- **THE PRUSSIAN HAWKS.** The besiegers flew hawks and falcons around Paris to strike the feathered messengers down — the sky had counter-programming. Lore ruling: every route has a predator; the predator also has a job. (Chain C.)
- **THE KNOCKER-UPPER.** Mary Smith's pea shooter, sixpence a week; the candle in the window = paid and home; the snuffer-outer put out the gas lamps on the same walk; the recursion ("we had a knocker-up, and our knocker-up had a knocker-up"); the trade died out 1940s–1970s. Lore ruling: the pea wakes the one, not the street. (Chain D.)
- **THE RECURSION.** The accountability chain is itself accountable — the watchclock watches the watchman, the knocker-upper has a knocker-upper. Lore ruling: in this world the watcher is always watched; THE WATCHED motif's third staging. (Chain D.)
- Background figures inventoried: THE TUBE CLERK — NEW (job = the capsule, motive = the pressure is the promise); THE PIGEON KEEPER — NEW (job = the loft, motive = the birds come back); THE KNOCKER-UPPER — NEW (job = the dawn, motive = the pea wakes the one); THE SUPERVISOR — established (job = the dial, motive = the puncture is the proof); THE NIGHT WATCHMAN — folded (job = the rounds, motive = the dial is the witness; the round staged five times — the supervisor carries this beat).

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (08:00 EDT) — HOP CHAINS

- **CHAIN E (seed: B-1273 "The Dumbwaiter Tray").** E1. The tray -> the name: "dumb" meant SILENT in old English; the word first appears in print ~1749 for rolling tiered shelves that let guests serve themselves without staff present (dumbwaiter history). E2. -> Monticello: wine dumbwaiters on either side of the dining-room fireplace brought wine up from the cellar; a revolving SERVING DOOR concealed in a niche moved dishes in and out "with fewer intrusions to diners" (monticello.org). Fresh angle: the architecture is the staff. E3. -> Horn & Hardart Automat, 818 Chestnut Street, Philadelphia, opened 9 June 1902 (nypl.org): nickel-operated miniature lockers with windows; "the food simply appeared, replenished from behind the wall by staff the customer never saw." E4. -> the first Automat equipment ship SANK; Hardart reordered and the second shipment arrived safely (nypl.org). Fresh angle: the second machine is the first. E5. -> the Automat's hot dishes were sent up from the kitchen VIA DUMBWAITER — "these earliest automats relied on dumbwaiter technology, so essentially, there was a kitchen underneath the dining room" (filmmaker Lisa Hurwitz via neatorama). The chain closes on its seed: the tray returns.
- **CHAIN F (seed: #205 NE-54 "The Night Porter").** F1. The porter's bell -> the hotel night bell: the desk bell is the building's summons after dark. F2. -> the night auditor: the lone front-desk worker (11pm-7am) who checks in late arrivals AND closes the day's books — part guest agent, part accountant; "if something goes wrong at 3 a.m., you're the first person guests turn to" (climbtheladder). Fresh angle: the building is held by one person. F3. -> the NCR 42 and the penny: "all those rolls of paper, folios, dockets all over the floor at 2am in the morning and searching for a PENNY because the figures didn't balance... you HAD to find that PENNY" (ex-night-auditor, quora). Fresh angle: the cent is the verdict. F4. -> the rollover: "the digital systems consider midnight to be the official end of the day... wait until midnight for the daily accounting close" (wubook). Fresh angle: the day ends by wheels turning, not by sleep.
- **CHAIN G (seed: B-1276 "The Attic Window").** G1. The attic window -> the lighthouse lens: the window that speaks in a pattern — each light's CHARACTERISTIC, a flash pattern charted and unique per station. G2. -> the clockwork: a 150-lb weight on a 65-foot cable drives the lens through gears; at St. Augustine the weight reached the bottom every 2.5 hours and the keeper cranked it back up, several times a night (staugustinelighthouse.org). A stopped rotation "silently converts a coded signal into an anonymous glow, which is arguably worse" (jacobsvillelighthouse). G3. -> Keeper Thorwald Hansen, Crooked River, January 1927: assistant ill, the nightly watch fell to him alone; he let the 150-lb weights descend ~12 hours, then wound them 80 feet back to the top before the lens halted (USLHS Keeper's Log). Fresh angle: the watch is kept by one. G4. -> the mercury float: Barnegat's 3-ton first-order lens, 1,024 prisms, "could be rotated by the pressure of one finger" (qsl.net). Fresh angle: the tons answer the touch.
- **CHAIN H (seed: the V-tilde wordmark drift — AD-314, B-1251/B-1269).** H1. The drifting tilde -> the proofreader's mark: red-ink marginalia, the trade's own glyphs (Chicago Manual of Style). H2. -> "stet": Latin "let it stand" — the mark that cancels a correction; the error is kept on purpose (Wikipedia list of proofreader's marks). H3. -> the caret (U+2038): inserts a word that was never there. H4. -> the dele: the swooping delete line. H5. -> the Corrections Desk: the network's own institution receives all three marks — the Desk that rules on every correction.

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (08:00 EDT) — 10-SECOND STUDY

- **10S-F20 — THE HAND THAT ISN'T THERE (from Chain E, the Automat).** Short-form comedy works when the CAUSE is off-frame and only the EFFECT is staged: the pie appears, the door turns, the wine rises — the servant is never shown. Production rule: stage the effect, hide the cause; the viewer's brain supplies the servant. The network already stages this (the wall refills at 9.5s); name it so pre-production drafts it on purpose.

A visible clock compresses time better than any montage: the wheel turning IS the edit. Production rule: no beat about waiting, closing, or ending ships without its clock in the composition.
- **10S-F22 — THE SECOND MACHINE (from Chain E, the sunken ship).** The take's best version is the re-fire — Shorts creators re-shoot without shame; the network's v2 correction discipline already lives this. Production rule: the re-fire is not a failure of the first take, it is the second machine — draft the named correction as a new performance, not a repair of the old one.

- **CHAIN I (seed: B-1255 "The Wind Pump" — the fen wind pump).** I1. The pump -> the project: April 1630, Charles I's letters patent to Francis Russell, 4th Earl of Bedford, and thirteen "Gentlemen Adventurers" to drain the Great Level of the Fens (~300,000 acres of marsh across eastern England); the Dutch engineer Cornelius Vermuyden — knighted 1628 after Hatfield Chase — contracted in 1630, ~1,500 Dutch workers on the cuts by late 1631 (wikipedia: Adventurers (land drainage); mlcpumping.info). Fresh angle: the pump in B-1255 is four hundred years downstream of the decision that made the land need pumping. I2. -> the cut: the 21-mile Old Bedford River (the Hundred Foot River), dug straight from Earith to Salter's Lode to cut off the Great Ouse's meander; the Lynn Law (Court of Sewers, King's Lynn, 13 January 1631) formalized the straight-line doctrine — long straight cuts get the water to the sea fastest. Fresh angle: the river as a correction OF the river; the straight line drawn on the landscape. I3. -> the deal: of the reclaimed land, 43,000 acres to the fourteen Adventurers, 12,000 acres to the king, and another 40,000 acres designated to provide income to maintain the works; the "Lynn Law" ruled the works "complete" in October 1637, the Royal Commission overturned it in 1639; costs ballooned past 100 investors, many Adventurers lost their fortunes (wikipedia; middlelevel.gov.uk). Fresh angle: the maintenance share is IN THE DEED — the repair was budgeted before the works existed; the project was declared finished twice and failed both times. I4. -> the opposition: the Fen Tigers — generations of fen folk who fished, fowled, and sedged the wild fen; their sabotage was infilling the newly cut drains, blocking what the Adventurers dug (middlelevel.gov.uk; docslib). Fresh angle: the refill is the works' own maintenance, performed by the other side. I5. -> the shrinkage: drained peat shrinks; the ground level sinks several feet below the surrounding land and fills again with water; windmill pumps first, then steam, then electric — the job never ends (howtohistory.substack). Fresh angle: the project was never completed, only continued — the level is a verb.
- **CHAIN J (seed: B-1252 "The Honey Extractor" — extends the 03:00 run's Chain 4D in place, which banked "THE MOURNING" and "THE SPENT HOUSE").** J1. The extractor -> the wax economy: bees consume roughly 8–10 pounds of honey to make a single pound of wax (beeculture); the extractor's whole point is capital preservation — the comb is the factory, the honey is the harvest. Fresh angle: the network's ledger register in the wild — the comb is the ledger, the honey is the transaction; crushing the comb is spending the principal. J2. -> the three versions: v1 = a tin box attached to a wire cord, with a funnel at the bottom and a glass fastened to collect the honey (slow, effortful); v2 = the same head on an arm at the top of a tripod; v3 = the round tub we recognize today — the first model built by Bollinger Manufacturer in Vienna, summer 1865; announced at the Brno beekeepers' conference, September 12–14, 1865 (encyclopedia.thefreedictionary). Fresh angle: the invention shipped three versions; only the third is remembered — the v2 rule as 1865 precedent. J3. -> the retired Major: by February 1867 he signs his letters "k.k. Major, retired, Dolo bei Venedig"; the garden hives all facing east for the first morning rays (wikipedia: Franz Hruschka). Fresh angle: the inventor demobilized by his own invention — the army lost an officer, the bees gained an industry; the signature is the retirement notice.
- **CHAIN K (plot research: real broadcast practice — the bumper's own history).** K1. The bumper's job -> the first channel bumper: 1926, the NBC chime — three notes (G-E-C) implemented to notify affiliate stations that the program had ended so they could cut to local news or announcements (nyucommclub). Fresh angle: the first bumper was a SOUND, not a logo — the 10s lesson in the wild; our sound events are the brand, the image is the frame. Extends the bank's earlier NBC-chimes node ("The Hand" episode) in place. K2. -> the mandate: mid-1970s, FCC rules required a clear distinction between programs and commercials in Saturday-morning children's blocks — "(Show) will be right back after these messages" (tvtropes). Fresh angle: the fence became federal — the delimiter exists because a regulator demanded one; the network's two-line bug is the law made visible. K3. -> the bookmark: in the VCR era the bumper became the fast-forwarder's signal to return to normal speed — a bookmark, not a border (mediaspy). Fresh angle: the take should be legible at 8x speed — the 2s event is the re-entry point. K4. -> the eyecatch: anime's short animation at the break and the return, produced WITH the show rather than by the network (tvtropes). Fresh angle: the mark belongs to the program, the fence belongs to the network — our bumpers are the shows' eyecatches.

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (09:00 EDT) — LORE DEEPENING

- **THE GENTLEMEN ADVENTURERS.** The 4th Earl of Bedford + thirteen investors, letters patent April 1630; the ranks swelled past 100 as the costs ballooned; many lost their fortunes; the 1637 "complete" ruling overturned in 1639. Lore ruling: the adventure is the investment, not the drainage. (Chain I.)

- **THE OLD BEDFORD RIVER.** The 21-mile straight cut, Earith to Salter's Lode; the Lynn Law's straight-line doctrine — long straight cuts get the water to the sea fastest. Lore ruling: the cut is the river's correction. (Chain I.)
- **THE FEN TIGERS.** The fen folk's sabotage: infilling the newly cut drains; fishing, fowling, sedging for generations before the Adventurers. Lore ruling: the refill is the works' own maintenance, performed by the other side. (Chain I.)
- **THE SHRINKING PEAT.** Drained peat sinks below the surrounding land and fills with water again; windmills, then steam, then electric pumps — forever. Lore ruling: the job never ends; the level is a verb. (Chain I.)
- **THE WAX CAPITAL.** ~8–10 lbs of honey to make 1 lb of wax; the extractor preserves the factory, not the product. Lore ruling: the comb is the capital; the honey is the interest; crushing the comb is spending the principal. (Chain J.)
- **THE THREE VERSIONS.** Tin box on a wire cord (v1) -> tripod arm (v2) -> round tub (v3); first built by Bollinger Manufacturer, Vienna. Lore ruling: the invention shipped three versions; only the third is remembered. (Chain J.)
- **THE RETIRED MAJOR.** "k.k. Major, retired, Dolo bei Venedig" (Feb 1867); the garden hives facing east for the first morning rays. Lore ruling: the inventor demobilized by his own invention; the signature is the retirement notice. (Chain J.)
- **THE FENCE.** The mid-1970s FCC mandate: a clear delimiter between program and commercial — "(Show) will be right back after these messages." Lore ruling: the delimiter exists because a regulator demanded one; the bug is the law made visible. (Chain K.)
- **THE SPEED SIGNAL.** The VCR-era bumper: the fast-forwarder's signal to return to normal speed — a bookmark, not a border. Lore ruling: the take must be legible at 8x. (Chain K.)
- **THE EYECATCH.** Anime's short animation at the break and the return, produced with the show, not the network. Lore ruling: the mark belongs to the program, the fence belongs to the network. (Chain K.)

## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (10:00 EDT) — HOP CHAINS

- **CHAIN L (seed: B-1274 "The Pattern Shop", bumper, shipped 2026-10-19 — the pattern loft).** L1. The shop -> the oversize: a wooden pattern is built DELIBERATELY LARGER than the product — the shrinkage allowance. Cast iron contracts 1/10–5/32 in/ft, steel 1/8–1.4, aluminum 1/16–5/32; the patternmaker knows the metal's shrink and builds the wood bigger (reliance-foundry.com; hdowns.co.uk: "iron contracts 1 mm every 100 mm, steel 1 mm for every 60 mm"). Fresh angle: the object is honest only because it was built as a lie — the lie is the allowance. L2. -> the double: the MASTER pattern carries DOUBLE shrinkage — it must survive two successive castings (wood -> metal pattern -> final casting), so it is oversized twice (testbook/practicalmachinist). Fresh angle: preparation can lie twice and still be honest. L3. -> the color code: the wooden pattern is painted red and black — RED is what will be metal, BLACK is where the core goes (hdowns.co.uk — the 1-tonne JCB counterweight pattern). Fresh angle: the pattern is a map of its own future; the paint is the legend. L4. -> the discipline: at Brooklyn Tech's pattern shop the teacher failed any student caught using sandpaper — patterns were pared with chisels and gouges, fillets of wax or leather (practicalmachinist). Fresh angle: the surface was never sanded — hand-cut discipline as the network's wordmark-gate energy. Starrett still sells shrink rules — rulers calibrated wrong on purpose for a specific metal (practicalmachinist). Fresh angle: the ruler that measures wrong on purpose.
- **CHAIN M (seed: B-1248 "The Quarry Face", bumper, shipped 2026-10-18 — the wedge set).** M1. The wedges -> the ringing tone: plugs and feathers are struck in sequence, and the audible tone CHANGES TO A RINGING SOUND when the wedges are tight; between each series of strikes, a PAUSE OF SEVERAL MINUTES allows the stone to react to the pressure (alchetron; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plug_and_feather). Fresh angle: the pause is part of the pressure — the stone needs time to agree. M2. -> the bronze age: variations used since ancient Egyptian times — bronze plugs and feathers driven into chisel-cut grooves at Aswan's obelisk quarries; also the Romans (alchetron; researchgate: "documented in quarries as early as Roman times"). Fresh angle: three millennia of the same wedge — the tool outlives the quarry. M3. -> the soaked wedge: another ancient method — dry WOODEN wedges driven into a trough, then soaked; the swelling wood splits the block (dondougan.homestead.com). Fresh angle: water is a wedge you cannot see. M4. -> the signed rock: Roman quarries in Cumbria and Northumberland carry INSCRIPTIONS on the quarry faces — pick and wedge marks alongside carved text; Dartmoor called it "feather and tare" and used it to split rails for the Haytor Granite Tramway (1820) (prehistoric-britain.co.uk; alchetron). Fresh angle: the quarry signs its work — the cut face is already a document.
- **CHAIN N (seed: B-1273 "The Dumbwaiter Tray", bumper, shipped 2026-10-19 — the service pass).** N1. The tray -> the silent servant: "dumb" meant SILENT, not unintelligent — the dumbwaiter was "a silent servant." First in writing ~1749 as rolling tiered shelves in France and England, parked near diners so servants didn't have to hover and overhear gossip (activerain.com; whitehousehistory.org). Fresh angle: the lift exists so nobody overhears — privacy is the original feature. N2. -> Jefferson's wall: at Monticello he installed revolving serving shelves between rooms and wine lifts hidden in the fireplace chimneys — a spring-touch turned shelves loaded with dishes into the room; servants brought dishes but NEVER ENTERED; Margaret Bayard Smith: the dumbwaiter "contained everything necessary for the progress of the dinner from beginning to end, so as to make the attendance of servants entirely unnecessary" (whitehousehistory.org). Fresh angle: the wall is the staff — the room serves itself. N3. -> the speaking tube: older dumbwaiter installations kept a speaking tube beside the lift — waiters talked to chefs through the tube; the voice travels, the body doesn't (eliteliftsltd.co.uk). Fresh angle: the silent servant's one allowed voice. N4. -> the patent: George W. Cannon's US Patent 260776 (Jan 6, 1883) for the dumbwaiter brake; the mechanical dumbwaiter's patent 1887 — he drew royalties until his death in 1897 (elevation.fandom). And the Bank of England's "bullion lift" — a dumbwaiter built to carry COINS AND GOLD BARS (eliteliftsltd.co.uk). Fresh angle: the silent lift has carried the national treasure.
- **CHAIN O (plot research: real broadcast practice — the test card and the sign-off).** O1. The sign-off -> the card after the anthem: RCA's Indian Head test pattern (introduced 1939) was broadcast AFTER the station signed off and played the national anthem — held through the downtime, phased out only when color television arrived in the 1960s (mediacollege.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian-head_test_pattern). Fresh angle: the card aired when nothing was on — the downtime was the program. O2. -> the one-image camera: the Indian Head was the standard image for RCA's TK-1 MONOSCOPE — a simple camera capable of producing ONLY the image embedded within it (wikipedia). Fresh angle: a camera with no lens — the only honest camera, because it cannot improvise. O3. -> the most-broadcast face: BBC Test Card F (1967–1998) — Carole Hersee, the engineer's daughter, playing tic-tac-toe with a clown doll; aired for thousands of hours — the most-broadcast image in UK television history (historyfacts). Fresh angle: the station's most-watched thing was a card, not a show. O4. -> the local variant: every station redrew the card — CBS's bullseye, WJZ-TV's Empire State card, the Canadian modified forms (historyfacts; videokarma). Fresh angle: the template spread by LOCALIZATION — each market drew its own version of the same card; the form is fixed, the hand is local.
