## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (20:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE EQUITY BULB (ghost light).** A single bare bulb on a stand, left burning on the empty stage. Practical: it lets anyone navigate the dark house without falling into the orchestra pit (the legend: a burglar fell in, broke his leg, and sued — the light as lawsuit prevention); some say mandated by Actors' Equity — the "Equity Light"/"Equity Lamp"; gas-lit theatres left the gas low overnight to relieve pressure on the valves; Shakespeare-era candles left burning to dispel the ghosts of past performances, especially the bad ones. Superstition: it keeps the ghosts company, or lets them perform, or keeps them at bay — the theatre can't decide; during the COVID closures, hundreds of ghost lights burned through the empty months as a symbol of hope (shakespearetheatre.org; aact.org; midhudsonciviccenter.org; superbcollections.com; fiveable.me). The cash ball -> LAMSON'S BALL: William Stickney Lamson, Lowell MA — a Civil War veteran who opened his "five and dime" (the Rachet Store); his 1881 patent: the cash rode inside a hinged wooden ball on sloping wood-and-leather rails, propelled by gravity; Lamson Cash Carrier Company incorporated Boston 1882; company lore has him first hollowing out cricket balls (ephemerasociety.org; sesquiotic.com; alchetron.com). Fresh angle: the cash ball is #206's ancestor — the network's trough is the same machine; the ball was wood before it was brass; gravity is free. AS2. -> THE HANDKERCHIEF THROW: before the ball, Lamson wadded money in a handkerchief and threw it across his store in the 1870s — the zero-budget prototype (cambridgemuseum.org.nz). Fresh angle: the throw precedes the track — the ball is the civilized throw; the handkerchief is the first cash carrier. AS3. -> THE BRASS CARRIER: the tube replaced the ball — metal cylinders under air pressure; the soft name "Lamson" became synonymous with something hard, percussive, fast (sesquiotic.com). Fresh angle: wood becomes brass, gravity becomes air — the upgrade chain; #206's ball sits one rung below the capsule. AS4. -> THE ROCKETEERS: NYC pneumatic mail 1897–1953 — 27 miles of 8-inch tube, 136 rocketeers, 2-foot 21-pound steel cylinders holding 500 letters, 30 mph; 95,000 letters/day, a third of the city's mail; the tubes ran 18 hours a day, round the clock when snow fell (barrypopik.com; inc.com). Fresh angle: the workers are named for the cargo's speed — the job is the visible end of the invisible network. AS5. -> THE FIRST TEST: Oct 7, 1897 — the first test shot carried a Bible wrapped in an American flag, the Constitution, McKinley's inaugural address — plus a live cat in a cotton sack ("a little dizzy, but he made it"), a dozen eggs, two magnums of champagne, and an artificial peach for Senator Chauncey Depew (tubetalk.media). ## 2026-10-19 Q0 research run (22:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE PAID STOP.** Western Union's 1928 booklet "HOW TO WRITE TELEGRAMS PROPERLY": "stop" is "known the world over as the official telegraphic or cable word for 'period'" — because punctuation was charged as a word each, and a period could be lost in transmission while a word could not; telegrams were priced per word, so articles, conjunctions, and punctuation came out first; the result was a compressed register that "reads today like a text message with better manners" (rip.so; tropedia.fandom.com). 200 million telegrams in 1929; the last US telegram Jan 27, 2006 (poynter.org; grunge.com). Fresh angle -> network plot: THE PRICED WORD — in this world every word costs; the one-line payoff is the telegram's descendant; brevity is not style, it is economy. Banked as "The Paid Stop" (plot-shaped, this run): want = say it short, obstacle = every word is money, turn = he pays for the STOP — the period is the purchase.

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (01:00 EDT) — hop chains

### CHAIN BH (seed: #208 A-61 "The Borrowed Memory" — the transfer slip, shipped 2026-10-19 ~20:45 EDT — UNC opens the morgue drawer; it holds one transfer slip; "It remembers elsewhere.")
1. **The transfer slip → the Deed of Transfer.** Every museum accession arrives with signed paperwork — date of preparation, donor name and address, description of contents, the donor's signature acknowledging the terms. The terms of acceptance are "outright and unconditional." Fresh angle: the transfer slip is the object's passport — the paper that says where it goes next; the paper travels WITH the thing. (Source: SPNHC accession documentation, spnhc.org)
2. **The Deed → deaccession.** The formal ritual of UN-OWNING: written recommendation, a bound deaccession book carrying a sequential log, a deaccession folder — and the rule that "the physical inventory number on the artwork will not be removed... to document its provenance for future researchers." Fresh angle: the un-owning is more paperwork than the owning; the number outlives the shelf — the stamp leaves, the object stays numbered. (Sources: DOI Museum Property Handbook 411 DM Ch.6; CU Art Museum collection policy, colorado.edu)
3. **Deaccession → deaccession without moving.** "An item can be deaccessioned without moving from its spot on a shelf" — disposal (the object moving) is a different, related process. Fresh angle: the purest network beat — the object never moves; only the file changes; the status is the event. (Source: Museum of Health Care, museumofhealthcare.ca)
4. **The un-moving object → the returned object.** The Huron County registrar's rule: deaccessioned objects are offered to "the museum in the area that is most relevant to the object" — 439 objects transferred 2013–2020, "returning them to the geographical areas where they truly belong." Fresh angle: the object goes home, and home is an administrative decision — the filing decides the belonging. (Source: Huron County Museum, huroncountymuseum.ca)

### CHAIN BI (seed: #206 L-53 "The Cash Ball" — "The money travels.", shipped 2026-10-19 ~20:45 EDT — the sawed ball rolling the inclined trough into the cashier's tray; arc extension of the 22:15 run's Chain AS, which took the Lamson ball route — this run takes the OTHER rung: the money's destination, not its vehicle)
1. **The cashier's tray → the mutilated note.** The Bank of England's Mutilated Notes service: "As a general rule, we will only reimburse you with the face value of a damaged banknote if you still have at least half of the banknote" — claims by post to The Manager, Dept MN, assessed within a month; you cannot deliver in person. Fresh angle: half the money is all the money — the money travels BACK; #206's ball goes one way, the torn note returns. "The money travels." → "Half returns." (Source: Bank of England, bankofengland.co.uk — primary)
2. **The half note → the tally stick.** The medieval English Exchequer's split tally: hazel/willow stick notched by denomination (£1000 down to a halfpenny), inscribed on both sides, split lengthways — the creditor keeps the longer half (the STOCK), the debtor the shorter (the FOIL); the wood's natural grain means only the true halves fit, "almost impervious to tampering." The word "stock" comes from this. Fresh angle: the receipt you can split — the halves prove each other; a half is a whole when it matches. (Sources: Christie/lot-art tally listing; Science Museum Group 1812 tally; MAA Convergence)
3. **The split → the fire.** 1834: after the Exchequer's abolition, six centuries of accumulated tally sticks were ordered burned in two furnaces at Parliament — the bonfire spread out of control and burned down the Palace of Westminster. Fresh angle: the receipts were so numerous they burned the parliament that issued them — the paperwork outgrew the building. (Sources: lot-art; MAA)
4. **The ash → the wooden money.** Tallies "began to circulate in a secondary market... fully transferrable and acceptable as a means to pay taxes" — a hazel stick spent like a coin; "the payer's name and date of the transaction were carved on both sides." Fresh angle: the stick is the coin's ancestor — wood spends when the grain says so. (Source: GIMMS; medievallondon/fordham)

### CHAIN BJ (seed: B-1280 "The Greenhouse Vent" — "The glass breathes.", shipped 2026-10-19 — the vent as the lung; the palace behind the vent)
1. **The vent → the glasshouse.** Joseph Paxton's Great Conservatory at Chatsworth (1838–41): 277 ft long, 67 ft high — the largest glass building in the world; Queen Victoria called it "the most stupendous and extraordinary creation imaginable." Fresh angle: a building made of nothing but air and light — the glass is the wall AND the window; the vent is where the building breathes on purpose. (Source: gardenhistorygirl.co.uk)
2. **The glasshouse → the Crystal Palace.** 1851: Paxton upscaled the greenhouse — 1,848 feet long, 293,635 panes, 900,000 sq ft of glass (a third of the country's annual output), built AROUND the Hyde Park elms with trees growing through the roof; six million visitors; moved to Sydenham, burned 1936. Fresh angle: the greenhouse scaled to a palace — the trees stayed; the building moved around them. LINEAGE: B-1280 "The Greenhouse Vent" (the vent vs the palace — flagged). (Sources: Wikipedia Great Exhibition; engines.egr.uh.edu)
3. **The palace → the sparrows.** The Crystal Palace's first crisis was not structural — thousands of sparrows trapped inside were messing on the exhibits; the Duke of Wellington's solution: "Sparrow hawks, Ma'am." Fresh angle: the grandest building of the century reduced to pest control — the deadpan line writes itself. (Source: wintercyclingcongress2016.org; achievers.amway.com)

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (02:00 EDT) — HOP CHAINS

### CHAIN BK (seed: #205 NE-54 "The Night Porter" — the single bell ring; "the single ring owns the dark"; shipped 2026-10-19 ~20:45 EDT — this run takes the OTHER rung of the bell: the house's ring, not the porter's)
1. **The bell → the front-of-house calls.** The AACT theatre-terms glossary: calls at the Half (35 min. before curtain), the Quarter (20 min), the Five (10 min), "calls normally accompanied by bar bells at 3, 2 and 1 minutes before the performance begins"; the final call is "Places" (US) / "Beginners" (UK), and the PSM confirms "We have Places." Fresh angle: THE HOUSE IS CALLED BY RINGS — the building speaks in a countdown; the bell is the house's voice; the rings ARE the schedule. (Sources: aact.org Theatre Terms; writeoutloud.net "PLACES PLEASE" bell; everythingbackstage.com.)
2. **The house bell → the ghost light.** The single bulb left burning on the empty stage: practical (the orchestra pit is ~ten feet below; the burglar-who-fell legend), superstitious (the ghosts of old actors), historical (James Fisher: gas-lit theatres, the dim gaslight "used to relieve pressure on gas valves"; sometimes called the "Equity Lamp"); during the COVID closures the light stayed on with nobody in the building as a symbol of hope. Fresh angle: THE BUILDING IS NEVER FULLY DARK — the theatre's night shift is one bulb; the empty building keeps a companion. STAGING NOTE: B-84 "The Ghost Light" (shipped 2026-10-11) already staged this — this chain riffs it as lore, not as a new item. (Sources: atlasobscura.com; shakespearetheatre.org; folklore.usc.edu.)
3. **The kept building → the watchman's clock.** The Newman Clock Company (Abraham A. Newman, 1878, Boston→Chicago; 30+ patents); the 1901 embossing patent — station key + mating die emboss the paper dial with station number + time; the keys chained at checkpoints; the tamper detector that punctures the dial if the case is opened (more than two perforations = tampering); the Guardsman tape model; mechanical line discontinued 31 Dec 2011 after 130 years. Fresh angle: THE ROUNDS PROVED — the walk leaves a paper trail; the patrol is paperwork; the night is filed. (Sources: locksmithledger.com Detex history; watchclocks.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchclock; digitalcommons.rockefeller.edu.)
4. **The paper trail → the whistled cues.** Playbill: before stage managers there were prompters who "cued music, special effects, and scene changes" by whistling or ringing bells; the practice borrowed from sailors hired as stagehands in the winter shipping lull; John Wilkes Booth's ca. 1861 Richard III promptbook marks a "W" for a whistle cue. Fresh angle: THE WHISTLE IS THE CUE — the show was run by code before headsets; the prompter's whistle is the first broadcast of the night; the sailor-stagehands. (Source: playbill.com.)

### CHAIN BL (seed: #207 PA-58 "The Flying Fox" — the capsule at the far office desk; "It flies."; shipped 2026-10-19 ~20:45 EDT — this run takes the OTHER rung of the capsule: the feathered courier, not the office desk)
1. **The capsule → the carrier pigeon.** The aircraft's pigeons carried message canisters strapped to their legs — White Vision's actual message: "Aircraft ditched safely N.W... Heavy swell, taxing S.E. No casualties." Fresh angle: THE CAPSULE IS OLDER THAN THE OFFICE — the message rode birds before desks; the tube is the envelope. (Source: pdsa.org.uk — primary, White Vision's story.)
2. **The pigeon → the Dickin Medal.** Created 1943 by Maria Dickin, founder of the PDSA; "the animals' VC"; bronze medallion inscribed "For Gallantry" and "We Also Serve"; 32 pigeons awarded alongside 38 dogs, 4 horses, 1 cat; the first three — Winkie, Tyke, White Vision — decorated 2 Dec 1943. Fresh angle: THE BIRD GOT THE MEDAL — the animal got the gallantry medal; the handler didn't; the courier is the hero. (Sources: theddaystory.com; historyfacts.com; pdsa.org.uk.)
3. **The medal → Winkie's flight.** 23 Feb 1942: a damaged Lockheed Hudson ditched in the North Sea; Winkie flew 120 miles covered in oil to Broughty Ferry; the RAF calculated the downed aircraft's position from her flight time + wind direction + oil-on-feathers; the crew was rescued 15 minutes after the search began — she carried NO message; her arrival WAS the coordinates. Fresh angle: THE BIRD WAS THE POSITION — the courier is the signal. (Sources: warhistoryonline.com; mrcvs.co.uk — Dundee statue, Nov 2024.)
4. **The signal → the besieged news.** Siege of Paris, 1870–71: Dagron's microfilm (11mm × 6mm, 0.05gm; 20 films to a bird, dozens of messages per film — one pigeon could carry 40,000 dispatches, "the contents of a substantial book"); 20-word limit, 5 francs each; received films projected by magic lantern onto a wall and transcribed by clerks; 302 pigeons left Paris, 57 returned; the Prussians flew falcons to intercept; the dogs flown out by balloon were never seen again — the pigeons proved reliable. Fresh angle: THE NEWS FLEW WHEN THE WIRES WERE CUT — the besieged city's mail was a bird; the whole newspaper rode one pigeon. (Sources: smithsonianmag.com; postalmuseum.si.edu — primary object record; artsandculture.google.com Postal Museum.)
5. **The interceptor → Gustav.** Gustav carried the first news of D-Day back across the Channel; he had flown Resistance messages out of occupied Belgium; the Germans used marksmen and trained hawks against the pigeons; NPS members supplied 200,000+ young pigeons. Fresh angle: THE HAWKS WERE THE CENSORS — the enemy's countermeasure was a bird; the sky had two couriers, one delivering, one intercepting. (Source: theddaystory.com.)

### CHAIN BM (seed: #204 O-118 "The Detected Lock" — the key held at the lock, the door never opening; "Detected."; shipped 2026-10-19 ~20:45 EDT — this run takes the OTHER rung of the lock: the lock that refuses, not the key that fits)
1. **The lock → the Bramah challenge lock.** Joseph Bramah, patent 1784; the Bramah Locks company at 124 Piccadilly; the challenge lock displayed in the shop window from 1790 on a board: "The artist who can make an instrument that will pick or open this lock shall receive 200 guineas the moment it is produced." Fresh angle: THE WINDOW IS THE TAUNT — the shop window as an advertisement of unpickability; the challenge hung in public for sixty years. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bramah_lock; lindahall.org.)
2. **The challenge → Hobbs at the Great Exhibition.** Alfred Charles Hobbs, 38, American, representing Day & Newell at the Crystal Palace; 51 hours over 16 days in 1851; the dispute over the sign's wording ("the sign had been hanging in public for roughly sixty years and was a little late to start adding conditions"); three arbitrators (Rennie, Cowper, Black); the 200 guineas ≈ £26,000 today; Bramah's reply: the lock was forty years old, iron not steel sliders. Fresh angle: THE FINE PRINT FELL — the challenge's own wording was the lock Hobbs picked first; sixty years of public hanging was the argument. (Sources: commonplacefacts.com; daniellucian.com; thingshavehistory.com.)
3. **The picked lock → the Chubb Detector.** The same morning, 22 July 1851: Hobbs picked the Chubb Detector vault door in exactly 25 minutes, then locked it again and picked it a second time in 7 minutes. Fresh angle: THE SECOND PICKING — the repeat is the verdict; he picked it twice to prove the first wasn't luck. (Source: thingshavehistory.com.)
4. **The trade → the pitch.** Hobbs came to London to SELL American locks — which meant demonstrating the British competition was worth replacing; the break-in was the sales demonstration. Fresh angle: THE PICK IS THE PITCH — the defeat was the advertisement. (Sources: thingshavehistory.com; daniellucian.com.)

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (03:00 EDT) — HOP CHAINS

### Chain BN — "the circulating tube" (from #206 L-53 "The Cash Ball")
1. #206's brass ball rolling along the trough → the Lamson cash railway: Victorian department stores shot small wooden and brass balls along overhead wires carrying change and the sales receipt (Lamson, 1870s); the wire was the cashier's desk stretched across the shop. Landing: "The Wire."
2. The cash ball on the wire → the pneumatic canister: the same shops later fired brass capsules through tubes under the counter; the bank drive-through still does it. The capsule is the signature in transit. Landing: "The Circulating Canister."
3. The shop tube → the Paris pneumatic post (1866–1984): telegrams and express letters shot across the whole city at up to 60 km/h through a dedicated tube network; the 22:00 last collection was the city's second evening post. Landing: LORE — THE CITY HAD A SECOND POST.
4. Paris → the Chicago mail tube (1897–1917): 60 miles of steel tube under Chicago linking 23 post offices; canisters ran at 25–30 mph; the motor truck killed it. The carrier never walked. Landing: LORE — THE TUBES NEVER WALKED.
5. The tube → the unsigned delivery (plot): A DELIVERY THAT MUST BE SIGNED FOR — the canister arrives at the exchanger's manifold; the signature card was never filed; the exchanger sends it back; the canister circulates. The circulation is the verdict.
6. The circulation → THE CIRCUIT motif (candidate): in this world messages circulate until filed; arrival is a rumor.

### Chain BO — "the undeliverable" (from #208 A-61 "The Borrowed Memory")
1. #208's transfer slip / forwarding address → the newspaper morgue: clipping libraries filed in envelopes by subject; the NYT morgue holds ~6 million photographs; "the memory left the building." Landing: LORE — THE MORGUE IS THE MEMORY.
2. The morgue's envelopes → the Dead Letter Office (the US Mail Recovery Center): undeliverable mail is opened by statute, read, resealed or auctioned; the office dates to 1775/1794. Landing: LORE — THE UNDELIVERABLE IS READ; "The Opened Letter."
3. The opened letter → the returned letter: returned to sender; the sender is gone too; by rule the letter becomes the property of the office. Landing: LORE — THE LETTER OUTLIVES THE ADDRESS; "The Returned."
4. The property rule → A LOST-AND-FOUND CLAIM (plot-shaped draft): want = claim the letter; obstacle = the claim form needs the sender's address; turn = the letter is already filed under the office's own name. REROUTED before banking — #202 PA-16 "The Lost Property Office" shipped 2026-10-19; research kept as lore only (self-cleaning).
5. The claim → THE DEAD-LETTER CLERK (background figure — NEW): job = the undeliverable; motive = every letter must end somewhere.

### Chain BP — "the sealed garden" (from B-1280 "The Greenhouse Vent")
1. B-1280's fogged glass and vent-crank → the Wardian case: Nathaniel Bagshaw Ward, 1829 — a fern grew in a sealed bottle on his windowsill; plants began crossing oceans in sealed glass cases. Landing: LORE — THE SEALED GARDEN.
2. The case → the tea trade: Wardian cases carried live tea plants to Assam; the sealed case made an industry possible. The glass is the passport. Landing: LORE — THE CASE IS THE PASSPORT.
3. The sealed case → "The Sealed Case" (LABS): the case at 0.5s; sealed at 4s; condensation inside at 9.5s — the breathing glass is the verdict. Line: "It crossed the ocean."
4. The conservatory → THE CONSERVATORY KEEPER (background figure — NEW): job = the sealed cases; motive = the glass is the passport.

- **THE TUBES NEVER WALKED.** The carrier never walked — the canister ran the route. The motor truck killed the tubes, not the telegram. (Chain BN.)
- **THE CASH RAILWAY.** Lamson, 1870s: brass and wooden balls on overhead wires carrying change and receipts across the shop; the wire was the cashier's desk stretched across the room. (Chain BN.)
- **THE CIRCUIT IS THE ROUTE.** In this world messages circulate until filed; arrival is a rumor; the manifold is the map. (Chain BN — motif-candidate statement.)
- **THE UNDELIVERABLE IS READ.** The Dead Letter Office, 1775/1794: undeliverable mail is opened by statute, read, resealed or auctioned. (Chain BO.)
- **THE LETTER OUTLIVES THE ADDRESS.** Returned to sender; the sender gone too; by rule the letter becomes the property of the office. (Chain BO.)
- **THE MORGUE IS THE MEMORY.** The newspaper clipping morgue — envelopes by subject, 6 million photographs; the memory left the building. (Chain BO.)
- **THE SEALED GARDEN.** Nathaniel Bagshaw Ward, 1829: a fern grew in a sealed bottle; plants crossed oceans in sealed glass. (Chain BP.)
- **THE CASE IS THE PASSPORT.** The Wardian case carried live tea plants to Assam; the sealed case made an industry. The glass is the passport. (Chain BP.)
- Background figures banked: THE EXCHANGER (job = the tube board; motive = the manifold is the map) · THE DEAD-LETTER CLERK (job = the undeliverable; motive = every letter must end somewhere) · THE CONSERVATORY KEEPER (job = the sealed cases; motive = the glass is the passport).

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (04:00 EDT) — HOP CHAINS

Seeds: #203 L-52 "The Claim Check" (shipped 2026-10-19 ~02:45 EDT — the torn ticket, halves matched, "the matched halves are the verdict"); B-1273 "The Dumbwaiter Tray" (shipped 2026-10-19 — the tray); B-1269 "The Glued Hinge" (shipped 2026-10-19 — the hinge).

### CHAIN BQ (seed: #203 L-52 "The Claim Check" — this run takes the PAPER rung: the ticket as a legal instrument, not the tear)
1. **#203's matched halves → the pawn ticket's two copies.** The North Carolina pawnbroker statute: the pledgor signs the ticket and receives an exact copy; the broker keeps the record for three years; "any person presenting a pawn ticket to a pawnbroker is presumed to be entitled to redeem the pledged goods." Fresh angle: THE TICKET IS THE DEED — the holder IS the owner by statute; the paper outranks the person. (Sources: NC Gen. Stat. §66-391; VT Stat. tit. 9 §3866.)
2. **The bearer rule → the lost ticket.** Vermont: lose the ticket, describe the article, examine the pawnbroker's books, and the broker "shall issue a second or stop ticket for the same" — the STOP ticket stops the original. Fresh angle: THE STOP IS A DOCUMENT — paperwork that cancels paperwork; the replacement outranks the original it replaces. Landing: [READY] "The Second Ticket."
3. **The torn ticket → the engineered tear.** Henry Archer's 1847 perforating machine; the Post Office bought it; perforated stamps from 1854. Fresh angle: THE TEAR IS DESIGNED — #203's tear was a match; Archer's tear is a manufacture. Landing: [READY] "The Perforation." (Source: the standard Archer/perforation history.)
4. **The perforation → the stamp's gum.** (Unbanked landing — future run fodder: the licked gum, the self-adhesive 1974 stamp, the stamp that sticks without ceremony.)

### CHAIN BR (seed: B-1273 "The Dumbwaiter Tray" — this run takes the DOOR rung: the tray's own family is banked ("The Silent Servant," "The Wine Lift," "The Revolving Shelf"), so this chain walks past the tray to the revolving door)
1. **B-1273's serving door → Van Kannel's commercialized door.** US patent 387,571, 7 Aug 1888, "Storm-Door Structure" — three radiating wings, "perfectly noiseless," excludes wind/snow/rain/dust AND "the noises of the street"; the original slogan was "always closed." STAGING NOTE: B-250 "Always Closed" (shipped 2026-10-11) already staged this — this chain riffs it as lineage, never as a new item. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolving_door; automaticaccess.co.uk.)
2. **The commercialized door → the uncommercialized rival.** H. Bockhacker of Berlin, German patent DE18349, 22 Dec 1881, "Tür ohne Luftzug" ("door without draft of air") — seven years before Van Kannel, and it never went into production. Fresh angle: THE DOOR THAT STAYED PAPER — the patent is the whole career. Landing: "The Unbuilt Door." (Sources: Wikipedia revolving-door history; automaticaccess.co.uk.)
3. **"Without draft of air" → the draft as the enemy.** Van Kannel's pamphlet promised to keep out "noxious effluvia" and "baleful miasmas." Fresh angle: THE SEALED ROOM — the draft is the subject, the door is the instrument; the test is whether the air moves. Landing: [READY] "The Draftless Door."

### CHAIN BS (seed: B-1269 "The Glued Hinge" — this run takes the JOINT rung: the glue already forgave in [READY] "The Reversible Glue" — this chain asks what the hardware forgives)
1. **B-1269's glued hinge → the loose-pin hinge.** The center pin taps out upward and the door lifts away — the joint is temporary BY DESIGN. Fresh angle: THE FORGIVING JOINT — "The Reversible Glue" was the forgiving bond; the loose-pin hinge is the forgiving hardware. Landing: [READY] "The Lifted Door." (Sources: hardwarebox.zendesk.com hinge types; first-law-comic.com.)
2. **The pin → the lettered hardware.** Butterfly hinges: leaves shaped like butterfly wings, surface-mounted, decorative; the trade names hinges by their shape (H, HL, T, butterfly). Fresh angle: THE HARDWARE IS LETTERED — door furniture carries an alphabet; the network's TEXT discipline could letter a hinge. Landing: "The Butterfly." (Source: thespruceah.pages.dev hinge types.)
3. **The hinge that moves the door upward.** The rising butt hinge: the door rises as it opens (clears carpet) and gravity recloses it when let go. Fresh angle: THE DOOR THAT CLOSES ITSELF — the hardware has the last word. Landing: [READY] "The Rising Hinge." (Sources: josephgiles.com technical sheet; engineerfix.com.)

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (04:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE THUNDER SHEET.** Thunder = shaking a large sheet of thin iron (Britannica; Van Dyke Browne, *Secrets of Scene Painting and Stage Effects*, 1900). The storm is a held object — the weather hangs backstage. Landing: [READY] "The Thunder Sheet."
- **THE WIND DRUM.** Wind = a piece of silk draped over a drum of wooden slats with spaces between; the drum is cranked (props.eric-hart.com). Landing: "The Wind Drum."
- **THE RAIN BOX.** Rain = a long box of pebbles on a center pivot, tilted (the rain-stick principle); the thunder run = cannonballs rolled in a trough above the audience. (Unbanked landings — future run fodder: the tilted weather; the rolling thunder.)
- **THE CRASH BOX.** A sealed box filled with glass and pennies for crash sounds. The penny returns — ARC to the Penny Ledger. (Unbanked landing — future run fodder: the penny that breaks.)
- **THE ORDERED WEATHER.** Circa 1930, Cleon Throckmorton Inc. advertised build-to-order "thunder and wind apparatus" — "every theatre should have its thunder and wind apparatus" (a thunder sheet ~$7, a 14" drum wind machine ~$15, when tickets ran $0.25–$1). The weather was catalogue furniture. Lore ruling: THE WEATHER WAS ORDERED. (Source: tsdca.org/history.)
- **THE COUGH DROP.** The announcer's cough button — the mic mute held while the human coughs; "a problem as old as radio" (bgs.cc Guest Gizmo; impact.hypable.com). The unheard is a profession; the forgotten mute is the gaffe. Landing: [READY] "The Cough Drop."

Fresh angle: THE SEALED WEATHER — the case waters itself. Landing: [READY] "The Wardian Case." (Sources: nzgeo.com; environmentandsociety.org.)

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (05:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE SIGN-OFF.** US: the legal minimum is the call sign + city of license; the custom added the anthem, then the test pattern with the 1,000 Hz tone, then static/snow. BBC: continuity announcement, clock, anthem (BBC One Wales added *Hen Wlad Fy Nhadau* first); Granada and Channel 4: announcement + clock + ident only; ARD started playing the anthem at closedown 23 May 1985. Fresh angle: the day ends in a fixed order — the ritual is the schedule. STAGING NOTE: staged as B-10 "Sign-Off," #90 PA-4 "The Sign-Off," [DRAFTED 2026-10-14] "The Sign-Off" (NETWORK), the "The Closedown" venture, and the live #459 "The Final Sign-Off" — riff as lineage, never as a new item. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sign-off; dejavu.org.)
- **THE PIPS.** 1924: Astronomer Royal Sir Frank Watson Dyson + BBC director John Reith commissioned it; 18-year-old engineer Harry Lampen Edwards built it with Marconi/Siemens. Six 1 kHz pips at one-second intervals — the first five 0.1s, the last 0.5s, the hour at the START of the last pip. Before 1972 all six were equal length and nobody could tell which was final; the last was lengthened so the hour can always be found. A leap second adds a seventh pip. Fresh angle: the hour is lengthened so it can be found. STAGING NOTE: staged as B-573 "The Sixth Pip," #94 N-54 "The Six Pips," B-333/#58 N-43 "The Seventh Pip" — riff as lineage. (Unbanked landing — future run fodder: the 1972 lengthening — the confusion → the fix.) (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Time_Signal; stackscale.com; europastar.com.)
- **THE THOUSAND HERTZ.** The sign-off's 1,000 Hz test tone with the pattern — audible proof the transmitter was alive. Fresh angle: the tone alone, no card. Landing: "The Thousand Hertz." (Source: the sign-off sequence.)
- **THE TIME BALL'S HEIR.** The pips replaced the railway-telegraph time system, which replaced the mechanical time balls (Portsmouth 1829, Greenwich 1833) that set ships' chronometers. Fresh angle: the instrument changes; the announcement doesn't. STAGING NOTE: the ball itself staged as B-226 "The Time Ball" — riff as lineage. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Time_Signal.)

### CHAIN BW (seed: B-1277 "The Returned Record" — this run takes the RETURN rung: the thing that went out and came back)
1. **B-1277's return → the Dead Letter Office.** Opened 1825; by 1893 over 20,000 items a day; in the 1860s women clerks outnumbered men 38 to 7 — "skilled dead letter detectives"; only DLO clerks had permission to open mail, and only to read the bare minimum; money found was turned over to the Treasury; unclaimed items were sorted, catalogued, held, then auctioned; the DLO Museum closed 1911, contents to the Smithsonian; renamed the Mail Recovery Center 1994 (Atlanta). Fresh angle: THE OPENED MAIL — the opening is a privilege, not a right. Landing retired pre-bank: "The Dead Letter" SHIPPED as #96 O-41 (2026-10-13) — lineage flagged, never re-banked. (Sources: postalmuseum.si.edu; smithsonianmag.com; atlasobscura.com.)

4. **The paddle → the return stamp.** The official mark of the failed delivery — and the DLO's own 1877 "Post Obitum" official seal, ordered for letters damaged in transit ("post obitum" = after death); 50,000 seals ordered for the ~1M letters passing through the DLO in 1877. ### CHAIN BX (seed: B-1103 "The Grate Lift" — this run takes the UNDERSTREET rung: the street has a below, and the below carries)
1. **B-1103's grate → the sewers → the Paris pneu.** The pneumatic post ran its tubes through the Paris sewers, 1866–1984; 427 km and 130 offices at the 1934 peak; 30 million messages in 1945; the "petit bleu" form — a fixed-cost message, officially a telegram, couriered the last leg from the nearest office; Debussy's 1911 pneu: "Yes my dear friend……. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_pneumatic_post; myfrenchlife.org; parisupdate.com.)

3. **The tube → the telegram.** Pneu messages were officially telegrams; per-word charging; the 1928 "HOW TO WRITE TELEGRAMS PROPERLY" booklet: "the celebrated word 'stop,' which is known the world over as the official telegraphic or cable word for 'period'"; the National Archives: each punctuation character cost the same as an entire word. Western Union ended paper telegrams 27 Jan 2006; India's state service ran to 2013. Fresh angle: THE PAID PERIOD — the sentence had a price. Landing: "The Stop" (banked below). (Sources: nationalarchives.gov.uk; poynter.org.)

6. **The tube → the courier.** The capsule arrived at the nearest office; a courier took it to the door — the tube ends, the legs begin. Fresh angle: THE LAST COURIER. ## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (06:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE GHOST LIGHT.** The bare bulb left on the empty stage: the gas-valve theory (a flame left burning overnight relieved pressure in the lines — Philadelphia 1816 to the Savoy's electric 1881, hundreds of theatre fires between); the thief who broke his leg in a dark theatre and sued ("Equity light"); the superstition — the light lets the resident ghosts perform at night so they don't curse the show; the pandemic resurgence — the Arden Theatre's ghost light turned on after a 13 March 2020 performance of A Streetcar Named Desire and never turned off. Fresh angle: THE UNEXTINGUISHED — the house is never dark. STAGING NOTE: staged as B-84 "The Ghost Light" (2026-10-11, "The theater is asleep. The light is awake.") and re-landed 2026-10-17 05:15 as "The Relieved Pressure" (the gas-valve root) — riff as lineage, never as a new item. (Sources: history.co.uk; carolineportante.substack.com; saltpillar.org.au.)
- **THE CLAQUE.** Nero's 5,000 soldiers chanting his encomium (the Angustals); 16th-c. poet Jean Daurat buying tickets for promised applause; 1820 — Sauton's Paris office systematizes it ("Assurance des Succés Dramatiques"); by 1830 an institution. The cast: the CHEF DE CLAQUE (judged where efforts were needed, signaled with a cough, a hand, a program); COMMISSAIRES (learned the piece by heart, pointed out the good bits between acts); RIEURS (laughed loudly at the jokes); PLEUREURS/PLEUREUSES (feigned tears into handkerchiefs — sometimes armed with tear-compelling lotions); CHATOUILLEURS (ticklers — bonbons, theatre bills, spicy stories, kept the room in good humor); BISSEURS (stood and cried "Bis! Bis!"); SIFFLEURS (hired booers — extortion: pay or be booed). The wage: 3–5 francs an evening for an ordinary claqueur, 15–20 for the head — a skilled worker's full day wage for applauding. Wagner withdrew Tannhäuser after the Jockey Club's claque derisively interrupted it. Fresh angle: THE PRICED APPLAUSE — applause is a job with a hierarchy, a wage, and rehearsals. STAGING NOTE: banked [DRAFTED 2026-10-20 04:15 EDT] "The Claque" (SATIRE, THE STALLS) — still live; riff as lineage, never as a new item. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claque; vocal.media; h2g2.com.)
- **PAPERING THE HOUSE.** Vaudeville lingo: complimentary tickets ("paper") given out to fill the house — often on opening night when critics attended — "to give the impression that the show was drawing large crowds" and keep the audience from "sitting on their hands"; the modern seat-filler industry is the same trade. Fresh angle: THE PAPER CROWD — the full house on paper. Landing: [READY] "The Papered House" (banked below). (Sources: marinaendicott.com; play-by-play.com; ballycast.com.)
- **THE CALLS.** The DSM's pre-show calls over front- and rear-of-house: the HALF (35 min before curtain UK, 30 min Broadway — "Ladies and Gentlemen of the [show] company this is your half hour call"); the QUARTER (20 min); the FIVE (10 min); BEGINNERS (5 min — "Beginners to the stage please"); front-of-house bar bells at 3, 2, 1 minutes; the GODSPELL half-hour ("Brethren, it's half hour to curtain and peace be with you"). Fresh angle: THE COUNTED CALLS — the show starts before it starts. STAGING NOTE: banked [DRAFTED 2026-10-17 07:15 EDT] "The Half Hour" (NETWORK bumper, THE CORRIDOR, the PA call) — still live; riff as lineage, never as a new item. (Sources: theatrecrafts.com; aact.org.)

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (07:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain A1 — the borrowed slip (start: #208 A-61 "The Borrowed Memory", shipped 2026-10-19: one drawer opened, one transfer slip, "It remembers elsewhere.")
1. **#208's transfer slip ("It remembers elsewhere") → the borrowed address.** A slip carries a new address — the thing is borrowed, the address is the thing that travels. Fresh angle: borrow the borrower, not the book — what if the lendable unit is a person?
2. **The person as the lendable unit → the Human Library.** Copenhagen, 2000: Ronni Abergel's Human Library launched at the Roskilde Festival as *Stop Volden* — instead of borrowing books, you borrow a person for 30 minutes and ask anything; titles are lived experiences ("Refugee," "Muslim Woman"). Now in 80+ countries. The only rule: listen with respect. Fresh angle: the due date is the whole premise — the conversation must end on time, every time. A borrowed person is a transfer slip with a return policy.
3. **Borrowed people → borrowed tools.** Berkeley, California, 1979: the Tool Lending Library opened with 500 tools in a portable trailer, $30,000 of federal CDBG money — one of the first tool libraries in the U.S., free to residents since 1988. 3-day and 7-day loans; no gas-powered or powder-actuated tools. Fresh angle: the library's collection is a maintenance shed — the due date stamps a wrench. (Historians note Berkeley was second generation — Grosse Pointe, Michigan had a tool library earlier; the bank of ideas honors the footnotes.)
4. **Tool lending → the Library of Things.** The German "Libraries of Things" extend the loan catalog past tools: kitchen appliances, camping gear, musical instruments — anything owned that sits idle. Fresh angle: the due-date card is the network's universal meme syntax (TITLE / BORROWED BY / DUE) — the whole of the network's lending philosophy fits on one card.

### Chain A2 — the rolling ball (start: #206 L-53 "The Cash Ball", shipped 2026-10-19: the wooden ball travels the trough, "The money travels.")
1. **#206's rolling ball → the ball that is never held.** The cash ball rolls its track once and is done. The bagatelle tables of the French court (1777) turned rolling balls into a parlor game; the Americans flattened bagatelle into the "pin ball" table. Fresh angle: the ball is money in motion — the game is the same object, played.
2. **Pin tables → the first coin-op.** David Gottlieb's Baffle Ball (1931): 50,000+ units, a penny a play — cheap Depression entertainment, the table that proved a ball on a track could be an industry. Fresh angle: the penny returns — the Penny Ledger and the Baffle Ball are both penny economies; the network's money travels, then gets spent.
3. **The nudged table → the machine that judges you.** Harry Williams invented the tilt mechanism in 1932 (deployed on Advance, 1935) to punish players who lifted or shook the game — a hanging pendulum inside the cabinet that kills the game when disturbed. Fresh angle: the equipment watches the player BACK — the only network object that enforces conduct. The tilt is the corrections desk of the game hall. Sources: museumofplay.org (Williams collection), techgnosis.com.

### Chain A3 — the crossed valley (start: B-1262 "The Viaduct", shipped 2026-10-19: the walk mid-span, "The valley is crossed.")
1. **The crossed valley → the clothed bridge.** The covered bridge: a wooden truss given a ROOF — not to shelter the traveler but to protect the timber from weather. The bridge is dressed; the walker is not. Fresh angle: the crossing is clothed, the crosser is naked — the network's lodging gag inverted. A roofed walk is a 10s of moving weatherless.
2. **The roofed crossing → the unroofed one.** Charles Blondin, June 30, 1859: first tightrope crossing of Niagara Falls, 1,100 feet, 160 feet above the falls, 25,000 watching. Then he upped it — carried his manager Harry Colcord on his back across (Colcord weighed about as much as Blondin; told to "rest like a dead weight"), and strapped a 55-pound coal stove to his back to cook an omelet mid-wire, lowering it on a rope to the *Maid of the Mist* below. Fresh angle: breakfast served at height — the crossing as a kitchen. The Colonel's line writes itself; the stunt is a broadcast. Sources: blogs.slv.vic.gov.au, mentalfloss.com, jackkellyattalkingtoamerica.substack.com.

### Chain A4 — the scoop (start: B-1279 "The Granary Scoop", shipped 2026-10-20: the scoop, the pile, the level)
1. **B-1279's scoop → the machine that scoops.** Buffalo, 1842–43: hat-and-fur merchant Joseph Dart built the first steam-powered grain elevator (engineer Robert Dunbar; belt of buckets in a wooden "marine leg" lowered into the ship's hold — it scooped like a trunk, 7x faster than men's backs). The schooner *Philadelphia*'s wheat came up in hours. Fresh angle: "Irish backs are the cheapest elevators ever built" — the skeptic's line is the network's line; the machine answered in hours. Sources: chriscarosa.com, criticalskillsblog.com.
2. **The elevator → the receipt.** Once grain goes into bins in bulk, no farmer gets his own grain back — the warehouse receipt trades while the grain sits still. The Chicago Board of Trade (1848) standardized grades (1856) and To-Arrive contracts (1851): the paper becomes fungible while the ton is just the ton. Fresh angle: the receipt IS the grain — the document is the product. This is the network's "this is the paperwork" at industrial scale; the ton never moves, the paper flies.

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (07:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

- **The counted beat is a free metronome.** When the take counts — twelve loaves, three piles, one stamp — the audience counts along whether they want to or not. The verdict inherits the count's tension: the thirteenth item, the last pile, the final thump. Production note: stage any divisible action (laying, stacking, counting, dipping) as an audible/visible count; the audience does the pacing work for free. Never narrate a count the frame already performs.
- **The one-breath line.** A deadpan line is at most ~7 words — "The money travels," "It flies," "The shelf remembers." If you can't say it in one breath, it's a speech, not a line. Production note: cut every drafted line to one breath before firing; the generator compresses two clauses into two mouth-openings, which breaks the one-utterance grammar (B-892 class).

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (08:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain C1 — the carried plans (seed: #210 S-43 "The Mile-Wide Lobby", shipped 2026-10-20 ~20:45 EDT: UNC crosses the empty lobby carrying the plans, NO-LINE; lore THE MILE-WIDE LOBBY — the crossing was the pitch, the order was the reward)
1. **#210's crossing → the pitch.** The order was the reward; the pitch is a walk. Fresh angle: THE CARRIED PLANS — the pitch happens in motion; the plans are carried, not presented.
2. **The pitch → the anteroom.** The lobby as the waiting place: the room before the room where you wait to be heard. Fresh angle: THE WAIT IS THE WORK (premise-2-adjacent: "a hallway is a room that forgot what it was for" — the anteroom is a room that remembers: it is for waiting).
3. **The anteroom → the uncalled.** Shipped S-11 "The Waiting Room" (#13, 2026-09-29) staged the game-show waiting room; banked B-990 "The Taken Number" staged the ticket. This run takes the OTHER rung: the anteroom of power, where the called name never comes. Fresh angle: THE UNCALLED — the name never called, not the number never drawn.
4. Landing: "The Lobbyist" + "The Uncalled" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on #210.)

### Chain C2 — the measured dish (seed: #209 L-54 "The Measured Dish", shipped 2026-10-20 ~20:45 EDT: hands-only; the dish measured at 2s, fitted into its wire compartment)
1. **#209's measure → the enforced standard.** Edward I, 1300: the statute — "no manner of vessel of silver depart out of the hands of the workers, until... it be marked with the leopard's head"; the Guardians of the craft went shop to shop assaying work (thegoldsmiths.co.uk). Fresh angle: THE MARK — the measure is enforced by a walk; the standard travels to the shop.
2. **The mark → the date letter.** 1478: the date letter introduced, changed every year, identifying the Touch Warden responsible for the assay (assayofficelondon.co.uk). Fresh angle: THE DATED MARK — the year is punched into the metal; the mark names its own inspector.
3. **The warden → the hall.** Goldsmiths' Hall, London: the mark struck in the hall is the "hallmark" — the building names the verb (plheineman.net). Fresh angle: THE HALL'S NAME — the room is the guarantee; the noun is the building.
4. **The hall → the leopard's head.** The crowned leopard (1478–1822), the uncrowned head since 1822 (sarasotaantiquebuyers.com). Fresh angle: THE CROWNED LEOPARD — the crown came and went; the head stayed.
5. Landings: "The Date Letter" + "The Leopard's Head" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on #209.)

### Chain C3 — the copper (seed: B-1285 "The Copper", shipped 2026-10-20 ~07:30 EDT: the copper vessel, "Held till morning.")
1. **B-1285's copper → the penny.** The penny is copper; bank line 103 mined the final strike (U.S. Mint's last circulating penny, 12 Nov 2025). This run takes the OTHER copper rung: the penny POST.
2. **The penny post.** Rowland Hill's 1837 pamphlet; the Uniform Fourpenny Post 5 Dec 1839 (lasted 36 days); the Uniform Penny Post 10 Jan 1840 — 1d prepaid, 2d if collected from the recipient; the Penny Black 6 May 1840 — the world's first adhesive stamp (Perkins, Bacon & Petch; Victoria's head from Wyon's medal); mail volume doubled 82M→169M pieces in a year (wikipedia; mysticstamp.com). Fresh angle: THE PREPAID — the letter pays for itself before it travels; the sender pays, the knock stops asking for money.
3. **The prepaid → the ended wait.** Before the reform, the postman waited at each door to collect payment — "time was wasted when the postman waited at each house" (wikipedia). Fresh angle: THE WAIT ENDED — the doorstep transaction died; the reform killed the knock's question.
4. **The post → the time-bill.** The mail coach ran to a time-bill — the timetable before timetables; the guard's horn kept the hours. Fresh angle: THE TIME-BILL — the road kept the hours before the railway did.
5. Landing: "The Prepaid" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on B-1285. Lineage vs 06:00 run's "The Pneu"/"The Stop" — the STAMP vs the TUBE/the PERIOD — flagged.)

### Chain C4 — the smokehouse door (seed: B-1284 "The Smokehouse Door", shipped 2026-10-20: 0 prior chains)
1. **B-1284's smokehouse → the slow fire.** Smoking as craft: the flavor takes hours; the door stays shut. Fresh angle: THE SLOW FIRE — the work is the waiting; the door is the instrument.
2. **The smoke → the signal fire.** Smoke as communication: the beacon. 1588: the Armada sighted off the Lizard 19 July; Plymouth→London by a chain of fires, news as far north as York within 12 hours; each beacon constantly attended, watch kept on all neighboring sites; no means to cancel a false alarm — one anxious watcher could set the whole county in an uproar for days (pharology.eu; wilcuma.org.uk). Fresh angle: THE CHAIN — the news travels at the speed of lighting; the alarm cannot be un-rung.
3. **The beacon → the kept light.** The attended fire becomes the kept light. Fresh angle: THE KEPT LIGHT — the watch never ends, it just gets a roof.
4. **The light → the dues.** Trinity House: first light at Lowestoft 1609, paid by a levy on vessels; the 1615 Dungeness patent empowered a penny-per-ton toll; 1836 compulsory purchase of all private lights (nationalarchives.gov.uk; trinityhouse.co.uk). Fresh angle: THE DUES — the light is a toll; the warning has a price.
5. Landing: "The Beacon Chain" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on B-1284.)

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (09:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain D1 — the neck (seed: #211 O-146 "The Last Sheaf", shipped 2026-10-20: UNC as THE REAPER cuts the last standing patch at 6s, lifts the sheaf at 9.5s; lore THE LAST SHEAF — the 'mell'/'neck')
1. **#211's sheaf → the neck.** Cornwall/Devon: the last sheaf cut is "the neck," cried three times — "I hav'et! I hav'et! I hav'et!" / "What hav'ee? What hav'ee? What hav'ee?" / "A neck! A neck! A neck!" — then "we yen!" (we have ended). (museumofcornishlife.co.uk; globalgreyebooks.com/Courtney.) Fresh angle: THE CRIED NECK — the end of harvest is announced, not observed; the call is the finish.
2. **The neck → the runner.** The neck's bearer runs for the farmhouse; the dairymaid waits at the door with a pail of water — seen, he is soused; unseen, he may kiss her. (Courtney.) Fresh angle: THE RUN — the end of harvest is a race; the prize is dryness.
3. **The run → the hung year.** The neck made into a miniature sheaf, decorated with ribbons and flowers, hung on a kitchen beam until the next harvest — then taken back to the field so the spirit of the corn returns in spring. (Courtney; museumofcornishlife.co.uk.) Fresh angle: THE RETURN — the spirit is lent for the winter; the loan has a due date in spring.
4. **The hung → the revived.** Crying the Neck died out and was deliberately revived in 1928 in St Ives by the Old Cornwall Society — the custom is itself a re-staging. (uncommonology.co.uk.) Fresh angle: THE REVIVED — the ceremony is performed because it was remembered, not because it survived.
5. Landings: "The Neck Runner" + "The Hung Year" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on #211; lineage vs shipped #211 — the RUN/the HANG vs the CUT — flagged.)

### Chain D2 — the machine (seed: #212 L-75 "The Winnowing", shipped 2026-10-20: the toss at 4s, the fan at 6s, the wheat settled at 9.5s; lore THE WINNOWING — the fan; the wind is the sieve)
1. **#212's toss → the beat before.** Before the toss comes the flail — stalks beaten on the threshing floor (The Farmers' Museum, Brooks Barn); or oxen trampling; or Washington's two-story threshing barn with horses on a turnstile. This run takes the MACHINE rung: the cradle-fan rung and the gentle-wind rung are owned by the 2026-10-19 20:15 run ([READY] "The Cradle", [DRAFTED] "The Gentle Wind") — lineage flagged.
2. **The machine → the fanning mill.** Late 1700s–early 1800s: the cabinet — sieves in a wooden box, paddle-wheel fan, gravity hopper; two people — one to fill the hopper and turn the crank, one to bag the grain. (worldclassantiques.com.) Fresh angle: THE TWO JOBS — the machine is incomplete without the pair; the jobs are the mechanism.
3. Landing: "The Fanning Mill" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on #212.)

### Chain D3 — the sorted (seed: #213 L-76 "The Sifters", shipped 2026-10-20: the pour at 4s, the picking at 6s, clean coal at 9.5s; lore THE BREAKER BOYS — Hine's Pittston photograph)
1. **#213's picking → the breaker.** Coal hoisted to the breaker, sorted and crushed into seven salable sizes — from "lump" and "egg" to "rice" and "barley"; the smaller sizes mostly for home heating. (hmdb.org.) Fresh angle: THE NAMED SIZES — the sizes have kitchen names; the sort is a menu.
2. **The sizes → the dyed.** Huber Breaker, Ashley PA: the company dyed its coal blue and sold it as "Blue Coal." (abandonedspaces.com.) Fresh angle: THE DYED PRODUCT — the brand is painted on the coal itself.
3. **The product → the wage.** Coal scrip: the substitute tender, good only at the company store; the booklet the owner must crack open and sign, acknowledging receipt — Black Diamond Collieries, Coal Creek TN, 1920s. (americanhistory.si.edu.) Fresh angle: THE CRACKED BOOK — the wage is sealed; the signature opens it.
4. **The wage → the waste (carried as lore).** The culm pile: slate, rocks, impure coal dumped into towering hills that "quickly became defining elements of the landscape." (hmdb.org.) Fresh angle: THE REJECTED LANDSCAPE — the waste defines the place. (Carried as lore, not an item.)
5. Landings: "The Seven Sizes" + "The Blue Coal" + "The Cracked Book" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on #213; lineage vs shipped #213 — the SORTED vs the PICKED — flagged.)

### Chain D4 — the kept birds (seed: B-1286 "The Loft Door", shipped 2026-10-20: the dovecote door shut by 4s, the closed loft at 9.5s; lore THE CLOSED LOFT — the loft closes whether or not the birds are in)
1. **B-1286's loft → the right.** Droit de colombier: in much of France the dovecote was the seigneur's privilege; his pigeons fed at the peasants' expense; the complaint rolls demanded abolition; abolished 4 August 1789. (encyclopedia.thefreedictionary.com/Dovecote; chateaudecourtomer.com.) Fresh angle: THE PRIVILEGE — the sky is owned; the birds eat at someone else's expense.
2. **The right → the rent.** 1309: Ralph Lemprière built a dovecote without permission, was ordered by the Justices Itinerant to pull it down, and bought the right back for a rent of one pound of pepper per annum forever — a rent still paid. (westfrancia.com.) Fresh angle: THE PEPPER RENT — the right is rented in perpetuity, in spice.
3. **The rent → the closed season.** The dovecote windows shut during planting season to protect the fledgling crops — the loft closes on a calendar. (travelfeed.com.) Fresh angle: THE CLOSED SEASON — the closing has a date; extends THE CLOSED LOFT.
4. Landings: "The Pepper Rent" + "The Closed Season" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on B-1286; lineage vs shipped B-1286 — the SEASON vs the DOOR — flagged.)

4. **The overflow → the shelves.** NRM blog: Prytherch's 1898 Railway Magazine survey of the Great Eastern Railway lost property — one year: 3350 pairs of gloves, 2280 umbrellas, 1000 hats, 300 books — plus a china figure, a glazier's diamond, three revolvers; hats put on high shelves, books in tin boxes, coats wrapped in brown paper against moths, live animals rehoused with staff until claimed (blog.railwaymuseum.org.uk — primary: Railway Magazine vol.2, 1898). Fresh angle: THE SHELVES — the lost are filed by species; the moth gets its own wrapping.
5. **The shelves → the rehomed (rerouted).** The auction rung (Hansard 1951 — unclaimed "sold at public auction sales") is owned territory (shipped B-483 "The Unclaimed" + banked draft 2026-10-12) — this run takes the ANIMALS rung instead: live animals rehoused with staff. Fresh angle: THE REHOMED — the lost things that are alive get fostered; the staff keeps what nobody claims.
6. Landings: "The Left Luggage" + "The High Shelf" + "The Rehomed" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on B-1288; lineage vs shipped B-1288 — the CLAIM vs the TEAR — flagged; vs shipped B-483 "The Unclaimed" — the STATION vs the LOBBY DESK — flagged.)

### Chain E2 — the designed weakness (seed: B-1288 "The Torn Ticket", shipped 2026-10-20 — second rung of the same seed; arc extension per the BI precedent: the TEAR's engineering, not its keeping)
1. **B-1288's tear → the engineered tear.** Before perforation, stamps were separated with scissors, razors, or by folding to a crease; Henry Archer's 1847 "Archer Roulette" cut too well (damaged the tables); his 1848 perforation patent (no. 12,340, bought £4,000 June 1853) punched rows of round pins; gauge 16 parted too readily → gauge 14; first perforated Penny Red, January 1854 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postage_stamp_separation; Smithsonian postalmuseum.si.edu). Fresh angle: THE DESIGNED WEAKNESS — the tear is engineered; gauge 16 vs gauge 14 is a moral. (Rerouted at research time: banked [READY] "The Perforation" (Chain BQ) owns the perforation title; this run banks "The Dotted Line.")
2. **The weakness → the unremovable.** Joseph Sloper, London printer, 1858: the railway ticket date-stamping problem — endorsements that "could not be removed"; a machine punching figures and letters through the tickets, changeable with the date (philatelic bulletin 322/349). Fresh angle: THE UNREMOVABLE — the hole is the endorsement; the date is punched, not printed. (Carried as lore.)
3. **The punched → the fingerprint.** Smithsonian: the Bonney-Vehslage punch, Southern Railway's Murphy Branch 1920s, "L"-shaped hole — "Each conductor had his own punch, which made a specifically shaped hole. The hole shape differed from punch to punch"; Canadian railways ~7000 designs — "Each punch, like a human fingerprint, leaves a mark that has no duplicate"; shapes: a lady's head, a high button shoe, a top hat (americanhistory.si.edu; churcher.crcml.org — 1954 Ottawa Citizen). Fresh angle: THE SIGNATURE — the hole is the man; the retiring conductor may keep his punch for sentimental reasons (CPR granted it).
4. **The signature → the stub (rerouted).** "The Kept Stub" is owned territory (shipped B-809 2026-10-14 + Chain 1/Chain 2) — this run banks the FILING rung instead. Fresh angle: THE FILED — the stub is not kept, it is archived; the album is the stub's afterlife.
5. Landings: "The Dotted Line" + "The Punch" + "The Filed Stub" (banked below). (Lineage vs shipped B-1288 — the ENGINEERED tear vs the TORN ticket — flagged; vs banked [READY] "The Perforation" (Chain BQ) — the DOTTED LINE vs the STAMP — flagged; vs shipped B-809 "The Kept Stub" — the FILING vs the KEEPING — flagged.)

### Chain E3 — the pin (seed: B-1288 "The Torn Ticket", shipped 2026-10-20 — third rung of the same seed; the PIN that pinned the half, not the half)
1. **B-1288's red pin → the porch board.** Cliffe parish history: the church porch held markets and deed-signings; "the notice board found on the West wall which is still reserved for local parish and area councils" (cliffehistory.co.uk). Fresh angle: THE PORCH BOARD — the pin holds the parish; the porch is the lobby's ancestor.
2. **The board → the rules.** Fulking parish notice boards: anybody may post, "but your notice may get removed if it lacks a date or is larger than A4" (fulking.net). Fresh angle: THE A4 RULE — the board has laws; the date is the price of the pin.
3. **The rules → the expired.** Diocese of Norwich visitor guidance: "Check that your notice board isn't faded or showing out of date notices" (dioceseofnorwich.org). Fresh angle: THE EXPIRED — the board is a calendar nobody turns; the notice outlives its event. (Carried as lore.)
4. Landings: "The Red Pin" + "The Notice" (banked below). (Lineage vs shipped B-1288 — the PIN vs the HALF — flagged.)

### Chain E4 — plot research (real show/media history): THE DETECTOR VAN
The town the signal reaches. Post-war Britain: TV licence £2 from 1 June 1946 (GPO); the first detector van unveiled 1 February 1952 — Hillman Minx and Morris Oxford estates with large roof aerials; the 1970s TV ad: "Yes, there's a TV set on at number 5. It's in the front room and they're watching Columbo" (edinburghlive.co.uk); the Science Museum: detectors "could detect TVs from 100ft and successfully located 90% of TVs in the UK in 1953" — but "the BBC never said how these vans worked," most felt they were "more effective as a deterrent than devices for actual detection"; "more often the authorities would simply find out who owned a TV from TV salespeople" (collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk — primary collection). Fresh angles: THE NAMING — the van announces what the street already knows (10S-F280); THE SCARE — the technology was the threat, the threat was the technology. Production rule: never stage a real programme or brand — the FORM (a van that names the watchers) is the researched fact; the CONTENT is network-native. Landing: "The Detector Van" (banked below).

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (11:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain F1 — the posted letter (seed: B-1287 "The Letter Box", shipped 2026-10-20: the flap fallen at 6s, hands gone at 9.5s, NO-LINE, "after six it is tomorrow's mail"; the street pillar box)
1. **B-1287's fallen flap → the collection plate.** Every pillar box wears its emptying times on a plate; the plate is the box's clock — once the flap has fallen for the last collection, the letter stops being today's mail. Fresh angle: THE PLATE — the deadline is scenery; the take's time limit is printed on the object itself. (Royal Mail collection plates; the seeded take's own verdict.)
2. **The plate → the collector's keyring.** Trollope's 1852 Jersey trial (Vaudin & Son, cast iron, olive green; Guernsey 8 Feb 1853; Carlisle first mainland 1853; red only from 1874 — en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillar_box; information-britain.co.uk). Every box on the route needs the collector's key. Fresh angle: THE KEYRING — the route is a ring of keys; the man who holds them holds the town's departures. (Carried as lore.)
3. **The keyring → the bellman.** Before the box there was the Bellman — "a fellow in a uniform who rang a bell to attract attention and collected letters from the public" (idler.co.uk/article/pillars-of-the-community). Fresh angle: THE BELLMAN — the man was the box; the bell was the first broadcast instrument; canon riff: the Bellman's bell is the ancestor of the network's announcement instruments (the Corrections Desk's stamp, the announcer's pips). First inventoried background figure this run.
4. **The bellman → the unread.** Letters that cannot be delivered go to the returns room — the office that reads the unreadable, the last room of the postal world. Fresh angle: THE UNREAD — the letter's afterlife is a night shift (carried as lore; the sorting room is its staging cousin).
5. Landings: "The Last Collection" + "The Bellman" + "The Sorting Room" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on B-1287; lineage vs shipped B-1081 "The Letter Slot" — the pillar box on the street vs the front-door slot — flagged at the B-1287 row; this run extends that row's world, not its beat.)

### Chain F2 — the hooked speaker (seed: B-1289 "The Hooked Speaker", shipped 2026-10-20: the hooking at 4s, the screen dimmed at 9.5s, "The picture starts."; the drive-in lot at dusk)
1. **B-1289's hook → the 1941 hook.** Early drive-ins used speakers mounted by the screen — muddy sound, neighbor complaints. In 1941 RCA introduced the in-car speaker "that hooked over the rolled-down window and put sound control directly in the hands of each driver" — it "removed most of the restrictions on locations" (clickamericana.com). Fresh angle: THE HOOK — the hook made the format possible; the smallest object decides where the world can exist.
2. **The hook → the unhook.** At the end of the night the attendant reverses the show: every speaker back on its post. Fresh angle: THE UNHOOK — the show ends backwards; the unhook is the closing ceremony. (Carried as lore THE UNHOOK.)
3. **The unhook → the two dots.** The projection booth's changeover marks flash 8 seconds before the end of a reel; the projectionist changes reels without the audience ever knowing. Fresh angle: THE TWO DOTS — the warning is the cut; the booth is the room where the film stays whole. (→ "The Cue Dots"; the projection booth is a NEW setting this run.)
4. **The dots → the lot walk.** The attendant walks the empty lot after the last car; the lot is checked the way a room is checked. Fresh angle: THE LOT WALK — the emptiness is inspected (carried as lore).
5. Landings: "The Unhooked" + "The Cue Dots" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on B-1289; Hollingshead's Camden opening 6 June 1933 and "the whole family is welcome, regardless of how noisy the children are" (driveinlist.com; lilesnet.com) carried as background color, never staged.)

### Chain F3 — the released hawk (seed: B-1275 "The Sparrow Hawk", shipped 2026-10-20: the release at 6s, the perched bird at 9.5s, "Pest control."; the glasshouse)
1. **B-1275's hawk → the airfield falconer.** At Comox Valley Airport, a 17-year-old Harris's hawk named Tuari patrols the airfield; her presence creates a "landscape of fear" that moves gulls, geese and crows off the runways — the kill never has to happen (thecollectivemags.ca). ## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (11:00 EDT) — LORE RULINGS

- **LORE-F1 — THE PLATE.** The pillar box wears its clock on its face: the collection plate is the deadline, printed. A fallen flap is a legal fact — after the last collection the letter is tomorrow's mail, and no hand can argue with the plate.
- **LORE-F2 — THE KEYRING.** The collector's route is a ring of keys: every box on it opens to the same hand. The keyring is the town's departures, carried.
- **LORE-F3 — THE UNHOOK.** The show ends backwards: the last job of the night is the reverse of the first. The unhook is the closing ceremony of every format that hooks.
- **LORE-F4 — THE HOURLY PATROL.** The sky is checked by hand, every hour, sunrise to sunset, all year. The round is the job; the catch is never the point. (From Botting, CFB Trenton — canadianbirdstrike.ca.)
- **LORE-F5 — THE LEGAL ID.** Once an hour the station says its true name: the callsign and the town. The naming is the law, and the law is the ritual.
- **LORE-F6 — THE TONES.** The analog day ended as a number: a burst of touch tones killed the remote transmitters. The last sound of the broadcast day was a code, not a word. (shakerdesignproject.com.)

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (11:00 EDT) — 10-SECOND STUDY

The viewer reads the stakes as scenery — no exposition, no setup line. Production rule: if a take has a time limit, print it on something in the frame. ## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (12:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain G1 — the lit landing (seed: B-1293 "The Lit Landing", shipped 2026-10-20: the stairwell, "The landing is lit."; lore THE LIT LANDING)
1. **B-1293's lit landing → the unlit lamp.** 15 December 1900: the steamer Archtor notes the Flannan Isles light is NOT operational; the relief tender Hesperus cannot sail from Breasclete until the weather breaks — she reaches Eilean Mòr at noon on 26 December. Relief keeper Joseph Moore lands alone to find the gate and main door closed, the beds unmade, the clock stopped — and THE LAMPS CLEANED AND REFILLED, trimmed and ready (NRS archive: "the lamp was cleaned. The fountain full. Blinds on the windows etc." — the morning's work of the 15th, completed). The men vanished; the routine did not. Fresh angle: the lamp trimmed and ready is the network's own register — the premise maintained by nobody. The last scheduled act outlived the actors. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flannan_Isles_Lighthouse; nrscotland.gov.uk.)
2. **The maintained lamp → the stopped clock.** Moore found the clock unwound — the one routine that cannot run itself. Fresh angle: the clock is the only object in the tower that admits nobody is there. Everything else got trimmed; the clock stopped telling. The kept light vs the stopped clock = the maintained premise vs the admitted absence.
3. **The stopped clock → the relief.** The relief's whole job is continuity: Moore + three volunteer seamen stayed to ATTEND THE LIGHT; Captain Harvie's telegram to the Northern Lighthouse Board went out the same day. Fresh angle: the relief is a plot — a boat six days late arriving to an empty routine, and the first act is to light the lamp anyway. The relief keeper is the network's newest background figure: job = the lamp, motive = the boat is already leaving.
4. Landings: "The Relief" + "The Trimmed Lamp" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on B-1293; lineage vs lore THE LIT LANDING — the LAMP vs the STAIRWELL — flagged.)

### Chain G2 — the emptied pocket (seed: B-1294 "The Emptied Pocket", shipped 2026-10-20: the lobby, "Nothing left.", one coin in the open palm; motif THE EMPTY POCKET candidate first staging)
1. **B-1294's "Nothing left." → the green channel.** At every airport: GREEN = "NOTHING TO DECLARE" (a green octagon), RED = "GOODS TO DECLARE" (a red square) — the Philippines NAIA order states the markings verbatim. And the walk through the green channel IS the declaration: legally, the step through is the sentence "nothing to declare"; if false, the smuggling offence is complete (anantamias). Fresh angle: a whole corridor where your FEET make a legal declaration. "Nothing left." is the same sentence, said with a palm instead of a walk. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custom_duties; elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph.)
2. **The declared nothing → the checked nothing.** The green channel is NOT exempt from examination — officers select by risk assessment and redirect passengers to the red; each channel is a point of no return: once entered, no going back to baggage claim. Fresh angle: "nothing to declare" can still be searched. The emptied pocket's palm gets turned over. This is a plot: want = pass; obstacle = the glance; turn = the search that finds nothing. The nothing is the verdict, but the search is the show.
3. Landings: "The Green Door" + "The Octagon" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on B-1294; lineage vs shipped B-1294 — the DOOR vs the PALM — flagged.)

### Chain G3 — the tare (seed: #214 PA-79 "The Tare", shipped 2026-10-20: the weighbridge, "The sack doesn't count."; lore TARE AND TRETT)
1. **#214's tare → the burned standard.** 16 October 1834: the Houses of Parliament burned because the Exchequer's obsolete wooden TALLY STICKS — the accounting system's own ledger, notched sticks — were being burned carelessly in the furnaces under the House of Lords. In the same fire the 1760 Bird/Graham imperial standard yard was found in the ruins, unfit for use as a standard (Pop Sci Monthly). Fresh angle: the tally sticks are the Penny Ledger's ancestors — a stick that IS a ledger. The Exchequer burned its own paperwork and took the definition of the yard with it. (en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Popular_Science_Monthly_Volume_19.djvu/672; citizendailypost.com.)
2. **The unfit standard → the recast.** The 1838 Royal Commission (Airy) refused to restore the lost yard from the seconds-pendulum data (unreliable) and rebuilt from comparison scales — two by Shuckburgh, one by Kater, two Ordnance bars. The imperial prototype masses were likewise destroyed in 1834; a new platinum prototype was cast in 1844 (IOP). The standard yard in use since 1855 is a copy assembled from copies. Fresh angle: THE COPIES ARE THE ORIGINALS — every ruler since 1855 measures against a reconstruction. The network's own canon does this: every hand-lettered card measures against a previous one. (spark.iop.org.)
3. Landings: "The Burned Standard" + "The New Yard" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on #214; lineage vs shipped #214 — the STANDARD vs the SACK — flagged.)

### Chain G4 — plot research: the pips (seed: B-1292 "The Raised Blind", shipped 2026-10-20: the control room, "The board is up.", the blind raised to reveal the board; lore THE RAISED BOARD)
1. **B-1292's control room → the pips.** The Greenwich Time Signal: six 1 kHz tones — the first five 0.1s, the sixth 0.5s; the hour changes at the BEGINNING of the last pip. First transmitted 9:30pm, 5 February 1924, introduced by Astronomer Royal Sir Frank Dyson; the mechanism was built by 18-year-old Harry Lampen Edwards for Marconi/Siemens. Before 1972 all six pips were equal length and nobody could tell which was the hour — the last was LENGTHENED so the hour can always be found. Fresh angle: THE LENGTHENED HOUR — five warnings and one verdict; the hour arrives inside the sixth. The lengthening is the fix for a confusion nobody admitted for 48 years. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Time_Signal; stackscale.com; miketodd.net/other/gts.htm.)
2. **The pips → the time balls.** The broadcast pips replaced the railway-telegraph time coordination, which itself extended from the Portsmouth (1829) and Greenwich (1833) TIME BALLS — a ball dropped at 1pm so ships could set their chronometers. Fresh angle: time used to be a FALLING OBJECT — the pip's ancestor is a drop. (Lineage vs shipped B-226 "The Time Ball" — the DROP vs the PIP — hop lineage only, not staged.)
3. **The pips → the maker.** The 18-year-old built the mechanism every BBC hour still descends from. Fresh angle: the commission outlives the commissioner — Dyson's name is on the history, the boy's hands are on the machine.
4. Landings: "The Lengthened Pip" + "The Boy Engineer" (banked below). (Seed verified: 0 prior chains on B-1292; the heavily-mined "The Sixth Pip"/"The Seventh Pip" rung NOT re-staged — shipped B-573, #94 N-54, B-333/#58 N-43 — this run takes only the unbanked 1972-lengthening rung.)

## 2026-10-20 Q0 research run (12:00 EDT) — LORE RULINGS

- **LORE-G1 — THE TRIMMED LAMP.** The premise is maintained even when nobody is left to maintain it. The Flannan lamps were cleaned and refilled by men who were already gone; the lamp trimmed and ready outlived the keepers. The routine is the institution, not the men.
- **LORE-G2 — THE STOPPED CLOCK.** The clock is the only object in the tower that admits nobody is there. Everything else got trimmed; the clock stopped telling. In this world the kept light is the premise and the stopped clock is the truth.

- **LORE-G4 — THE COPIES ARE THE ORIGINAL.** The imperial standard yard found in the 1834 ruins was unfit for use; the Commission refused the pendulum and rebuilt from comparison scales. Every yard since 1855 is a reconstruction from copies. The standard is a decision, not a fact.
- **LORE-G5 — THE LENGTHENED HOUR.** Before 1972 all six pips were equal and nobody could tell which was the hour; the last was lengthened so the hour can always be found. In this world the verdict event runs longer than its brothers.
- **LORE-G6 — THE REFERENCE.** The chicken is a reference, not a prop. Day 47 names it in the ledger; no take ever shows it. The naming is the whole bit; the showing would break it.
